Feeding behavior and mechanics of sharks: past, present and future. P.J. Motta. Department of Biology,
Universny of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida, 33620 U.S.A.
Knowledge of the feeding behavior of sharks is based on a rich history of descriptive studies, and understanding of
the feeding mechanism is rooted in anatomy. These works posed as many questions as they answered. Questions
about the feeding mechanism and the function of jaw protrusion remain, the degree of stereotypy of prey capture
behavior, the role of jaw suspension in feeding, and how a relatively simple morphological system evolved to the
current diversity of feeding forms. Research is now addressing these questions.' Utilizing anatomical techniques,
computer imaging, electromyography and kinematic analysis, models of the feeding apparatus are being proposed.
Prey capture behavior appears not to be a modal action pattern, many sharks exhibiting variability and modulatory
abilities. Jaw suspension is not clearly related to feeding behavior as was once thought, and our work has revealed
evolutionary shifts that influenced the diversity of feeding forms. We are now posed with additional questions of the
evolution of suction feeding and the scaling of prey capture kinematics. The feeding behavior and mechanics of
elasmobranchs continue to be an exciting and relatively unexplored area that promises to further our understanding
of these apex predators and augment our knowledge of lower vertebrate feeding mechanisms.

Preference for static and dynamic criteria in Physalaemus pustulosua. J. Bosch and M.J. Ryan, Department of
Zoology, University of Texas at Austin. Austin, TX 78712 USA.
Anuran call properties were classified as static or dynamic based on vrlthin-male variablltiy during bouts of calling.
Females exert stabilizing or weakly directional selection on static propertties, and highly directional selection on
dynamic properties. Selection pressure was examined in two cal) characteristics; a static character (dominant
frequency of the whine), and one dynamic character (intervals between whines). Six phonotaxis experiments were
conducted with gravid females using synthetic calls. Stimuli presented for both characters are based on the mean
and standard deviation of those characters in the study population, to compare preferences between static and
dynamic characters. For each character, 3 distinct intervals of variation have been used (1SD, 2SD, and 3SD), that
which is translated in 3 different experiments: mean-1.5SD vs. mean-0.5SD, mean-1.5SD vs. mean+0.5S0 and
mean-1.5SD vs. mean+1.5SD. As expected, preference was strong in the dynamic character, increasing in
proportion to the increase in the interval between stimuli. Preference for the static character remained constant. The
degree of ‘motivation’ in the choice made by females was measured as the time taken to make the choice, the
number of speakers visited, and the number of females necessary to get 20 valid responses. For both characters an
increase in female 'motivation' was observed in proportion to the increase in the intenral of variation between stimuli.
Furthermore, all these measures of 'motivation' were greater in the dynamic character than the static character.

Acoustic competition In Physalaemus pustulosus, a differential response to calls of relative frequency.
Bosch and M.J. Ryan, Department of Zoology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712 USA.
The response of male Physalaemus pustulosus to conspecific whines of different frequencies was examined. In the
first block of playback experiments (fixed response), three types of synthetic stimuli (HFR, MFR, LFR) were used that
corresponded to calls of high frequency (mean+2 SD), mid-frequency (mean), and low frequency (mean-2 SD) for
the study population. In the second block of interactive playback experiments (relative response) whines of relative
frequency to that of the male subject were used: male frequency + 2 SD (HRR), male frequency (MRR), and male
frequency - 2 SD (LRR). In the fixed frequency experiments, no modification of male vocal response was observed.
However, in the relative frequency experiments, males responded with greater rates of whine production, and above
all, with more complex calls (adding secondary notes) to stimuli of similar or higher frequency than to stimuli of lower
frequency than their own. In other words, male vocal competition is greater only when competitors have similar or
relatively higher whine frequencies to their own, and does not increase when competitors have call frequencies
which are at the mean or higher for the population as a whole. Nevertheless, this differential response cannot be
explained only as an effect of competition between males of different sizes, given that the relationship between
frequency of the whine and male size is very weak.

Effects of changes in hydration and temperature on jumping ability in two species of Puerto Rican frogs. Y.
Sanchez. Department of Biology, University of Puerto Rico, San Juan, PR 00931-3360.
Variation in temperature and hydration may significantly affect the jumping performance of amphibians and therefore
their foraging efficiency, habitat selection, survivorship and fitness. We compared locomotor abilities of two
neotropical frogs Eleutherodactylus anb’llensis and E. cochranae. Jumping performance (maximum jumping
distance) was measured at three temperatures (20°C, 25°C and 30°C) and two hydration levels (100% and 75%). E.
antillensis showed a significant decrease in jumping ability under dehydration condition at 25°C and 30°C. However
at 20°C, there was no significant decrese in jumping ability for E. antillensis. E. cochranae showed no differences in
jumping ability. E. cochranae seems to have greater tolerance to changes in temperature and hydration.

thestimuius.

Radiotrackfng amphibians: lessons from implant and external attachment procedures. D.M. Madison and
V.S. Lamoureux, Department of Biological Sciences, State University of New York at Binghamton, Binghamton, New
York 13902-6000.
   Year round radiotracking of Ambysloma maculatum, A. tigrinum, Cryptobranchus alleganiensis, and Rana
clamitans has lead to improved package design, surgical procedures, field release and recovery, and positioning
techniques. External packages are generally unacceptable for tracking amphibians. Amphibian skin is too
physiologically active, delicate and moist for the attachment of external units by waist bands, harnesses, collars,
glues or sutures. Packages fixed to the amphibian integument has caused tethering and even injury and death in the
animal's struggle to free itself. External packages can also prevent amphibians from entering or turning around in
small mammal tunnels, ainways, vegetative tangles and rock crevices. External packages, stomach inserts, and
surgical (coelomic) implants were userf on aquatic hellbenders to test the various methods in a natural setting. The
implants worked best, followed by the inserts, which were defecated after 10 days. External packages were
unsatisfactory.
Radiotransmitter implants were used successfully in all the above species, but precautions with design, implant
surgery, and field deployment must bs taken. Implant packages should be small enough to allow amphibians to turn
around in tight spaces and be coated with beeswax instead of paraffin. Sutures should be more closely spaced in
colli weather, and cyanoacrylate should bs avoided. Animals should be released at the beginning of their daily
activity cycle in the same pulse of ecological/social events from which they were removed. Finally, "local
triangulation* should be used to obtain positions; visual fixes should normally be avoided.

A laboratory study of foraging behavior in young northern water snakes {Nerodia sipedon): The effect of
water depth, habitat structure, and ontogeny on foraging proficiency. C.A. Conaway and A.R. Gibson,
Cleveland State University, Department of Biological, Geological, and Environmental Sciences, 2399 Euclid Avenue,
Cleveland, Ohio 44115 USA.
I earned out a laboratory study of foraging proficiency in young northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) presented
with different water depths (0.25, 0.50, 1.00, 2.00 in.), and the presence or absence of artificial habitat stnjcture.
Over a seventeen month period and using two litters of young water snakes, I performed three laboratory
experiments in which I measured the time requited to capture and ingest live minnows in a small feeding arena
during 30-minute trials. Snakes generally took less time to capture fish in shallower water than they did in deeper
water. Ingestion times largely were unaffected by depth. Larger/older snakes took less time to capture fish than did
smaller^oung snakes, and larger snakes also captured more fish than did smaller snakes. In an experiment using
one litter of young snakes, I found that capture and ingestion times generally were unaffected by the presence of one
form of habitat structure, despite its importance as documented in other studies.

Comparative behavior of two parthenogenetic and one bisexual species of Cnemidophorus lizards from
souttiem Texas. M.A. Paulissen. Department of Biological & Environmental Sciences, McNeese State University,
Lake Charles, Louisiana 70609, USA.
Two species of the all-female, parthenogenetic Cnemidophorus laredoensis complex (Teiidae) coexist with the
bisexual species Cnemidophorus gularis in the Rio Grande Valley of southern Texas and northern Mexico. I studied
the behavior of the two parthenogenetic species, provisionally designated 'LAR-A' (= C. laredoensis) and 'LAR-B',
and C. aularis through focal animal observations of free-ranging lizards in a state park in Texas. Focal animals were
followed for a minimum of 10 minutes and all behaviors were recorded into a tape recorder. Playback of the tapes
allowed determination of the amount of time lizards spent performing various behaviors. Observations were made
during the May to June breeding seasons of 1994-1996. The major differences were between males of C. gularis
and LAR-A, LAR-B, and C. gularis females. In general, C. gularis males spent a significantly greater percentage of
time interacting with other lizards (most often courting conspecific females or parthenogenetic females), moved
greater distances during the time they were observed, and moved faster than C. gularis females and females of the
two parthenogenetic species.        There were few behavioral differences between C, gularis females and
parthenogenetic females. The two parthenogens did devote a greater percentage of their time to searching for food
than did C. gularis males and females; however there was no significant difference in the rate of capture of arthropod
prey. Overall, the results suggest that the behavioral differences between sexes are greater than the behavioral
differences between species in this group of lizards despite differing reproductive modes.

Environmental cues used by juvenile com snakes {Elaphe g. guttata) for spatial learning and memory of an
escape task. T.J. Nyberg. Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY
14627, USA; A. Jain and W. Amaya, Neuroscience Program, Oberlin College, Oberlin, OH 44074, USA; D.A.
Holtzman, Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, University-of Rochester, Rochester, NY 14627, USA.
Spatial orientation is necessary for snake survival, mediating important behaviors such as den localization and
predator escape responses. To characterize cues used for spatial orientation, eight juvenile com snakes were
trained to find the only open hole within a circular arena, given a choice of eight holes. During training, snakes
showed significant decreases in the latency to find the goal and in the path length taken to find the goal. A
significant increase was found in ths percent movement in ths goal quadrant. Manipulations of controlled
environmental cues (rotation of a cue card, rotation of the arena, release from a new position in the arena, and
removal of the cue card) were done to examine the effects on orientation to the goal. The results indicate that no
one particular cue was used by all of the snakes, although rotation of the cue card and arena affected the most
snakes. Individuals were affected differently by different cue manipulations, and some snakes appear to use multiple
environmental cues for this task. Snakes also appear to use cues which were not manipulated, such as extra-arena
(e.g. overhead lights) and intra-arena cues (e.g. variation in the arena surface).

Structural differences In gill vasculature among batiod elasmobranchs. R.L. Sherman. Nova Southeastern
University Oceanographic Center, 8000 N. Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA.
Classic studies of gill vasculature indicate the gross anatomy of elasmobranch gills is similar in most spedes, and in
general, resembles those of teleosts. Studies of fine gill stnicture of several species of batoid elasmobranchs have,
however, reported some structural differences. These differences include the presence, in urolophids (Urolophus
jamaicensis, U. mucosus, U. paucimaculatus), of 1) a tip channel, possibly an extension of the afferent filament
artery that nrns along the top of the filament corpus cavemosum, and 2) a vascular arcade, a vessel which connects
the afferent filament arteries of a hemibranch near the tip of each filament. To date, these stnictures were believed
to be unique to the urolophids as they were not found in either rajids {Raja erinacea, R. davata} or the shark
Scyliorhinus canicula. Research with the cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) and other batiod elasmobranchs,
however, indicates the tip channel and vascular arcade are not unique to urolophids. Additional research is required
to determine the phylogenetic and physiologic significances of these structures.

Chondrocranium and Internal oral anatomy of Hyla chrysosceiis. S.F. Soear. C.C. Swart and R.O. de Sd,
Department of Biology. University of Richmond,, Richmond, VA 23173 USA.
Hyla chrysosceiis, family Hylidae, ranges from Southern Canada south to Texas and Rorida. Internal oral
morphology and chondrocranial anatomy for this species have not been described. However, chondrocranial data is
available for eight species within the family Hylidae. Herein, we describe the internal oral anatomy using scanning
electron microscopy (SEM), chondrocranial anatomy, and ossification sequence for H. chrysosceiis. Specimens were
field collected in Beaverdam, Virginia, and preserved in 10% formalin. A total of 43 tadpoles, ranging from Gosner's
stages 30 to 46, were cleared and double-stained for bone and cartilage using standard techniques. A table of
ossification sequence is presented. In addition, two tadpoles were prepared for SEM using standard techniques.
Hyla chrysosceiis differs in several characteristics from the other described members of the family Hylidae. It is
most similar to the previously described H. puchella and H. lanciiormis. However, in H. chrysosceiis the anterior tipS
of the cornua trabeculae are laterally expanded. Hyla chrysosceiis has an otic process connecting the
palatoquadrate to the otic capsule. This process was reported absent in H. lanciiormis. The muscular process of H.
chrysosceiis is smaller than that of H. pulchella . The internal oral anatomy of H. chrysosceiis is similar to that
reported for other hylids.

Development of the suprarostral plate in pipoid frogs. C.C. Swart and R.O. de Sa, Deptartment of Biology, ,
University of Richmond,, Richmond Virginia, 23173 USA.
The ethmoid plate of anuran larvae is formed by the fusion of the trabecular and parachordal cartilages early in
development. From the antero-lateral edges of this plate, the cornua trabeculae arise as two separate and anteriorly
diverging projections. Usually, at their most anterior tips, the cornua trabeculae articulate with the suprarostral
cartilages, the element supporting the upper jaw. Modification of the cornua has been demonstrated in several taxa
(Wild 1996). In pipids, cornua trabeculae and suprarostral cartilages are not identifiable as separate elements even
in relatively early larvae (Neiuwkoop and Faber stage 50). Instead, a single and continuous cartilaginous plate
covers the entire area, the suprarostral plate (Trueb and Hanken 1993). This plate has been reported in Xenopus,
Pipa, and Rhinophrynus. Hymenochirus boettgen lacks a suprarostral plate and possesses a further modified
ethmoid area. Tadpoles of Xenopus laevis , Rhinophrynus dorsalis and H^enochinjs boettgeri were studied using
whole-mounted cleared and stained specimens and paraffin and plastic embedded cross-sectioned material. Herein
we describe the development of the suprarostral plate in Xenopus iaevis , Rhinophrynus dorsalis with comments on
the condition in Hymenochirus boettgeri

Ultrastructure of gymnophione scales and their utility as phylogenetic characters. A.L. Soroston. Natural
History Museum and Department of Systematics and Ecology, The University of Kansas USA.
Since Taylor's Atlas of Scales (1972), interspecific variation among caecilian scales has been virtually ignored, and
only the presence or absence of sc^es has been used as a phylogenetic character. The issue of variation has
focused on scale morphology within and among individuals of a single species. Considerable variation has been
found in the size, shape, arrangement, and number of scales, and thus, scales have been regarded as too variable
to be phylogenetically informative. The surface morphology of scales has been investigated in detail in only a few
taxa. The outer-most layer of caecilian scales is comprised of mineralized squamulae. The objectives of this study
were to investigate intraspecific and interspecific variation in the arrangement and shape of the squamulae,' and to
address whether there are scale characteristics, besides the presence or absence of scales, that can be utilized in
reconstructing phylogenies. Scales from representative of the four caecilian families ttiat possess scales were
removed and analyzed using light and scanning electron microscopy. Little intraspecific variaition was found in scale
ultrastructure, while a good deal of interspecific variation was identified. Variation in scale ultrastructure among taxa
is quantified and scale characters are discussed.

butterflyfishes. W.L. Smith and J.F, Webb, Department of Biology, Villanova University, Villanova, PA 19085

Lateral line canal morphogenesis in the cichlid, Archocentrus nigrofasclatua. M.L. Tarby and J.F. Webb.
Department of Biology, Villanova University, Villanova, PA 19085 USA.
The development of the supraorbital and mandibular canals was analyzed in Archocentnjs nlgrofascialus (n=26, 4.5
-11.5 mm SL) in order to evaluate conflicting descriptions of canal morphogenesis and the manner in which they are
incorporated into dermal cranial bones. Neuromasts of the dorsal aspect of the head were examined (n=6,4.5 - 8.0
mm SL) using SEM to clarify their identity as presumptive canal or superficial neuromasts. Four developmental
stages were identified. Neuromasts arise in the epithelium (Stage I) and a bony plate ossifies under each
neuromast. Epithelial ridges arise on either side of the neuromast and ossify intramembranously forming canal walls
(Stage II). The epithelium fuses over the neuromast (Stags III) and canal walls fuse medially (Stage IV)> forming the
lateral line canal roof. Thus, the supraorbital and mandibular canals appear to develop as outgrowths of the
underlying dermal bone, not as separate ossifications. In addition, regression analyses reveal that neuromast width
and canal width exhibit a positive linear relationship with fish size in both the supraorbital and mandibular canals
indicating that there are probably ongoing interactions between neuromasts and dermal bones after initial canal
ossficiation.

The effect of chronic Aroclor® 1242 exposure on metamorphosis of ranld tadpoles. M.J. Rybitski. Virginia
Institute of Marine Science, College of William and Mary, Gloucester Point, VA 23062 USA.
Aroclor® 1242 is a polychlorinated biphenyl (PCS) formulation reported to have endocrine disrupting activity in many
animals. To examine its effects on amphibian metamorphosis, tadpoles resulting from two morphologically disparate
egg masses were orally dosed daily throughout the larval period, approximately eight months. The effects on ranld
metamorphosis varied between the egg masses. In the first egg mass, tentatively identified as R. sphenocephala,
there was no statistical difference between treatments in the number of metamorphs at the end of the experiment. In
the second egg mass, tentatively identified as R. palustris, PCB treatment was correlated with an increase in the
number of tadpoles completing metamorphosis, significantly in the highest dose. The apparent stimulation of
metamorphosis in the second egg mass by PCB exposure may be due to an endocrine disrupting effect on the
corticosterone "stress" axis. A thyroid-mediated mechanism of effect is also possible. The increase in
metamorphosis in the PCB treated groups was only significant at the highest dose (1000 pg/g). This levd of
contamination exceeds concentrations likely to occur in the wild. Based upon these results, it is unlikely that PCB
exposure in the wild is altering time to metamorphosis to a degree that would detrimentally effect amphibian
populations. Interpretation of these results is hampered by the difficulty in identifying the ranid larvae. Efforts are
ongoing to resolve the identification of the tadpoles and froglets.

Ontogenetic cranial allometries and their Impact on vision in snakes. C.L. Caorette. Evolution, Ecology, and
Organismal Biolog, Ohio Slate University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210 USA, Ohio State University,
1735 Neil Avenue. Columbus, OH 43210 USA.
Changes in head size and shape during development occur in all vertebrates. One general observation is that the
eyes of most vertebrates are large early in development and that the remainder of the head tends to grow around
them. This paper presents a comparative study of the relative size and position of the eyes within and among
different groups of snakes. Of particular interest are changes associated with head size in left and right visual field
overlap, with respect to both quantity and direction of overlap. For example, in some arboreal species, the eyes are
rotated about the dorsal-ventral axis towards the frontal plane during ontogeny. This increases the frontal .binocular
overlap, while sacrificing some of the postero-lateral visual field. These changes may be the consequence of
structural changes to increase gape and the development of larger, more powerful jaw musculature in larger
individuals for capturing and ingesting larger prey. Correlations with natural history and phylogeny are discussed
together with some hypotheses of ultimate causation.

 Stocks of Couesius plumbeus (Cyprinidae) in the Keweenaw Peninsula, Michigan. R.M. Bailey. Museum of
Zoology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Ml 48109-1079, U.S.A.
The lake chub {Couesius plumbeus), the most widespread minnow in northern North America, ranges from Alaska to
New England. Couesius is regarded as monotypic, but its relationships have been debated and there have been
questions as to whether or not the species is polytypic. Several recent studies cited in the literature remain
unpublished.
In 1941, Hubbs and Lagler reported that two subspecies, occasionally sympatric though usually separated
ecologically, occurred on the Keweenaw Peninsula. Later these authors suggested that the two forms verged on full
specific distinction. Restudy of their abundant material supplemented by new collections indicates that there are. in
fact, two morphs of the lake chub in the area, one chiefly in creeks, the other in Lake Superior shorewaters and
rivermouths. The creek form has a smaller eye, a shorter and slightly more rounded dorsal fin. and significantly
fewer vertebrae. I suggest that these reflect different ecological conditions during development. Downstream drift of
creek fish has resulted in sympafry of the lake and creek morphs at the mouth of Eagle River. The relationships of
Couesius are discussed.

Morphological and genetic variation In northwestern longnose suckers, Catostomus catostomus-the Salish
sucker problem. J. D. McPhail and E. B. Taylor, Dept, of Zoology, University of BC, 6270 University Blvd.,
Vancouver, BC, V6S 1Z4.
A distinctive form of longnose sucker, ths Salish sucker, occurs in southwestern British Columbia and western
Washington. Salish suckers differ from other western longnose suckers in both their morphometry and mitochondrial
genome. Thus, both morphometric and molecular data indicate taht Salish suckers have divereged from other
northwestern longnose suckers; however, our molecular data suggests an even ‘deeper* divergence between
western and eastern longnose suckers, and the Salish sucker is unambiguously part of the western lineage. This
implies that the Salish sucker evolved after the divergence of western and eastern longnose suckers. The
geographic distribution of Salish suckers is consistent with a pre-Wisconscinan origin south of Puget Sound and post
glacial dispersal north into southwestern B.C. The Salish sucker is in decline throughout its geographic range and
probably will be extinct in southwestern B.C. within a decade. THe diagnostic mitochondrial haplotypes
characteristics of the Salish sucker argue that a unique part of the evolutionary history of the longnose sucker will be
lost with the extinction of the Salish sucker. As such they constitute and Evolutionarily Significant Unit and warrant
some protecton in Washington State where there still is at least one large population.

Lessons from E.J. Crossman - The relevance of a comprehensive approach to fish taxonomy.                   J.D. Reist.
Fisheries and Oceans Canada, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB, R3T 2N6.

In his direction to students. Dr. E.J. Crossman emphasizes and encourages a comprehensive approach to questions
and problems of fish systematic and taxonomic studies which, at the time I was doing my degree work, were
dominated by morphological and osetological approaches. Recently such studies have become dominated by
genetic approaches which often rely solely upon tissues provided to laboratories rather than the fish themselves, and
focus solely upon variation at the molecular level. Little or no reference is usually made to other character systems
such as morphology, osteology, ecology or biology. For well known groups and studies at higher taxonomic levels
this bias may not matter, and genetic studies add another dimension to our knowledge. However, for poorly known
groups and lower taxonomic levels, working solely with tissues can limit understanding, may bias results, and result
in erroneous conclusions. External morphology is often the first clue to undiscovered diversity. Genetic variation may
be present but without associated knowledge of morphology may not be interpreted correctly. Thus, quantifying and
understanding morphological diversity is important in the development of hypotheses which can then be tested using
other approaches such as genetics. Morphological diversity within an esociform (Olympic mudminnow, Novumbra
hubbsi) and morphological and genetic diversity within a salmoniform group (Arctic and Dolly Varden chars,
Salvellnus spp.) are used to illustrate the need for close association of various approaches to achieve fuller
understanding of diversity and relationships of fishes. In keeping with the legacy of Dr. Crossman, I advocate a more
comprehensive approach to systematic and taxonomic studies which should include reference to morphological,
ecological and biological chararactes as well as genetic characters.

Evidence of mate competition and mate choice In Atlantic cod. J.A. Hutchings. T.D. Bishop and C.R. McGregor-
Shaw, Department of Biology, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3H 4J1.
We quantified individual differences in reproductive behaviour of Atlantic cod under simulated natural conditions. At
field spawning densities, 16 individually marked cod (7 males, 9 females) were observed twice daily and videotaped
continuously for 9 weeks at ambient photoperiod and temperature in a large tank. Males established an aggression­
based dominance hierarchy with 96% of all agonistic interactions being initiated by the 3 largest males.
Microsatellite DNA analysis of 1 female's brood identified paternal gene contributions from the 3 behaviourally
dominant males. Interactions between sexes were dominated by male circling of females. After descending to the
bottom, a motionless female was circled an average 2.4 times (range: 1 to 11), usually by 1 male per circling bout but
by several males throughout the spawning period. Circling may provide opportunities for males to gain individual
access to reproductive females and for females to assess the quality of potential mates. Given the prevalence of
sound communication among reproductive cod and other gadids, sexual differences in the size of sound- producing
muscles in haddock provide indirect evidence of mate choice. The mating conditions of cod and haddock are
consistent with the hypothesis that these fish reproduce in leks.

Another look at the Batesian-Mullerlan mimicry spectrum.                R.W. Van Devender. Department of Biology,
Appalachian State University, Boone, NC 28608 , USA.
In 1976 James Huheey used a functional feeding model to simulate the effects of adding weaker models to simple
Mullerian Mimicry system. Huheey concluded that weaker models decrease the survivorship of the stronger models
and have the same impact on the models as would Batesian mimics. This conclusion contradicts a number of earlier
theoretical and logical assertions, but has apparently survived the test of time rather well. I used a similar functional
model of feeding to ask whether specific changes alter the conclusion that Mullerian Mimicry cannot exist. The newer
feeding model included both positive and negative values for noxiousness and a wide range of relative proportions of
model species. Individuals of the second mimic species were ADDED to a resident pool of noxious model instead
of replacing them. This modification was added because models and mimics only share their appearance not
necessarily their ecological space. Success, or lack of success, was measured In terms of mortality rates for both
species. Results of the simulations delineate situations with "viable" proportions of "models" and "mimics". In all
situations where the second species was at all noxious, overall sunrivorship for the original species increased.
Mullerian co-models have exactly the impact that Fisher suggested in 1930. The model used extended the ranges of
possible attractiveness beyond the usual limited range of palatable vs. unpalatable and suggests ways of
incorporating these variables into more general systems.

Structure and frequency of multiple apermatophores of Ambystoma                    texamm.      E.J. Zallsko. Blackbum
College, Carlinville, IL 62626, USA.

Soermatophotes of Ambystoma texanum collected in the field from Macoupin and Jackson Counties, Illinois, consist
of a sperm filled cap supported by a gelatinous base. This structure is consistent with prior reports for this and other
Ambysttxna species. Multiple structures consisted of up to 7 spermatophores stacked vertically. Individual
spermatophores within multiple structures have a morphology consistent with single spermatophores.
Spermatophores within multiple stnjctures adhere to each other. The base of each stacked spermatophore typically
covers the subjacent spermatophore cap, leaving only the cap of the top spermatophore exposed. Ave
spermatophore fields of 21-535 spermatophores were examined. The percent of spermatophores in multiple
structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (19%, N = 21;
73.8%, N = 112-120; 83.7%, N = 378-535 spermatophores). Further, the number of spermatophores within multiple
structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (22% of all
spermatophores were in structures of 4 or more spermatophores for N = 378-535; 15.7% for N= 112-120; and 0%
for N = 21 spermatophores).

metamorphosis limits the feeding ability of these individuals, thus, contributing to their short term post "metamorphic"

 Evolutionary Relationships of spiny-tailed Iguanas (genus Ctenosaura} and their Implications for Mexican
and Central American biogeography. L. Bucklev. Rochester Institute of Technology, Department of Biological
Sciences, Rochester, NY 14623.
Several important geophysical trends in Mexico and Central America are reflected in the pattern of relationships
among lizards of the genus Ctenosaura. The spiny-tailed iguanas are primarily lowland species whose current
distributions wpearto have been influenced by both fragmentation and dispersal. Identifiable events cluster into one
of two general categories which include those which are fairly recent (< 3 mya) or those which are relatively older (>
5 mya). Species or spedes groups whose divergences reflect relatively older events may have resulted from uplift
of interior highlands, isolation of the Baja peninsula and previous isolation of Lower Central America from Nuclear
Central America and Mexico. More recently diverged species may be the result of episodes such as the emergence
of the isthmus of Tehuantepec, the formation of the Mexican tiansvolcanics, the fragmentation of Pacific coastal arid
habitats and isolation on islands.

Variation in the scleral ossicles of cryptodiran turtles. K.D. Andrews, Dept. Biol., Glendale Community College,
Glendale, AZ 85302, USA; J.L. Carr. Dept. Biol., Northeast Louisiana University, Monroe, LA 71209 USA.
Among tetrapods, scleral ossicles form a ring of small bony plates in the eyes of Sphenodon, lizards, turtles, and
birds. The number of ossicles and their pattern of overlap have been used as taxonomic characters for lizards and
birds; however, the ossicles of turtles have been considered too variable to be phylogenetically inforrnative. We
undertook a more comprehensive survey to assess levels of variability in scleral ossicles and their potential utility as
taxonomic characters among chelonians. Ossicles in 432 eyes from 73 species representing nine out of 10
cryptodiran families were cleared and stained. The ossicles were counted and the pattern of ossicle overlap in the
ring for each eye recorded. Bilateral symmetry, and extent of intraspecific and interspecific variation were analyzed.
Number of ossicles ranged from 7 to 14 per eye. The most common numbers of ossicles were 10 (39%) and 11
(35%). There was a high degree of bilateral symmetry in the number of ossicles present. Within a species, the
extent of bilateral symmetry in overlap patterns ranged from 39% to 100%. For the most common numbers of
ossicles, overlap patterns were predominated by one or two vry common patterns. Although number of ossicles
alone may be useful in distinguishing some closely related species, it has limited use at higher taxonomic levels.
The overlap patterns are very consenrative and therefore of limited phylogenetic utility.

Behavioral habituation In the green frog, Rana ctem/tana, S. Perrill and P. Owen, Butler University, Department
of Biology, Indianapolis, IN 46208, USA.

Habituation and its role in the dear enemy effect were Investigated in a population of green frogs, Rana clamitans.
Green frogs have a prolonged breeding season In which males vocalize from territories to attract mates. We tested
the prediction that male green frogs will habituate to broadcast synthetic conspecific stimuli. Our results indicate
that male green frogs can discriminate familiar from unfamiliar stimuli. We infer that habituation helps to mediate the
territorial interactions between male green frogs. Strangers present a greater threat than familiar neighbors. Males
can habituate to the advertisement vocalizations of their near-neighbors, allowing them to focus more attention on
the unfamiliar vocalizations of a territorial intruder. This would save energy that could be invested in a male's
advertisement calls and in the defense of his territory.

Striking In bold snakes. D. Cundall and A. Deufel, Lehigh University, Biological Sciences, 31 Williams Dr.
Bethlehem PA 18015-3190 USA.
Boid strikes resemble predatory viper strikes. Quantitative analysis of video records (30fps, 1/1000 s exposure) of
160 strikes made by 18 bold snakes representing eight species show that although at least three kinematic patterns
may be used, the majority of strikes are made by dropping the mandible and accelerating the braincase over the
prey. The snake's teeth slide over the prey surface and do not engage until the prey moves In the direction of the
strike. Gape rarely exceeds 60 degrees and jaw closure may begin at or just prior to contact with the prey. The
strike terminates with a bite involving ventral flexion of the snake's head during formation of the first constricting coil.
The rapidity and variability of strikes suggest that suspensorial design in bold snakes acts in part to absorb shocks.
Anatomical and behavioral comparisons to other alethinophidian snakes suggest that the rapid strike may have
coevolved with macrostomate gape size because features of skull design that increase gape size also increase
shock absorbing potential during strikes.

 Pressure/immobllfzation as first aid for venomous snakebite In the United States. D.L .sr Hardy. 585 S Main
Av. Tucson, AZ, 85701; S.P. Bush, Loma Linda University. School of Medicine.
Pressure/immobilization (P/I) is a first aid method used in Australia for elapid snakebite which consists of elastic
bandage wrapping and splinting of the extremity. It has recently been suggested that it be used following venomous
snakebite in the United States. However, most physicians do not recommend P/I for pitviper bite because local
necrosis may be increased due to venom sequestration, and clinical experience in terms of outcome after pitviper
envenomation is lacking. In addition, correct application of P/I requires knowledge of the technique and immediate
availability of appropriate materials, its use may increase the incidence of compartment syndrome, and
implementation of P/I can delay transport to a medical facility. Advocates say possible Increased local necrosis from
P/I use is an acceptable trade off if systemic venom effects can be delayed. We recommend the use of P/I in the
U.S. be limited to bites by captive Australian elapid snakes and only on a case by case basis. Passive
immobilization and immediate travel to a medical facility remain the only first aid measures universally accepted.
P/I is not recommended following pitviper envenomation as it has not been shown to improve outcome and may
cause additional injury.

Comparl&one of temporal display structure across contexts and populations In male Anotta camHnanaia:
signal stability or lability? M.B. Lovern. T.A. Jenssen and K.S. Orrell, Dept, of Biology, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg.
VA 24061 USA.

We examined the relative stability versus lability of temporal display structure in males of the lizard, Anolis
carolinensls. We videotaped headbobbing displays across field and laboratory environments, social contexts, and
populations for males from Georgia, Rorida, and Hawaii, and subsequently generated display-action-pattem (DAP)
graphs of these displays for statistical comparison. Anolis carolinensls is known to be a recent (circa 1950) colonizer

Perch height and movements of the arboreal lizard Anolis nebulosus from a tropical dry forest of Mexico. A.
Ramirez-Bautista, Institute de Biologia. Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico. Apdo. Postal 70-153. Mexico
D.F. 04510; M. Benabib. Institute de Ecologia. Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico. Apdo. Postal 70-275.
Mexico D.F. 04510.
We studied perch height and individual movements of the lizard Anolis nebulosus from Chamela, Jalisco, Mexico.
Males used higher perches than females. Adults used significantly higher perches than juveniles and hatchlings,
and overall, perches were significantly higher during the wet than the dry season. Perch height increased with body,
environmental, and microenvironmental temperature, suggesting that perch height plays a role in thermoregulation.
Distance moved by each individual was not related to SVL. Females moved longer distances than males, but
females remained longer in the study area than males. Significant differences among age classes were found in the
time period that lizards lived in the trees. The number of days lizards remained in the area was inversely related
with the distance traveled. A larger proportion of lizards that moved longer distances died before the reproductive
season, in comparison to those that moved shorter distances or did not move at all from ths tree where they were
originally caught, suggesting that it is dangerous to move, and lizards should establish soon in a territory to increase
their fitness.

Mother-offspring interactions in the ground skink, Scincella lateralis. j.A,-Al9n and G.S. Sonnier. Department

Parental care is relatively rare in reptiles and cannibalism of offepring even occurs in some taxa. Yet. young often
remain near their parents with little, if any dispersal. Using hatchling ground skinks (Scincella lateralis) reared from
eggs laid by known mothers, wo examined the responses of female ground skinks to each of three conditions; her

Structure and evolution of shark ribosomal DNA Internal transcribed spacers.    M.S. Shivii. Nova Southeastern
University, Oceanographic Center, 8000 North Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA; M,J. Stanhope, School of
Biology and Biochemistry, The Queen's University, Belfast, BT9 7BL„ N. Ireland, UK; S.O. Rogers, College of
Environmental Sdence & Forestry, State University of New York, Syracuse, NY 13210, USA.
Internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) are DNA regions separating the multicopy, nuclear ribosomal RNA
genes. We have obtained complete ITS2 sequences from several sharks representing different lineages, and report
here on aspects of the comparative structure and evolution of this locus.
Shark ITS2 regions are ths largest reported for any eukaryote, a size explained in part by the insertion of sequence
elements strongly resembling group I introns. These insertion elements appear to be present in all major shark
lineages. They are, however, conspicuously absent from hammerhead sharks, arguing for an ancient origin of these
elements with subsequent loss in the presumably derived hammerhead lineage. The insertion element is also absent
from the ITS2 of the one stingray (Urolophus Jamaicensis) we have examined thus far.
We have also explored the phylogenetic utility of ITS2 sequences for resolving some relationships within the family
Carcharhinidae. The precise affinities of Prionace and Negaprion to Carcharhinus are currently unsettled, with
hypotheses proposed about Prionace being either a derived species within or sister taxon to Carcharhinus.
Preliminary phylogenetic analysis of 1TS2 sequences places Prionace well within the Carcharhinus clads, arguing
against ths current status of the blue shark as a separate genus.

Shivji, Oceanographic Center, Nova Southeastern University, 8000 N. Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004, USA.
Blue sharks are highly vagile elasmobranchs with a circumglobal temperate and tropical distribution. This species
displays complex reproductive and migratory behavior, making it difficult to realize a clear picture of genetic stock
structure. Wo report here our examination of the utility of mitochondrial (mt) DNA control region sequences for
assessing blue shark genetic structure on a global scale. Complete control region (1069 bp in size) sequences were
obtained from 16 blue shark individuals collected from 5 globally distributed sites. Contraiy to ths case in most
vertebrates, this locus is remarkably conserved in blue sharks. The 11 haplotypes observed differed from each other

12 variable sites) was restricted to the 350 bp region adjacent to the tRNA-proline gene, with no variation observed
in the central 400 bp section of this locus. Phylogenetic analysis revealed no indication of geographic population
structuring. We infer from these data that either the blue shark mt control region may be too conserved to be useful
for population genetic studies, or that dispersal over a global scale is occum'ng, or has occurred in the recent past.

Mechanics of ventilation in the swellshark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum (Scyliorhinidae).                       L.A. Ferry-
Graham. University of California, Irvine, CA 92697-2525 USA.
Most fishes are faced with one of two options for gill ventilation: physically moving their gills through the medium
(“ram" ventilation), or actively pumping the medium over their gills via “buccal pumping“. The basic pattern of
mechanical movements during buccal pumping was studied over 40 years ago. However, unique patterns of water
flow through the head of the swellshark during feeding suggested that the generation of respiratory currents might
not be as simple as once thought. Using pressure transducers implanted into the buccal and gill cavities of actively
respiring swellsharks, it was discovered that pressure traces vary within and among individuals. These data,
combined with both video and electrical impedance data for the displacement of the lower jaw and gill septum,
suggest that although the classic pattern of pressure generation regularly occurs, at least one novel pattern of
pressure generation exists. During this novel pattern, pressure reversals exist over a much longer duration than
previously thought possible, and at much larger magnitudes. It is questionable whether the classic alternating
“suotion“ and “pressure“ pumps are always used for moving water over the gills unidirectionally, and whether
continuous water flow over the gills exists for large intervals of time in this species.

Ontogenetic changes in energetics and active and passive ventilation of the swell shark {Cephaloscyllium
ventnosum} egg capsule. S.R. Meehan. Department of Environmental Protection, Lignumvitae Key, Florida USA;
A.P, Summers, Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, UMASS Amherst, Massachusetts USA; T.J. Koob, Shriner's
Hospital for Children, Tampa, Florida USA.
The swell shark. Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, is an oviparous chondrichthyan fish. Each egg capsule contains a
single embryo that is incubated on the sea floor for 7.5 to 10 months. The homy capsule material is not sufficiently
permeable to oxygen to supply the needs of a late stage embryo, however, after about one third of development four
slits open in the sides of the egg case to admit seawater. We investigated ontogenetic changes in metabolic rate and
mechanisms of capsule ventilation. Mass specific rate of oxygen consumption decreases as the embryo grows. Early
stage embryos have a relatively large tail appendage that is used to generate a water current through the capsule.
During development this appendage decreases in relative size and just before hatching the embryo ventilates the
capsule by oropharyngeal pumping. In addition to the active pumping, the capsule is ventilated passively. When in a
current, pressure differences along the capsule induce flow through the capsule interior. Sufficient water to supply
the oxygen needs of a near term embryo will be induced to flow at current speeds of just 0.2 knots. This passive flow
comes at no metabolic cost to the embryo.

Validation of otolith age estimates for the rainbow darter, Etheostoma caeruleum, in the James River of the
southwest Missouri Ozarks. D.W. Beckman. Department of Biology, Southwest Missouri State University,
Springfield, Missouri 65714, USA.
In the past 15 years there has been an emphasis on validation of age estimates for fish population studies.
However, age estimates have been validated for few freshwater stream fish species; with a dearth of published age
validation studies for North American darters of the genus Etheostoma. Traditionally darter ages have been
obtained from scales or by length-frequency analysis, methods now known to be unreliable for many species.
The purpose of this study was to evaluate otolith and scale age estimates for the rainbow darter, Etheostoma
caeruleum, from the James River in the southwest Missouri Ozarks. Validity of age estimates was assessed by
following the progression of annulus formation at the growing edge of scales and otoliths in fish captured throughout
the year (edge analysis). Samples of 10-15 fish were taken by seine in each of 8 months from July 1996 through
May 1997. Otoliths were viewed whole and in transverse section, and scales were viewed mounted between glass
slides. Edge analysis of whole or sectioned otoliths indicated that one opaque annulus was formed per year in the
otoliths, primarily during summer months. High agreement between sectioned and whole otolith ages (75% exact
agreement, 99% within one year) indicates that consistent, valid ages can be obtained for Etheostoma caeruleum
using either otolith method. Otolith age estimates ranged from 0-4 years. There was no clear pattern discerned in
timing of scale annulus formation, and scale age estimates tended to be lower than otolith age estimates. Our
results suggest that scale age estimates for darters should be made with caution.

Development of the lateral line system In the shovelnose sturgeon, Scaphirhynchus platorynchus. M.A.
Gibbs and R.G. Northcutt, Dept. NeurosciencQs. UCSD, 9500 Gilman Dr., La Jolla, CA 92093-0201, LISA.
The shovelnose sturgeon, Scaphirhynchus platorynchus, normally develops over a 10 day period at 18 °C. During
the first 45 hours post-fertilization, three preotic (anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic) ano three postotic (medial,
supratemporal and posterior) lateral line placodes arise within the cephalic ectoderm. Lateral line ganglia are formed
in each placode from endogenous neuieblasts which migrate from the placodes at 60 hours post-fertilization.
Placodes begin to elongate into sensory ridges a few hours before hatching, and by the time hatching occurs, at
about 106 hours post-fertilization, neuromasts are erupting in the central zones of the otic and caudal anterodorsal
sensory ridges. By four days post-hatch, an exposed mechanosensory lateral line extends from the dorsal zone of
the anteroventral sensory ridge to the supra- and infra-orbital zones of the anterodorsal ridge. At 10 days post-hatch,
the larva is feeding and has a mechanosensory lateral line that extends from the rostrum to ths trunk and includes
neuromasts from all six dorsolateral placodes. Electroreceptive ampullary organs, which arise from ths
anteroventral, anterodorsal, otic and supratemporal placodes begin to enjpt just before the onset of feeding, and are
fully developed by the time canals begin to form around the neuromast lines at twelve days post-hatch.

Lack of negative effect of ambient ultraviolet radiation on development of eggs and larvae of the
southernmost anuran of the world near the ozone hole. S.F. Fox. Department of Zoology, Oklahoma State
University, Stillwater, OK 74078 USA; D.J. Bruggeman, Department of Zoology, Oklahoma State University,
Stillwater, OK 74078 USA; H. Nunez, Seccion Zoologfa, Museo Nacional de Historia Natural, Casilla 787, Santiago,
Chile; R.A. Van Den Bussche, Department of Zoology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK 74078 USA; J.A.
Bantie II, Department of Zoology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK 74078 USA.
One possible cause implicated in worldwide amphibian declines is increased ultravlolet-B radiation (UV-B) brought
on by anthropogenic thinning of the ozone layer. Due to the ozone hole, increased UV-B is most pronounced over
Antarctica in winter, but ozone-poor air drifts northward over the southern cone of South America in early spring
when frogs there begin to breed, thus potentially exposing their eggs and larvae to damaging amounts of UV-B.
Damage from UV-B at that time is expected to be intense, especially since UV-B levels there prior to the first
appearance of the ozone hole were not high. We report preliminary results from a multi-year study of potential UV-B
effects on survival, growth, malformations, and DNA damage of developing eggs and larvae of Pleurodema bufonina
in southern Argentina. In none of four populations studied so far have we found evidence of a negative effect of
ambient UV-B.

Variability in exposure of amphibian embryos to uv-b radiation.       P.S. Com. USGS Midcontinent Ecological
Science Center, Aldo Leopold Wilderness Research Institute, PO Box 8089, Missoula, MT 59807 USA.
In ihe last 20 years, thinning stratospheric ozone has resulted in a 5-10% increase in UV-B radiation at the Earth's
surface, poleward above 40° latitude. Field experiments that have shown increased mortality of amphibian embryos
exposed to ambient sunlight, compared to those exposed to sunlight with UV-B removed, have lead to a hypothesis
that increased UV-B radiation has contributed to amphibian declines. However, measurements of incident UV-B are
missing from most of these studies, and variability in UV-B has not been examined. There are several sources of
variation in the UV-B radiation to which embryos may be exposed, including annual variation in UV-B, seasonal
gradients in UV-B, annual variation in amphibian breeding phenology, and local geographic variation in breeding
phenology. I used satellite-based estimates of UV-B radiation and observations of amphibian breeding phenology in
northern Colorado to estimate the range of variation in UV-B. Erythemal exposure (UV-B weighted by the action
spectrum for human skin irritation) increases by 80% from 1 May to 30 June, and breeding activity may vary by 30
days from year to year and 14 days across an elevation gradient. Mean 10-day erythemal exposure for two
populations of boreal chorus frogs, Pseudacris maculata, ranged between 192 and 388, and the mean exposure
between populations of P. maculata and boreal toads, Bufo boreas, on elevation gradients increased by 21 and 28%,
respectively. The increase in UV-B radiation due to ozone thinning is small relative to variation in UV-B to which
embryos may be exposed.   85                .           14:45 Friday                                 CA2                                CHM

Nest-site choice in a turtle with temperature-dependent sex determination. F.J. Janzen. Department of Zoology
& Genetics, Program in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Iowa State University, Ames, lA 50011 USA.
The role of nest-site choice in the population biology of species with temperature-dependent sex determination
(TSD) is virtually unexplored despite its importance in theoretical models for the evolution of sex ratio in such
species. In those models, the evolution of sex ratio is largely determined by heritable variation in maternal choice of
thermal qualities of nest sites. This ongoing 3-year field study examined thermally-dependent nest-site choice in a
marked population of painted turtles that has been the focus of long-term studies of TSD. Analyses to date indicate
that individual turtles exhibit significant fidelity to nest sites with similar amounts of surrounding vegetation cover. In
other words, some turtles consistently prefer unshaded sites and vice versa. Because vegetational cover is a
reasonable predictor of nest thermal environments and offspring sex ratios in this population, these findings suggest
that nest-site choice and, hence, TSD may be able to evolve in response to environmental change. Supported by
NSF grant DEB-9629529.

Modeling organismal growth In turtle populations:            assumption validation and practicality.M.J..Dce£lik,
Center for Biodiversity, iTlinois Natural History Survey, 607 East Peabody Drive, Champaign, IL 61820 USA; L.
Comerford, Department of Mathematics, Eastern Illinois University, Charleston, IL 61920 USA.
For the last decade, interest in modeling chelonian growth has increased and provided a framework for better
understanding of this life history trait. Modeling growth generates variables that can be used as life history
descriptors, and in unified comparative studies. With a long list of models, the question becomes which one to use?
To choose among models, we must first understand the basic assumptions of the typical linear, guadratio, allometric,
Johnson, Putter, von Bertalanffy, Gompertz and Logistic algorithms: 1) age is known, 2) growth follows the specified
algorithm, 3) seasonal effects are absent and 4) genetic effects are minimal. Assumption one is circumvented using
mark/recapture analogues of the aforementioned models, while assumption two is eliminated by using robust models
like the Richard's, Schunte, Baker and Francis. New insights into modeling have allowed us to include seasonality;
however, our knowledge of genetic effects does not presently allow us to correct existing models. We will discuss
and present the value of certain mark/recapture growth models, by fitting mock and actual data sets to the von
Bertalanffy, Gompertz, Logistic, Richard's and Schnute mark/recapture analogues.

Maternal effects, nest-site choice, and the maintenance of temperature-dependent sex determination. CX,.
Milne and F.J. Janzen, Department of Zoology and Genetics, 339 Science II, Iowa Stale, University Ames, lA 50011
USA.
The adaptive value, if any, of temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) is uncertain in reptiles. Suggested
mechanisms include differential fitness between offspring sexes, dependent on maternal condition. Thus, females
with the ability to assess environmental conditions that produce the sex whose fitness benefits most from maternal
condition would have a selective advantage. This presentation reports a three-year field study on nest-site choice in
the painted turtle, Chrysemys picta, a species exhibiting TSD. No relationship was found between egg mass and
nest-site choice for the three years of the study. Although egg mass may not influence nest-site choice in painted
turtles, other maternal effects that remain unexplored may play a role in nest-site choice and the maintenance of
TSD.

Hearing in elasmobranchs: a review. AA. Mvrbera (Jr.1. Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science,
University of Miami, Miami Florida 33149, USA.
A brief history is provided of the studies which established that elasmobranchs not only detect underwater sounds,
but respond to them in ways that suggested a rapid ability to locate specific sound-sources. The latter included
acoustical features that mimicked sounds produced by stnrggling prey as well as providing a point-source to observe
the behavioral activities of such predators. The rapid speed in locating sound-sources by free-ranging sharks
created controversy, however. An important theory, at the time, precluded fishes, and particularly sharks, from
directional hearing in the acoustical far-field (distances beyond one wavelength of a sound). Repeated confirmation
that sharks could accomplish such a feat during the late '60s - mid 70s resulted in several new theories that could
account for rapid directional hearing by these animals. These theories will also be briefly reviewed as will be the
findings that resulted from a renewed interest in the neural mechanisms of elasmobranch hearing in the '80s. The
report will end with ideas concerning future directions of hearing research in elasmobranchs.

The biological function of the mechanosensory lateral line in relation to ecology and behavior is essentially unknown

Electroreception: Mechanisms for detecting weak signals in noise. D. Bodznick. Dept, of Biology, Wesleyan
University, Middletown, CT 06459-0170 USA.
The elasmobranch electrosense is known for its extraordinary sensitivity which Is necessary for detecting the feeble,
behaviorally-relevant electric fields in the sea. But a cost of this sensitivity is vulnerability to electrical noise including
that produced by the fish's ovm behaviors. Behavioral, morphological and physiological specializations are ail
necessary for extracting the important weak signals from noise. Each of these types of specializations will be
discussed and recent work on the physiological mechanisms for extracting weak signals from noise will be reviewed.
Physiological adaptations include receptors that can operate over an extended voltage range without loss of
sensitivity, simple subtractive circuits in the hindbrain and sophisticated adaptive filter mechanisms that involve the
development of an expectation of the noise typically associated with each of the fish's different behaviors. The end
result of these mechanisms is that all traces of the noise can be eliminated in the hindbrain without any loss of
sensitivity to the signals important for behavior.

What is the current status of chemical shark repellents? J.A. Sisneros. Department of Biological Sciences,
Florida Institute of Technology, 150 W. University Blvd., Melbourne, FL 32901-6988 USA.

Efforts by the US Navy to develop a chemical shark repellent during the post W.W.II years were unsuccessful and
later abandoned. Interest in chemical shark repellents was renewed by the discovery of pardaxin, a natural shark
repellent secreted by the Moses sole (Pardachinis manmoratus}. The surfactant-like nature of pardaxin led
researchers to test the shark repellency of various surfactants. The most effective surfactant tested to date is the
alkyl sulfate surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS). Swim-through repellency tests were conducted in a
roundabout test tank using swell sharks, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, to determine if repellent efficacy of alkyl
sulfate surfactants was affected by carbon chain length, ethylene oxide (EO) groups, and counterions. Results
indicate repellency increases as all^ chain length increases from octyl to dodec^, decreases with the addition of EO
groups, and is not affected by counterions. SDS is the most effective known chemical repellent, but it does not meet
ttie Navy's potency requirement for a classic surrounding-cloud type repellent of 100 parts per billion. Thus, SDS is
only practical as a directional repellent such as in a squirt application. Recent work on semiochemicals may offer a
new prospective direction for the search of a more effective chemical shark repellent.

 The cerebellum of elasmobranch fishes denranstrates a wide range of variation in size and complexity across taxa.

Biology of ozark cavefish In Logan Cave national wildlife refuge, Arkansas. J.E. Johnson and J.Z. Brown,
Arkansas Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR 72701 USA.
Amblyopsis rosaa is a threatened species endemic to the Springfield Plateau of Arkansas, Missouri, and Oklahoma.
One of the largest reported Ozark cavefish populations is in Logan Cave, Arkansas, and was surveyed 25 times
between 1993 and 1995. During the study, 113 cavelish were marked with visual implant tags. Half (56) of the
tagged fish were recaptured 163 times; 30 tagged fish were never recaptured, and the other 27 were unavailable for
recapture. Gross movement exceeded 1,000 m, with a mean movement of 1.2 mriish/d. Movement was positively
correlated with cavefish length. The Logan Cave population was open to migration, with a mean of 3.8 untagged fish
captured monthly. Jolly-Seber population estimates ranged from 12 to 93 fish monthly, with a mean of 32.3 fish and a
mean survival of 0.990/d. Most fish gained in length during April-October, the period a maternity colony of gray bats
(Myotis grisescens} also occupied the cave. The Logan Cave population of Ozark cavefish appears to be a subset
of a larger population, most litely inhabiting the recharge aquifer. Cavefish that moved through the aquifer and into
Logan Cave generally survived there less than two years. No cavefish were believed to have move upstream into
the aquifer or downstream out of the cave.

Genetic variability of Eurasian and North American Perea. T.N. Todd. M.K. Bumham-Curtis and C.O. Hatcher,

Population genetic structure, phylogeography, and spawning philopatry In walleye {StUostedion vibeum}
from mtDNA control region sequences. C.A. Steoien and A.I. Brokaw, Case Western Resenre University,
Cleveland, OH 44106-7080 USA; J.E. Faber, University of West Virginia, Parkersburg USA.
Mitochondrial DNA control region sequences (1200 base pairs) tested the genetic and phylogeographic structure of
230 walleye Stizostedion vitreum among spawning sites, lake basins, lakes, and glacial refugia in the Great Lakes
region. Polymorphisms included different copy numbers and sequences of tandem repeats, and base substitutions
in the left and right domains. Results indicated significant phylogec^raphic structure among glacial refugia, lakes,

Correlation, between the extent of reproductive Isolation and morphological specialization among sympatric
lake whitefish ecotypes {Coregonua sp.) as revealed by microsatellite and morphological analyses. GJjj
and L. Bematchez, University Laval Department de Biologie, GIROQ , Sainte-foy, Quebec, G1K 7P4.
Il is generally recognized that the evolution of sympatric fish ecotypes found in post glacial lakes is the result of
processes driving ecological and phenotypic changes. If the same forces driving phenotypic divergence are also
responsible for the development of reproductive isolation, one predicts a correlation between the extent of tropic
specialization and that of reproductive isolation being reached in a given environment. We test this hypothesis by
comparing morphological and genetic divergence between sympatric dwarf and normal whitefish ecotypes from six
different lakes of the St. John R. basin (eastern Canada and northern Maine). An analysis of molecular variance was
performed using 8 microsatellite loci while 9 meristic and 19 morphometric variables were selected to quantify
morphological differentiation. Significant differences in allele frequencies between ecotypes were found in 5 lakes,
confirming that they represent genetically distinct populations. This translated into significant but variable Fst
estimates between ecotypes, ranging from 0.041 to 0.225. Similarly, dwarf and normal ecotypes were significantly
different in morphological traits, the squared Mahalanobis distance (D) varying from 1.81 to 12.69. The extent of
morphological specialization reached between ecxjtypes in each lake was negatively correlated with the extent of
gene flow among them (Nm = 7.5265 - 0.2633 x D, r = - 0.67). These results supported our hypothesis that the
extent of reproductive isolation reached between ecotypes may be related to the potential for occupying distinct
tropic niches, and therefore to the same selective forces driving morphological specialization In each lake.

A study of the North Atlantic redfish species complex (genus Sebastes}: usefulness of microsatellites for
inter- and intra- specific differentiation. S. Roques and L. Bematchez, GIROQ, Departement de Biologie,
Universitd Laval, Quebec.
Four species of redfish are potentially found in sympatry in the Atlantic Ocean: Sebastes marinas, S.vMparus,
S.fasciatus and S.mentetia. A combination of several characters can potentially distinguish these taxa at adult stage,
but no character alone can discriminate them, and none can be used for young stage identification. Low levels of
intraspecific and interspecific genetic variation have in general been found in those species.We developed specific
microsatellites loci, and the usefulness of 8 of them was investigated by measuring inter- and intraspecific genetic
diversity between two samples (n=30-50) of each of the four species. Results confirmed the high polymorphism of
these markers with a mean of 32 alleles per locus, and high overall heterozygosity from 0.65 to 0.82. Exact tests
revealed highly significant differences in alleles frequencies among species at all loci. Unique alleles or alleles size
ranges observed in a given species were absent or found at very low frequencies in the others. This resulted into a
highly significant interspecific genetic variance (up to 49%). At the intraspecific level, significant differences in allele
frequencies were obsen/ed between samples in all species. However, they translated into very small levels of
divergence.These results will be discussed in the context of both the evolutionary history and the management of
this species complex.

A mtDNA and microsatellite assessment of single vs multiple origins of landlocked Atlantic salmon (Salmo
salar L.) from Lake St-Jean, Quebec, (Canada). N. Tessier and L. Bematchez, Universite Laval, dept, biologie,
Ste-Foy, Quebec, G1K 7P4.
We r^orted inter-population genetic divergence among landlocked salmon associated with distinct tributaries in
Lake St-Jean. The erdent of differentiation between one of these populations from the others was more important
than that reported among any anadromous populations. Two alternative hypotheses may potentially explain these
observations: the lake was postglacially recolonized by a single founding population and subsequent founder events

Phoxinux eos-neogaeus are all-female fish from the northern United States and southemCanada that reproduce by
gynogenesis, a form of clonal reproduction. These fish were formed by hybridization between a female of Phoxinus
neogaeus and a male of Phoxinus eos; they express one enzyme allele (allozyme) of P. eos and one allozyme of

Application of M-FiSH to fish chromosomes. R.B. Phillips and K.M. Reed, Department of Biological Sciences,
University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, Wl USA.
Multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (M-FISH) is a new technique which allows localization of multiple DNA
probes on chromosomes from a single metaphase. We have used this technique to localize different families of
repetitive sequences to the chromosomes of zebrafish (Danio rerio) and several species of salmonid fishes including
rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush). Chromosome preparations were
obtained from a diploid cell line of zebrafish and from cultured blood of the salmonid species. Cloned probes were
labeled with either Spectnjm Organe or Spectrum Green using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and slides were
counterstained with DAPI. Images were captured with a CCD camera and analyzed with QUIPS software (Vysis,
Inc.). Different families and sub-families of repetitive DNAs were localized at different centromeric, subcentromeric,
and subtelomeric locations in each species. These probes will be useful for Identification of fish chromosomes in
gene localization experiments using M-FISH.

Preliminary Investigation of microsatellite loci in red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) in the northern Gulf
of Mexico. E.J. Heist and J.R. Gold, Department of Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences, Center for Biosystematics and
Biodiversity, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX USA.

Toward the phylogeny of the family Lacertidae: implications from mitochondrial DNA 12S, 16S and COI gene
sequences (Reptilia: Squamata). JJEu, Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum,
100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario, Canada M5S2C6.
A phylogeny of the family Lacertidae was derived from mtDNA gene sequence data. Thirty-two species, representing
22 currently recognized genera and subgenera, were included in the analysis. A total of 3,600 base pairs was
obtained and aligned from 12S, 16S and COI gene sequences. A preferred tree was selected based on weighted
parsimony and functional ingroup and outgroup analyses. Decay analysis, bootstrap and permutation tail probability
were used to evaluate support for the recovered nodes. The genus Gallotia was resolved as the basal taxon and the
sister group of all remaining lacertids. Takydromus branched off next. All African lacertids grouped together, and
formed a monophyletic clade with the Eurasian genera Eremias and Ophisops. The remaining Eurasian lacertids
sequentially branched off near the base of the tree in a 'comb-like* fashion. The basal position of Gallotia and ths
monophyly of African lacertids are consistent with previous hypotheses. The European-origin hypothesis of lacertids
is favored, and the distribution of lacertids in Africa is likely a dispersal event.

Snake vertebrae do the twist. B.R. Moon. Dept Biology, Univ. Michigan, Ann Arbor Ml 48109, USA.

The zygosphene-zygantrum articulations of snake vertebrae are hypothesized to restrict or eliminate vertebral
torsion. This hypothesis is apparently based solely on the inference of function from structure, despite contradictory
evidence. Gasc (1974, Mem. Mus. Nat. Hist. Nat., Paris Ser. A Zool. 83:1-182) measured vertebral torsion of 1-
2°/joint in dried P^hon skeletons, but his results are seldom cited. I observed axial torsion during lateral undulation
and feeding in Pituophis melanoleucus. To determine whether apparent axial torsion results from differential
movement of the left and right body walls, combined lateral and vertical bending, or actual torsion at the vertebral
joints, I examined close-up video images of crawling P. melanoleucus and digitized macro video images of torsion in
fresh sections of the trunk. To measure vertebral torsion, I clamped sections of 10 vertebrae at one end and twisted
the free end by hand; the limits of twisting were clearly detectable and were reached before the movement produced
any axial bending. Freely crawling P. melanoleucus exhibited negligible lifting, moderate differential movement of
the left and right body walls, and apparent torsion of 0.02-2.4'’/vertebra. Fresh trunk sections allowed actual torsion
of 0.3-1.1’/vertebra, which produced substantial overall torsion when added over several vertebrae. Therefore, the
observed torsion was likely produced by differential movement of the left and right body walls combined with real
torsion at the vertebral joints. Despite the mechanical restrictions imposed by the complex articulations, vertebral
torsion occurs in snakes and appears to be functionally important in many kinds of snake movements.

Evolution of germ-cell determining genes in amphibians. M.E. White and B.l. Crother. Department of Biology,
Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402; A.D. Johnson, Rorida State University, Dept, of Biology,
Tallahassee, FL 32306.
Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates.
Although much of the early development of all amphibians is very similar, frogs and salamanders differ strikingly in
the way they determine the germ cell lineage (the cells that will form eggs and sperm). The pattern observed in frogs
is quite different than the one seen in other vertebrates; the salamander mechanism is apparently much more similar
to that of birds and mammals. Although the pattern of germ cell formation has been elucidated in a wide variety of
species, little is known about the genes governing this process. Because most major embryological events are
controlled by genes that have been highly conserved evolutionarily, it is logical to conclude that genes involved in
germ cell determination will also be similar in a wide variety of species. Three genes- daz, oct-3/4 and vasa- have
been shown to be critical for germ cell determination in mammals. We have used phylogenetic methods to analyze
the homologous genes from frogs and salamanders to investigate whether the evolution of germ cell specific genes
reflects the mode of germ cell determination (salamanders being more similar to mammals) or the phylogenetic
relationships of the organisms (salamanders and frogs being more closely related). Our preliminary results suggest
that germ cell determining genes from two different salamanders are more closely related to the mammalian
homologues than to anuran ones, supporting the idea that the evolution of the genes tracks the mode of cell
determination rather than the anlm^ phylogeny.

Impacts of Bufo boreas anti Bana lutalventrla tadpoles on algae and snails In ponds of Yellowstone National
Park. W.E. Roberts. Mountain Research Center. P.O. Box 173490, Montana State University. Bozeman, MT 59717.

  Decline in frog and tadpole populations may alter trophic structures and ecosystems. During summer 1997 I
investigated impacts of tadpole populations on food webs in ponds of Yellowstone National Park. The field
component of this project involved two phases - experimental manipulations in enclosures and landscape-level
comparison of unmanipulated ponds with and without tadpoles. In separate experiments, I stocked three blocks of

biomass. Results of the two phases of this projed suggest that enclosures accurately mimicked conditions in whole
ponds, and that tadpole grazing had a complex influence on algal biomass, rather than a direct negative impact.

Seasonal variation in hatchling sex ratios of Chrysemys picta from eggs incubated near a pivotal
temperature. R.M. Bowden. M.A. Ewerf and C.E. Nelson, Dept of Biology, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN
47405 USA.
Seasonal variation in sex ratio is well documented for many species of turtles, and is largely attributable to a
seasonal increase in temperature. In contrast, we found a seasonal decrease in the proportion of males for
Chrysemys picta even though all of the eggs were incubated at or near the pivotal temperature. This trend occured in
each of the four years examined and at each of up to three sites per year. Although this trend was not always
significant for the individual samples, it was significant (p = 0.005) when the years and sites were combined. If this
trend were due to a minor systematic shift in incubator temperature, the lower proportions of males should have been
associated with a decrease in incubation time (laying to hatching) as both incubation time and proportion of males
decrease with increasing temperature. However, the sex ratio of the individual clutches was not significantly
associated with incubation time in either the site or individual year samples, nor in the samples combined (p = 0.84).
The slight trend for all samples combined was toward more (not fewer) males with no change in incubation times (p =
0.83). The seasonal shift in sex ratio here thus appears to be independent of temperature.
