The evolution of herbivory in modern fishes. R. Winterbottom. Department of Zoology, University of Toronto &,
CBCB, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queens Park, Toronto, Ontario; F. Santini, Department of Zoology, University of
Toronto &, CBCB, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queens Park, Toronto, Ontario.
Herbivory is a derived feeding characteristic that has evolved independently several times in all the major phyla and
classes of metazoans. Bony fishes are no exceptions to this. In fact herbivory might have evolved up to 7 times
independently in the percomorph fishes in a very short span of time at the beginning of the Cenozoic era and another
time in the Ostariophysans. Given the fact that herbivory has evolved in lineages that used to have different trophic
habits, and that it is performed in different ways, it is hypothesized that there has been a physiological preadaptation
that has allowed the evolution of this new feeding strategy. The available data are presented and discussed. In
additions, the evolution of herbivory is strongly connected to the evolution of modem coral reefs. The implications of
tttis association are also discussed.

Biomass vs. abundance measures of variation In stream fish community structure. KA. Chandler, D.M.
McElroy and R.D. Hoyt, Department of Biology. Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green , Kentucky 42101
USA; D. Stites, Department of Agriculture, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, Kentucky 42101 USA.

Both biomass and abundance data are commonly utilized in characterization of ecological system dynamics:
however, questions exist as to which approach is best-suited for long-tenn studies. While potentially providing more
information than abundance data, biomass sampling may be irxrre detrimental to ecosystem stability. We examined
this trade-off by comparing results derived from abundance and biomass indicators in ichthyofaunal samples from
Buck Creek, an Order III tributary of Drakes Creek in southcentral Kentucky, collected twice yearly from Fall 1992 to
Spring 1996. Principal components analysis was used to summarize patterns of spatial and temporal variation
among samples for both biomass and abundance data. Correlations in patterns of loadings on corresponding PC
axes were used to compare the two approaches. PCI-Ill from the biomass data accounted for 59.1 % of the total
variation; eigenvalues for each axis were comparable to those obtained from abundance data. Both biomass and
abundance measures suggested season, station and year effects on community structure; however, taxa driving
seasonal differences in biomass were responsible for station differences in abundance, and vice-versa. These
contrasting patterns suggest a potentially complex life history patterns in species within this community. Mors
importantly, our results indicate that different sampling strategies may lead to qualitatively distinct impressions of
community dynamics.

Hatching success of Bog Turtle (Clemmys muhlenbergO} eggs in a Pennsylvania population under natural
and laboratory conditions. R.T. Zappalorti. M.E. Torocco and P.J. Drake, Herpetological Associates, Inc, Plant
and Wildlife Consultants,, 536 Seaman Avenue, Beachwood, New Jersey 08722 - USA.,,.
The hatching success of bog turtle (Clemmys muhlenbergO) eggs from a single population was examined at a site in
eastern Pennsylvania. Between 1993 and 1994 we compared naturally incubated hatching success with artificially
incubated eggs. Bog turtles lay their eggs in various types of Carex grass tussocks within their marshy habitat. In
1993,17 eggs in four clutches (four separate nest locations) were discovered. Seven eggs (two clutches) from two
separate nests were left in the field to incubate naturally. Eggs were hatched in the laboratory at ambient cycling
temperatures between 32.5 °C. during the day and 19.0 °C. at night (Mean 25.5 °C.}. Of the seven eggs, 3 hatched
(42.8%) and 4 (57.2%) were removed by an unknown predator prior to hatching, whereas 90% of the 10 eggs
incubated in the laboratory hatched successfully with only one infertile egg. In 1994, seven nests containing 10
clutches (33 eggs) were discovered. Twenty-one eggs at seven nests were left in the field and 12 were removed to
ths laboratory. All eggs removed from the field in 1994 were replaced with exact-size paraffin wax eggs. Ten
(47.6%) of the real eggs left in the field were removed from the nests by a predator (possibly a small mammal), two
(9.5%) were broken (presumably by another nesting female at the same site), and three (14.3%) failed to hatch. In
addition, four of the wax eggs were removed by a predator. All of the eggs incubated in the laboratory hatched
(100%). The results of this study suggests that predation on eggs by an unknown small mammal is a contributing
source of mortality at this colony. Natural hatching success may also be reduced by infertility and poorly understood
developmental problems.

Neuroecology of elasmobranch fishes:           Relating the brain to the real world.     T.C.Tricas, Department of
Biological Saences, Florida Institute of Technology, 150 W. University Blvd., Melbourne, FL 32901-6988 USA.
Ethological studies on elasmobranch fishes have attempted to explain the adaptive value of specific behaviors. For
example, laboratory studies have characterized the taxis responses duritig orientation to acoustic, olfactory, electric
and visual stimuli. These studies complement field research that describes the motor patterns involved^ in natural
behaviors such as reproductive interactions and feeding. Although lab and field studies have provided good
descriptions of behavioral motor patterns, relatively little infonnation is obtained on how sensory and central
processing systems initiate and form these often complex behaviors. The ampullary electrosense of the
elasmobranch is presented as a model system in which the peripheral morphology, neural response prrpperties and
central neuroanatomy can be interpreted in relation to the ecological factors that shape their behavior^. Vector
analysis of the peripheral organization of the ampullary canal system and neural response properties provide useful
tools for predicting different ecological functions for the ampullary clusters. Chronic recording of electrosensory
neurons in the alert swimming animal permit integration of neural activity with motor behavior. The mechanisms by
which sensory input and central processing shape elasmobranch behavior can bo better understood when
interpreted in relation to the natural ecology of each species.

Orientation and navigation in elasmobranchs: Which way forward? J.C. Montgomery and M.M. Walker, School
of Biological Sciences, University of Auckland, Auckland New Zealand.
Elasmobranchs possess a multiplicity of mechanisms controlling posture and short distance orientation. Vestibular
contributions to posture and locomotion are well documented. So too, are the contnljutions of vision, olfaction and
the octavolateralis senses to short distance orientation, particularly orientation to specific environmental stimuli such
as those generated by prey. Less well understood are the mechanisms guiding orientation over longer distances.
Anecdotal and systematic observations of behavior show tidal, daily, repeat long distance, and even seasonal
movement patterns. Tnje bi-coordinafe navigation has not been demonstrated in elasmobranchs. The mechanisms
underlying the above movement patterns are largely speculative, however, they are likely to include responses water
currents, physical parameters such as temperature and pressure, and the geomagnetic field. Of particular interest in
elasmobranchs is that geomagnetic orientation could be mediated directly via a magnetite based sensory system, or
indirectly via ttie electrosensory system. Systematic studies of movement patterns, and experimental studies of the
underlying mechanisms of orientation are required to gain an understanding of orientation and navigation in this
intriguing group.

Elasmobranch behavioral ecology: oxymoron or opportunity? W.R. Strong. Dept, of Evolution, Ecology and
Marine Biology, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106-9610, USA.
Behaviorally and ecologically, sharks and their allies exhibit remarkable diversity. Over the past several decades,
Don Nelson and his contemporaries made enormous progress in the understanding of shark behavior. The vexing
task of relating this behavior to species and community ecology now stands in plain view. The study of behavioral
ecology can, in the broad sense, be construed to include almost anything the animal does within the context of its
environment. As a discipline, however, behavioral ecology has specific stated goals, principally to understand the
evolution of animal behaviors. Sharks in general are not well suited to these goals. As a result, empirical work is
often limited to descriptions of life history, distribution and abundance and basic investigations of morphological and
behavioral adaptations. Critically assessing how the latter affect survivorship and fitness is a formidable task, one
that largely remains in the domain of those who study teleosts, birds, etc. Nonetheless, elasmobranchs possess a
number of unique traits. And given their long-held positions as apex predators of the world ocean, much work
remains to be done in the area of predation. Understanding sharks' roles in the ecosystems they inhabit is central to
species management and, ultimately, to the "holy grail" of successful, system-wide management.

Tagging programs provide valuable means to Increase our biological understanding of sharks and to obtain
information for rational resource management. Shark tagging programs throughout the wortd have been directed

Physiological telemetry of elasmobranchs: taking the laboratory to the field. C.G. Lowe. Hawaii Institute of
Marino Biology, PO Box 1346, Kaneohe, HI 96744, USA; K.J. Goldman, VIMS Fisheries Dept., PO Box 1346,
Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA.
 Physiological telemetry is a powerful tool in studying elasmobranchs in the laboratory and field. Controlled
laboratory studies of the physiology of elasmobranchs has increased our understanding of the behavior, life history,
and ecology of many species. However, extrapolating results from laboratory studies alone may misrepresent these
biological aspects of animals in the field. Additionally, some elasmobranchs are too large, logistically difficult to
maintain, or have low survivorship in captivity making them extremely hard to study in the laboratory. Physiological
telemetry offers a bridge between the laboratory and the field providing an opportunity to elucidate similarities and
differences. Previous studies have coupled a variety of sensors to acoustic transmitters to remotely relay information
on swimming speed, tailbeat fr^uency, muscle contraction rate, heart rate, muscle, cranial and stomach
temperature, and neural activity. These techniques have been used on elasmobranchs ranging from stingrays to
white sharks, but have been restricted by the size of the electronic components, attachment methods, or logistical
difficulties in conducting long-term tracks. Recent developments in sensor technology and miniaturization of
electronics have increased the diversity and applications of physiological telemetry. Acoustic modem and satellite
telemetry may offer a means of downloading archived data collected from animals in the field.

The energetics of calling in frogs. K.D. Wells. Dept of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut,
Storrs, CT 06269-3043.
The investigation of calling energetics in frogs provides an opportunity to integrate studies of behavioral performance
with whole animal physiology, muscle structure, and muscle biochemistry. Measurements of oxygen consumption by
calling males have shown that metabolic rates increase by up to 25 times resting rats. Structural features of the
trunk muscles that provide the power for call production, including mitochondrial density, capillary density, and
abundance of lipid reserves, are all positively correlated with calling rate. Activities of enzymes that are important in
aerobic metabolism and fatty acid metabolism are much higher in species with high calling rates than in those with
low calling rates. Pairwise comparisons of dosely-related species show the same pattern: those with high calling
rates have muscles that can sustain higher levels of call production than do those with low calling rates. Patterns of
energy substrate use reflect patterns of call production. Species with high calling rates depend more heavily on
stored lipids for call production than do species with low calling rates, and species with short breeding seasons
deplete their energy resenres more rapidly than do those with prolonged breeding seasons and long chorus

Auditory Tuning and Phonotactic Preferences in Anurans.               H.C. Gerhardt. Division of Biological Sciences,
University of Missouri, Columbia, MO 65211 USA.
Advertisement calls of anurans usually have one or two emphasized frequency bands, which match fairly well with
the maximum frequency sensitivity of one or the other, or both, of the two auditory organs, the basilar and amphibian
papillae. At a finer scale of analysis, however, mismatches often occur between their mean frequency of conspecific
calls in a species or population and the maximum frequency sensitivity of the auditory system. Such discrepancies
could be a mechanistic basis for sexual selection, but the question arises: How well do the usual threshold measures
of frequency sensitivify reflect frequency selectivity at the much higher signal levels at which anurans normally
communicate? Although threshold measures and frequency preferences estimated from the same individuals
correlate poorly with respect to small, but behaviorally effective, differences within a single frequency band, such
estimates do predict reliably which of the two frequency bands is preferred by females in species that have calls with
bimodal spectra. In some of these, thresholds determined centrally and preferences correlate well with estimates of
frequency sensitivity ar ther peripheral level, but this is not true of other species. Examples from behavioral and
neurophysiological studies of several species of treefrogs will be discussed.   181            _________ 14:30 Saturday_______                              14
Acoustic communication and neural processing in the Pacific treefrog. E A. Brenowitz, Depts. Psychology and
Zoology Univ of Washington, Seattle WA 98195 USA; G.J. Rose and T.B. Alder, Dept, of Biology, University of
Utah, Salt Lake City UT 84112 USA.
Male Pacific treefrogs, Hyla regilla, use advertisement and encounter calls to regulate inter-male spacing within
breeding chonjses. Encounter calls are produced when the advertisement calls of a neighbor exceed a threshold
amplitude. These aggressive thresholds are plastic; i.e. males resume advertisemenl.calling (areommodate) to
repeated presentation of advertisement calls at amplitudes 4 dB above their aggressive threshold. Correspondingly,
a male’s aggressive threshold for the advertisement call is positively correlated with the maxirnurn amplitude of
advertisement calls of neighbors, measured at the focal male's position. The aggressive thresholds of males for the
encounter call also are plastic but are not significantly correlated with the maximum call amplitude of their neighbore.
This disjunction stems from the fact that males in stable choruses are not exposed to supra-threshoW encounter
calls Accommodation to one call type fails to significantly alter a male’s aggressive threshold to the other call type.
Plasticity of aggressive thresholds, like plasticity of aggressive signalling, appears to be important in balancing the
costs and benefits of aggressive behavior.                                             .     ,,       . .. .
The capacity of males to selectively accommodate to the advertisement or encounter call supports the hypothesis
that these two call types are processed, in part, by discrete neural 'channels'. Because these two call types are
hlohly similar spectrally, selective accommodation cannot result from sensory adaptation in the penphery. ine two
c^l types however, differ markedly in their temporal structure, particularly their pulse repetition rate. These
obseivatio'ns support the notion that separate temporal filters exist in the central nervous system for processing
these two call types. Recent neurophysiological studies have provided insight into the mechanisms that underlie this
temper^ pattern recognition and discrimination.

405 Hilgard Avenue,, Los Angeels, CA 90095 USA.
Ectothermy is the norm among animals. It is known that aspects of both acoustic signal production and reception in
ectotherms are temperature-dependent. Since female preference in some ectothe^s is also temperature­
dependent, understanding the genesis of this dependence in detail becomes cruaal. The inner ear of ariurans is
unique in that it contains three organs which are specialized for sound reception. The amphibian papula (AH), the
basilar papilla (BP) and the saccule (S) are anatomically distinct, spatially-separate organs each with its own

The western hognose snake {Heterodon nasicus) has been separated into three subspecies (H. n. nasicus, H. n.

Traditional studies of snake systematics emphasize univariate variation in some characters, and often ignore
multivariate differentiation.   I utilized discriminant function analysis to examine multivariate morphometric
differentiation in head shape among four putative subspecies of Ninia sebae, a small semi-fossorial colubrid snake
found at intermediate elevations in Central America. Linear discriminant function analysis can be used only if
covariance matrices are the same amongst groups. If this assumption is not met, then quadratic discriminant
fonction analysis can be used, however, this test is less powerful. Techniques which compare the structure of
covariance matrices can be used to construct matrices constrained by commonality of matrix components, which
may then be used in linear discriminant function analysis to more powerfully lest a hypothesis. Using these
methods, I found that the described subspecies of Ninia sebae are not well differentiated. The species appears to
consist of two distinctive subspecies, with one wide-ranging group spread throughout southern Mexico southwards to
Costa Rica, and another narrowly confined to the Pacific versant of southern Mexico and Guatemala, isolated by the

As currently recognized, the Yarrow's Spiny Lizard (Sceloporus jairovii complex) exhibits amazing intraspecific
variation in male dorsal coloration, such that the range of basic colors among populations is nearly as great as that
among all reptiles (e.g.,. green, black, red, blue, yellow, gray, brown). In this study, we use phylogenetic methods to

and consists of at least four evolutionary species, (2) striking color variation exists both within and between the
evolutionary species currently referred to S. jarrovii, (3) most of the conspicuous male color morphs seem to have
evolved independently from relatively dull colored monochromatic ancestors, and the blue color morph has evolved
twice.

Trematode parasitism of the Canadian red-sided garter snake {Thamnqphls sirtalls parletalis): A study in
prevalence and Intensity. D.R. Kelly and R.W. Krohmer, Science Department, Saint Xavier University, 3700 West
103 Street, Chicago, Illinois 60655 USA.
One-hundred and ninety-four Canadian red-sided garter snakes were collected from the Interiake region north of
Winnipeg, Manitoba, over a two year period, in the spring and fall seasons of 1996 and 1997. This snake is host to a
lung inhabiting digenetic trematode of the family Pfagiorchiidae. The infection is acquired by the comsumption of
tadpoles and frogs. These intermediate hosts harbor the metacercarial cysts that may further develop into mature,
egg producing adults, when consumed. It has been reported that the minimum time requirement for the appearance
of an adult trematode in the lung is greater than eight weeks. All snakes examined for trematode infection were
preserved, measured for length, and gender determined. The adult trematodes were counted and removed, with their
locations being recorded. The data were used to evaluate ths prevalence (percent rate of infection) and intensity
(number of parasites per host). The prevalence of the trematode infection was higher in females (35%) than in males
(15%). The mean intensity was also higher in females (10+2, range: 1-65) than in males (5+1, range: 1-13). No
significant correlation between intensity and snout-vent length was found in either sex. However, there is evidence to
suggest that prevalence increses with snout-vent length. A group of long term captive (> 12 weeks) snakes were
compared to the sample of wild snakes. There were no significant differences in the mean intensities of the wild and
long-term captive animals. However, the prevalence in the females increased from 35% to 53% and increased in
males from 15% to 30%.

Fisheries Science Center, NMFS, NOAA, Hatfield Marine Science Center, Newport, Oregon 97365 USA.
Under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark photoperiod, juvenile walleye pollock displayed a diurnal schooling and activity
pattern, characterized by cohesive shoaling during the day, with a cessation of shoaling and decreased swimming
speeds at night. Juvenile walleye pollock were not characterized by a distinct light threshold for shoaling; shoals
gradually dispersed as light levels decreased and gradually recoalesced as light levels increased. At light levels
below 2.8x10 ° mEs 'm’^ juvenile walleye pollock were so dispersed as to no longer constitute a shoal.
Exposure to simulated predation had differing effects upon fish behavior under light and dark conditions. Brief
exposure to a model predator in the dark, caused fish to swim faster than fish which had been exposed in the light.
Chronic exposure to a living predator produced similar results; fish tended to swim slower when a predator was
present in the light, but faster when a predator was present in the dark. In the light, predation can result in cohesive
shoals, but in the dark. Increased activity may accelerate shoal dispersal, suggesting that perceived predation risk
has opposite effects upon the spatial distribution of shoaling fish under light and dark conditions.   205                       , 13:30 Saturday                                CF3                                AXL

The estuarine artenmlnimum: evidence from the lower Chesapeake Bay. C.M. Wagner. College of William &
Mary, School of Marine Science, P.O. Box 1346, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA.

The dramatic biological, chemical, and physical changes in the low salinity habitats of estuaries are thought to limit
the number of resident faunal taxa. Remane (1934) first described this phenomena, a species minimum occurring
near oligohaline salinities (5-8 %»), from invertebrate assemblages of large stable brackish lakes. It has since been
proffered as a general feature of the estuarine gradient, though examples from the primary literature are rare. Two
possible complications to the location of this pattern in estuarine fishes are: (1) the large number of seasonal
migratory species who exhibit changing salinity preferences with ontogeny; and, (2) ths failure to standardize species
richness estimates to a measure of sample size (i.e., rarefaction). I applied rarefaction techniques to seine and trawl
survey data to investigate whether this phenomena is evident in fish assemblages from three tributaries of the lower
Chesapeake Bay. Results of the analysis indicate a minimum can occur, and is most evident in systems with a
physically long salinity gradient. Beta diversity calculations confirmed the region of highest species turnover was
displacer] upstream from the minimum (near 0-2 %e), and coincides with the most severe changes in ionic ratios.
Hence, distance to source pools of marine and freshwater taxa appears to interact with salinity preferences to
establish ths minimum. Excursions from most favorable habitats by a highly mobile species appears spatially similar
to recnjitment survival in sessile invertebrates, and may explain the similarity in pattern between the two groups.

Sciences, University of Auckland; C. Thornbum, Kelly Tarlton's Underwater World, Auckland.
Elasmobranchs have some sophisticated feeding strategies, ranging from tail clipping bill-fishes, to locating
concentrations of patchily distributed prey. These strategies are underpinned by an equally sophisticated array of
sensory systems. To fake one example, many rays feed on buried bivalves, and dig where the prey densities are
high (Hine ef al. 1997). Behavioral studies (Montgomery and Skipworth, 1997) illustrate the potential importance of
mechanosensory systems in this feeding behavior. Both mechanosensory and electrosensory systems share a high
level of sensitivity, to the extent that behaviorally relevant inputs could be swamped by self-generated noise. One
interesting aspect of the sensory biology of elasmobranchs is that hindbrain signal processing effectively resolves
this problem (Montgomeryand Bodnzick, 1994).

Selective foraging behaviour of basking sharks on zooplankton in tidal fronts. D.W. Sims and V.A. Quayle,
Department of Biological Sciences, University of Plymouth. Drake Circus. Plymouth. PL4 8AA. U.K.
 Individual and grouped basking sharks {Cetorhinus maximus} filter-feeding on zooplankton at the water's surface
were tracked visually together with zooplankton sampling from their feeding paths. Along tidal slicks they exhibited
area-restricted searching behaviour and actively selected areas containing high densities of large zooplankton
above a threshold level. Basking sharks remainerf in the most profitable patches transported by tidal currents for up
to 27h and moved between patches over 24-48h periods. Between years, the location of shark foraging areas
changed according to ths effects of prevailing weather conditions on frontal boundary sharpness and the
maintenance of frontal upwellings. Our results snow that basking sharks are selective filter-feeders on specific
zooplankton assemblages and therefore useful as biological indicators of abundance trends in zooplankton species
influenced by climatic fluctuations of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO).

Evolutionary Innovations in the feeding mechanism of elasmobranchs. C.D. Wilga. Department of Ecology and
Evolutionary Biology. University of California. In/ine. Irvine. CA 92697 USA; P.C. Wainwright, Department of
Biological Science, , Florida State Univeristy, Tallahassee, FL 32306 USA; P.J. Motta, Department of Biology,
University of South Florida, 4202 Fowler Ave., Tampa. FL 33620 USA.
A major conclusion from comparative studies of feeding mechanisms in lower vertebrates is that some of the
biomechanical couplings involved in mouth opening have been retained throughout evolution. However, recent
studies of the jaw mechanism indicate that elasmobranchs differ from other lower vertebrates in that the
geniohyoideus coupling is the primary mechanism for lower jaw depression rather than the rectus cervicus coupling.
In addition, previous studies of the feeding mechanism in lower vertebrates indicate that structural differences among
taxa may arise by the addition of a novel stnrcture or as a result of modification of the existing musculoskeletal
apparatus. Accompanying such changes, the ancestral motor pattern may be retained or the timing of motor activity
may be altered. Evolutionary innovations in the musculoskeletal apparatus mediating upper jaw protrusion in
elasmobranchs has involved both the addition of a novel feature, the dorsal preorbitalis coupling, and by the
modification of an existing structure, the levator palatoquadrafi coupling, while retaining the ancestral system, the
ventral preorbitalis coupling. These changes in the musculoskeletal apparatus have Involved conservation of the
motor pattern in the ancestral mechanism and alteration of the motor pattern in the modified mechanism.

Suction feeding in sharks: a kinematic analysis of feeding in the nurse shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum. PJ._
Motta. University of South Florida, 4202 East Fowler Ave., Tampa, Florida, 33620 U.S A.
Despite relatively simple feeding mechanisms, sharks exhibit a variety of feeding types. Ancestral cladodont sharks
presumably grasped and possibly swallowed their prey whole. Modern sharfe have radiated to include biting,
gouging and biting, ram-feeding, suction-feeding, filter-feeding, and crushing types. Convergence and specialization
for suction feeding have arisen in a variety of divergent extant taxa. The orectolobiform nurse shark, Ginglymostoma
diratum, is a specialized and apparently obligate suction feeder. Kinematic analysis from high speed video of five
sharks reveals a conservative feeding sequence involving mandible depression and labial cartilage protrusion,
followed by mandible elevation and labial cartilage retraction. The expansive anti compressive phases are very rapid,
with a mean duration of 92 ms. Similar to other elasmobranchs, there is significant variability among sharks in nine
kinematic variables. Within sharks, bite durations are very constant as the sharks become satiated. The suction
feeding nurse shark differs from ram feeding carcharhinid sharks by its short and relatively constant durations of
mouth expansion, minimal contribution of palatoquadrate protrusron and cranial elevation, reduced dentition,
formation of a laterally enclosed and anteriorly directed mouth, and hypertrophied abductor muscles. Continuing
studies seek functional and evolutionary patterns in shark feeding.

specific attributes of the prey item Sharks are generally presumed to be highly visual predators and, thus, it is

investigated the effect of both prey size and elusivify on prey capture kinematics in a species with a more
generalized diet, the leopard shark, Triakis semitasciata. Sharks were filmed using high speed video feeding on two
sizes of ths same prey (shrimp pieces) and two mors elusive prey (earthworms and live mud shrimp). In leopard
sharks, size effects were noted for kinematic parameters related to buccal cavity expansion. Elusivity effects were
not detected for any parameters, but a performance consequence was also not detected with increasingly elusive
prey. These studies cumulatively suggest that rather than possessing a single attack behavior, generalists are
capable of kinematic modulation. They also suggest that the phrase ‘master of none* that is typically used to

A review of the South African literature over ths last decade shows that more than 20 papers have been published

data collection in ths wild, thereby augmenting direct obsenrations. This promising area of research has the potential
to clarify details of behaviour and feeding ecology that otherwise would be unobtainable.

Dietary changes associated with life history and sex for the sevengill shark: Implications for Intraspecific
comp^ition and resource partitioning. D.A. Ebert. US Abalone, P.O. Box 254, Davenport, CA. 95017, USA.

Dietary changes associated with life history stage and sex for the sevengill shark are analysized and discussed. Data
collected over a 15 year period were used to analyze ths sevengill shark's dietary habits. The size categories were
grouped so as to approximate this shark's life history stage; juvenile, adolescent, and adult. In addition, the diet of
male and female sharks of each life history stage was compared to note any differences between the sexes. Dietary
changes associated with an elasmobranchs life history and sexual stage of development may explain how food
resources within a given territory are partitioned such that competiton between conspecifics at different stages of life
may be reduced. A reduction in competition between conspecifics may have evolved to ensure that resource
partitioning and cannibalism would be reduced between conspecifics at different stages of life. Thus increasing
survivorship for the species during the critical early stages of life. The implications of dietary changes as related to
life history and sexual stage of development may be complex and far reaching, yet may play a critical role in the
success of elasmobranchs as a group.

Tapeworms as Indicators of elasmobranch feeding biology. J.N. Caira. Department of Ecology and Evolutionary
Biology, Univeisity of, Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA.
Tapeworms are potentially valuable indicators of elasmobranch feeding biology because their life cycles require
more than one host species and transmission between these host species is accomplished through predation. Thus,
tapeworms enter their elasmobranch hosts when the intermediate hosts in which they reside as lanrae are consumed
by elasmobranchs. The lack of life cycle data and lack of infonnation on degree of specificity for their final
Intermediate hosts currently limits the specific predictive value of tapeworms. However, some generalizations can be
made from the complete tapeworm assemblage observed in a host. Inconsistencies in the tapeworm assemblages
of related elasmobranch species can provide indirect evidence of differences in food habit. For example, the
tapeworms of megamouth are fully consistent with this shark's status as a filter feeder rather than an apex predator.
Changes in the tapeworm fauna of a host species over time may reflect age related changes in diet. For example,
the differences in the tapeworm fauna between small and large individuals of the Atlantic nurse shark may be
indicative of a shift in food habit. Depending on their specificity tor their intermediate hosts, tapeworms may act as
indicators of specific prey species consumed by a host species or Individuals.

Standardized diet compositions and trophic levels of sharks. E. Cortes. Institute for Fishery Resource Ecology,
National Marine Rsheries Service/Florida State University, 3500 Delwood Beach Road, Panama City, FL 32408,
USA.
Sharks are marine consumers believed to occupy top positions in marine food webs. But surprisingly few
quantitativo estimates of trophic levels (TL) exist for this group. With the hope to better define the ecological role of
sharks in marine communities, this paper presents standardized diet compositions and trophic levels for a suite of
species. Dietary compositions were calculated from published quantitative studies using a weighted average index.
TL values of the eleven food types used to characterize the diet were obtained from published accounts and used to
calculate fractional trophic levels for 151 species representing seven orders and 21 families. Sharks as a group are
tertiary consumers (TL>4), and significant differences were found among six orders compared, attributable mainly to
differences between orectolobiformes and all other orders. Among four families of carcharhiniform sharks,
carcharhinids had significantly higher TL than triakids and scyliorhinids, but not sphymids. When compared to TL for
other top predators of marine communities obtained from the literature, mean TL for sharks was significantly higher
than for seabirds, but not for marine mammals. Trophic level and body size were positively correrated, with the fit
increasing when the three predominantly planktivorous species were omitted and when considering carcharhinids
only.

Review of rate of consumption, food transit and digestive efficiency in sharks.              B.M. Wetherbee. Zoology
Department, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, HI, USA.
Sharks are important apex consumers In the marine environment and quantification of energy flow through sharks is
important for understanding their impact in marine ecosystems. However, there have been relatively few studies on
rates of consumption (daily ration) in sharks and it is difficult to generalize about the role of sharte in the flow of
energy in an ecosystem. Estimates of the daily ration of sharks generally either incorporate data on the duration and
rate of food emptying from the stomach and field observations on prey items ingested, or involve bioenergetic
models based on a balanced energy budget. Several factors that may influence rates of consumption are poorly
understood in elasmobranchs. There have been few studies on the efficiency of food digestion, absorption and
conversion to growth, and the passage of food through the digestive tract, despite the importance of these factors on
energy flow through the trophic level occupied by sharks. This study reviews the current state of knowledge on rates
of consumption, rates of food transit through the stomach and entire digestive tract, and the efficiency with which
ingested food is converted to energy stored as growth in sharks.5K6.

levels In this paper we summarize the feeding habits of the spiny dogfish in B.C. waters analyzing several data sets
collected during the 197O's and 198O's. and comparing them to published literature. In particular, we examine the
spatial and temporal variability in dogfish feeding habits and discuss the importance of recognizing bias when
attempting to estimate consumption rates of dogfish prey.

reproduction. Many aspects of communication are dependent on, influen^d by, hormones associated with
reproductive state. Less clearly appreciated is the fact that communication signals influence hormonal state in a

testes and changes in testes histology compared to control animals. In frogs, therefore, vocal communication signals
trigger changes in reproductive physiology as well as reproductive behavior.

comparing diploid, triploid and tetrjqiloid green toads on the basis of morphometrical and acoustical parameters.

attention is given to their differences. Diplcrid toads show signficantly larger body size and proportionally larger head

Testing morphometric theories on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses: examples from characid and
atherinopsid fishes. B. Chemoff. Department of Zoology Field Museum Roosevelt Rd. at Lakeshore Drive
Chicago, IL 60605 USA.
The diversity of sizes and shapes within and among groups of fishes is one of the principal features of their
evolutionary history. To understand as much as possible about the history of size and shape evolution, two
important components must be explored: phylogeny and environment. The evolution of size and shape have often
been discussed in the context of development^ theories involving differential growth (allometry), differential timing
(heterochrony), developmental integration, etc. The purpose of this presentation will be to examine ways in which
developmental theories of size and shape diversity are tested on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses. The
data comprise ontogenetic series of landmarks from clades of characid (Bryconops) and atherinopsid {Atherinella}
fishes, fit to a reference form, from which the relative waqis and relative-warp scores are calculated. Phylogenetic
and environmental components of fomi change among species within clades is analyzed from both partial least
squares confirmatory factor analyses. The results show that in contrast to expectations derived from the literature,
large amounts of the variance in form-change among species are explained by phylogenetic hypotheses of species
relationships.

Did vicariance mold phenotypes of cyprinid fishes In western North America? Evidence from the Gila River
basin of Arizona. M.E. Douglas and W.L. Minckley, Department of Biology and Museum, Arizona State University,
Tempe AZ 85287-1501 USA; B.D. DeMarais, Oklahoma Biological Survey, University of Oklahoma, Norman OK
73019 USA.
Patterns of morphological variation in a group of western North American cyprinid fishes (the 'Gila robustd complex
of the Gila River basin of Arizona and New Mexico) has long puzzled fish taxonomists. Three different forms, (G.
robusta, G. intermedia, and G. nigra) are recognized, yet their basin-wide distributions are a disjunct mosaic. Several
hypotheses have been offered to accommodate this aberrant pattern: ecotypy/ecophenotypy (i.e., individual or
populational response to local conditions), hybridization/intergradation (i.e., gene flow between differentiated species
or races); and vicariance (an historical explanation related to regional hydrographic evolution). To represent these
hypotheses, 33 sample locations were scored within the basin with regard to stream size, stream elevation, stream
barriers, and paleodrainage pattern (the latter accomplished by supenmposing sites onto maps depicting drainage
patterns during six different geologic epochs). Moqihometric data, collected from 25 individuals at all 33 sites, were
then contrasted against the 9 test matrices using two- and three-way Mantel tests. A vicariance model was the only
hypothesis proficient in explaining extant diversity of fish phenotypes. Of those reconstructions used in this model,
only the Pliocene epoch was significantly associated with extant distributions of phenotypes.       241                        09:00 Sunday                                  CF5                               CHM
    Coevolutlonary hypotheses and evolution of mate discrimination in a gynogenetic species complex of
    Amazon mollies. L.A. Dries. Dept, of Zoology. University of Texas, Austin, TX 78712 USA.

    Gynogenetic female Amazon mollies (Poedlia formosa) mate with sexual males (P. latipinna} for success^
    reproduction Studies show that of males distinguish between conspecific females and gynogens, and preferentially
    mate with the former. However, the existence of gynogens indicates mate discrimination is imperfect. The Red
    Queen Hypothesis has been applied to this system suggesting the evolution of mate recognition in is a
    coevolutionary "arms race'; the lack of genetic contribution by males to gynogenetic offspring imposes selection for
    male discrimination that favors sexual females. This, in turn, imposes selection on gynogens to evolve characters
    that override male discrimination. This assumes gynogenetic females have evolved since their origination. Amazons
    originated with a hybridization between P. mexicana and P. latipinna at least several thousand years ago. If a
    coevolutionary hypothesis is true, extant gynogens should differ from ancestral gynogens. In ^s study first
    generation sexual hybrids were used as an analog for the ancestral gynogens to test this hypothesis. The predictions
    are gynogens will have an enhanced ability to attract sexual males, males will prefer gynogens over hybnds, and
    females will differ in agonistic behavior. The results of this study do not support these predictions. This suggests
    application of such hypotheses to gynogenetic systems be preceded by studies documenting the presence of
    evolutionary change in the species of interest.

Female preference for trait symmetry in addition to trait size in swordtail fish. M.R. Morris, Department of
Biological Sciences, Ohio University, Athens OH 45701 USA.
Interest in fluctuating asymmetries, random deviations from perfect bilateral symmetry, has spread to studies of
sexual selection because of the intriguing idea that females could use the degree of asymmetry of a male trait to
assess the genetic quality of potential mates. The evidence that females prefer males with symmetrical sexual
signals, however, has remained controversial. A problem that applies to most previous studies is that preference for
trait size can be misinterpreted as preference for symmetry, even when overall trait size is held constant, if females
assess trait size by the largest minimum on one side. If overall trait size is equal between males, the asymmetrical
males will have the maximum and minimum trait size, and so preference to mate with symmetrical males could
actually reflect a preference to avoid males with the minimum trait on one side. Xiphophorus cortezi females
preferred males with symmetrica! bar numbers when the minimum number of bars was held constant. The strength
of female preference for the symmetrical males with fewer bars was negatively correlated with the strength of
preference the same females had for bar number. These results clearly demonstrate that females preferred trait
symmetry in addition to trait size.

of three species of sculpin (Cottidae) to compare their roles in detemriining the taxonomic coposifion of the diet.

correlated with differences in the occurrence of these prey types in the diets of the three species. Performance
played a greater role in detemiining the occurrence of calanoid copepods in the diet than did choice. Species and
individuals with high capture success on calanoids did not choose to attack this prey type more often than those with
lower capture success. This study indicates that classic measures of selectivity will only reflect active choice or
avoidance when capture success on a prey type is high.H. Jonesi (163 and 124 informative characters, respectively). Parsimony analysis of the data was performed in X.

perch. We anticipate that recruitment of round gobies will increase substantially in Lake Erie owing to the presence
of artificial reefs (shipwrecks) and the ability of guarding males to defend nests effectively.

abundance and distribution in early July 1997 on six offshore petroleum platforms. Hurricane Danny passed through

Molecular phylogeny of the gobloid fishes. C.E. Thacker. Museum of Zoology, Division of Fishes; University of
Michigan;, Ann Amor, Ml 48109 USA.
The perdform suborder Gobioidei contains an estimated 2000 species in 270 genera, found throughout the world
oceans and freshwaters. This lineage is very diverse and reductive evolution is common, m^ng traditional
morphological systematic studies particularly difficult. In an attempt to resolve relationships among gobioid groups, I
sequenced a 2022 base pair fragment of the mitochondrial penome, comprising the entire ND1 and ND2 genes for
40 gobioid species and performed phylogenetic analysis using cladistic parsimony methods. My data set includes
representatives of the Gobiidae (including all subfamilies: Gobiinae, Gobionellinae, Oxudercinae, Amblyopinae and

phylogeny for which Bremer support and jackknife indices indicated weaker support in the deeper nodes. Analysis of
translated amino add data yielded two phylogenies differing only in the placement of one taxon; this phytogeny is
congruent in many respects with pobioid relationships suggested by morphological characters. My analysis provides
a broad view of gobioid relationships and, in particular, provides evidence for the relationships of the paedomorphic
Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae within the Gobioidei.

Speciation studies in the Percina subgenus Swainia (Percidae: Etheostomatinae). TJ. Near. Illinois Natural
History Survey.
Hypotheses concerning modes of allopatric speciation make expHcit predictions regarding patterns of phylogenetic
and biogeographic diversification. This investigation will test allopatric speciation models using phylogenetic and
biogeographic information for the subgenus Swainia, a monophyletic group of four described species in ths genus
Parana. Complete gene sequences of the mitoohondrially encoded cytochrome b have been collected from all
species of Swainia, including individuals from multiple populations of P. phoxocephala and P. nasuta. Patterns of
nucleotide variation were investigated and phylogenetic relationships were estimated using maximum parsimony,

using both maximum parsimony relative rate tests and a likelihood ratio test. Inferred phylogenetic relationships,
biogeographic patterns, and relative amounts of nucleotide divergence are used to develop hypotheses of speciation
in Swainia.

Biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes: patterns of faunal occurrence in southeastern Australia. P.J.
Unrnack. Biology Department, Arizona State University, Tempe AZ 85287-1501, USA.
This presentation is part of a wider study of the biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes. Southeastern Australia
is hereby defined as coastal drainages from the Fitzroy River through Gulf of St. Vincent, including the inland Murray
system separated from coastal drainages by the Great Dividing Range. It has the following biogeographic
relationships of fishes restricted to freshwater 1) 5 of 8 species from southern Victoria also occur in the Murray
system: and 2) 18 of 27 spedes (or spedes pairs) co-occur between coastal Queensland drainages and ttie Murray
system. The relationships of an additional 6 species endemic to the Murray system are more obscure.
Biogeographic connectivity between the Murray and surrounding drainages thus appears high. Past biogeographic
explanations for these relationships have relied heavily upon river captures, making faunal distributions easily
explained. However, the last 15 years have seen a paradigm shift in the proposed evolution of the Great Dividing
Range including evidence that river captures are either non-existent or very old (> 30-60 mba). Most patterns are
congruent with present geological scenarios although exceptions exist. The new geologic conclusions are assessed
on the basis of biological evidence and new hypotheses are provided to explain present distribution patterns.                               11:45 Sunday                                GS1                              MCN

Gopher tortoise {Gophenis polyphemus} movement patterns In large and small habitats: how much land Is
enough? J.O. Ott. Department of Zoology, Auburn University, Auburn AL 36849, USA., JW Jones Ecological
Research Center, Ichauway, RR 2 Box 2324 Newton, GA 31770, USA; W.K. Miohener, JW Jones Ecological
Research Center, Ichauway, RR 2 Box 2324 Newton, GA 31770, USA; M.T. Mendonga and C. Guyer, Department of
Zoology, Auburn University, Auburn AL 36849, USA.
The geographic range of the gopher tortoise has declined due to habitat desfroction and fragmentation. Protection
strategies typically include preserving patches of habitat or conserving areas occupied by tortoises, even if those
areas are restricted in size and quality. However, the patterns observed in these sites can differ from those in large,
contiguous areas where conditions may more closely resemble those under which the spedes evolved. We tracked
131 tortoises via radio-telemetry for one year on an 11,700 ha longleaf pine reserve in southwest Georgia. Male
tortoises utilized an average of 9.3 + 4.6 burrows and traveled an average total distance of 83.7 + 73.8 m during the
study period. Females utilized 4.8 ± 2.4 burrows and traveled 48.2 ± 57.7 m. The longest movemements were 6.4 km
by a male tortoise and 480 m by a female. The results of this study emphasize the need to preserve large,
contigucHJs habitats for use by gopher tortoises. Furthermore, it suggests that movement by tortoises is limited in
smair habitats, especially those surrounded by vast inhospitable areas. Data gathered within large study sites may
provide better information for the long-term preservation of this species.

Intraspecific phylogeny of the lizard Cnemidophorus sexlineatus: To conserve or not?                      P. Razzano.
Department of Biology, Hofstra University, Hempstead, NY, USA, 11549.
Mitochondrial DNA sequence analyses were used to inter phylogeographic relationships among individuals of the
lizard species Cnemidophorus sexlineatus, as well as to determine whether a population of C. sexlineatus in
Michigan is endemic or recently introduced. Individuals were obtained from Colorado, Oklahoma, Indiana, Michigan,
and Florida. A PCR generated fragment which spans the mtDNA ND3 to ND4 gene region, and including the
Argenine fRNA, was sequenced for each individual. Sceloporus grammicus and C. gularis sequences were used as
outgroups.
The preliminary data cannot rule out the possibility that the Michigan population is endemic. The Florida individuals
are in a dade basal to a clade that contains Micnigan, Indiana, and Oklahoma individuals. Sequence divergence
values of the Michigan specimens range from 1.2% to 5.8%. The Indiana and Oklahoma specimens have sequence
divergence values of 1.6% to 2.3% and 1.1% to 1.5% respectively. One Colorado sample forms a clade with the C.
gularis sample, its sequence divergence is 8.3%.

Department of Natural Resources, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-3001, USA.
Human activities tend to create highly fragmented landscapes, thereby exposing remaining habitat to the effects of
edges. I am interested in the impacts of forest-pasture edges on the dynamics of frog and lizard populations. Using a
paired-plot design, I described the abundance and distribution of lizards {Norops. spp.) and leaf-lifter frogs
{Eleutherodactylus spp.) in 10 forest fragments near Las Cruces, Costa Rica, The study took place from February to
June, 1997, and covered both dry and wet seasons. No species was definitively absent from the edge plots.
Nocturnal leaf-litter frogs were generally equally abundant near forest edges and in forest interiors. The single diurnal
eleutherodactylid species, however, was consistently more abundant in the forest interiors, suggesting that abiotic
edge effects may be stronger during the day than at night. Anoline lizards were more abundant at the edges during
the dry season, but became more abundant in forest interiors during the wet season. This seasonal variation adds a
new dimension to our understanding of edge effects, and carries important practical implications for future studies.
The reproductive period of the lizards, which coincides with the rainy season, as well as lower rates of parasitism on
anoline lizards near edges, are offered as possible explanations for the observed seasonal pattern.

Genetic diversity in drought-impacted populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clommys marmorata
pallida. C.M. Ingram and J.W. Archie, Department of Biological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach.
Long Beach CA 90840-3702 USA.

Populations that experience a large reduction in effective size are expected to exhibit a bottleneck effect which will
include loss of heterozygosity and loss of alleles. Populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata
pallida, in Central and Southern California were impacted by an extended drought that occurred from 1987-1992 and
exhibited local population size decreases up to 85% during this period. I examined changes in genetic diversify in
four populations of C. marmorata in the drought affected area by comparing miorosatellite DNA allele frequencies
from tissue samples collected before and after this drought period. Genotypes of five microsatellite loci were
defemiined to assess the genetic diversity within these samples. Heterozygosity was used as a measurement of
genetic diversity. Although no significant decline in heterozygosity was shown in the five loci, there was a decrease
in the number of alleles present in the most severed impacted population. Since most individuals that were present
in the post-drought samples were sunrivors of the drought, the first sign of decreased genetic diversity would be the
loss of alleles. Changes in the level of genetic diversity (heterozygosity) would only be detectable in subsequent
post-drought generations.

Amphibian abundance and community structure in fragmented peat bogs.                    M.J. Mazerolle. Department of
Biology, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, B3H 4J1.
Peatlands are increasingly exploited in Europe and North America due to the demand for peal in horticulture. As a
result, these wetlands are threatened, particularly in New Bronswiok and Quebec, North America's principal peat
producers. I used drift fences and pitfall traps to investigate amphibian populations in pristine bogs and disturbed
bogs (i.e., bog remnants adjacent to peat harvesting operations) of southeastern New Brunswick. Results following
20, 592 trap nights indicate that species richness is higher in pristine bogs than disturbed bogs (range 2-7 spp.).
Rana clamitans was the only specieS sensitive to peat harvesting, while the abundance of Rana sylvatica, Rana
pipiens, Bufo americanus americanus and Rana septentrionalis did not differ between pristine bogs and bog
fragments. Captured individuals consisted almost exclusively of ranid Juveniles in both types of bogs. These data
show that peat bog harvesting has a definite influence on adjacent amphibian communities. However, additional
work will be needed to differentiate natural population fluctuations from the impacts of peat harvesting on amphibian
movements and resource (i.e., bog ponds) utilization. *

For amphibians that breed in temporary pools. Juvenile dispersal is an important life history movement linking the

years old) to recently clearcut habitat (2-11 years old). Similarly, in the powerline experiment. Juvenile wood frogs
showed a dispersal preference for closed-canopy habitat immediately upon metamoqjhosis, with the highest capture
rates occum'ng in microhabitats characterized by dense foliage in both the understory and canopy layers. Our
results suggest that populations of wood frogs, spotted salamanders, and other vernal pool breeding amphibian
species are likely to benefit from efforts to maintain connectivity between upland forest habitats and aquatic breeding

Response of salamander distribution to forest canopy gaps created by selective timber harvesting.                M.T.
Messere. Department of Biology, Albany University, Albany, NY 12206 USA; P.K. Ducey, Department of Biological
Sciences, SUNY at Cortland, Cortland, NY 13045 USA.
Selective timber harvesting (removal of individual frees or small groups of trees), which creates gaps in the forest
canopy, is widely practiced in public and private forests. However, the effects of this technique on herpetofaunal
populations has been incompletely studied. We examined the effect of forest canopy gaps, created by selective
harvesting, on the distribution of ths northern redback salamander, Plethodon cinereus, in a maple-hemlock forest in
central New York State. Distributions of individual salamanders were determined by searching 1 m x 1 m quadrats
along transects extending from the center of gaps into the surrounding forest. In the first year following harvest, we
found that salamander distributions did not indicate significant movement from or avoidance of gap sites. However,
salamander densities were somewhat elevated on ths edges of gaps. Data for the second year following harvest
are being analyzed.

program. S.C. Ribev. S.L. Walker and E. Porter, Environment Canada, National EEM Office, 351 St. Joseph Blvd,

In 1992, the Canadian government passed amendments to the Pulp and Paper Effluent Regulations (PPER) under
the Fisheries Act, which included a requirement for mills to conduct an Environmental Effects Monitoring (EEM)
program. The purpose of EEM is to assess the adequacy of national regulations for protecting fish, fish habitat and
the use of fisheries resources. One key component of EEM is a fish survey (FS), which involves sampling two
sentinel species from an exposure area and examining gross population oharaderisfics. EEM requirements specify
growth, reproduction and survival as key assessment endpoints for fish. The primary objective of the first sunrey
(Cyde 1) was to determine variability in the measured parameters and determine sample sizes using power analysis
for subsequent cycles. Following the completion of Cycle 1, a number of refinements to the EEM program have
been implemented. The purpose of this paper is to review the changes to the FS component of EEM and discuss
the use of the FS data in decision making. Difficulties with the FS component and alternative approaches to the fish
survey {e.g., mesocosms) currently being explored will also be presented.                                                                              P3                                  PCH

The influence of evolutionary history on signal recognition In tungara frMS.                 MJ. Rvan. Department of
Zoology, University of Texas, Austin TX 78712 USA; A.S. Rand, Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, 900
Jefferson Drive, Suite 2207, Washington DC 20560.
We have been using the advertisement call system of tungara frogs {Physalaemus pustuiosus) and their close
relatives to attempt to understand the evolution of communication systems. We have analyzed the advertisement
calls and phylogenetic relationships of members of the Physaiaemus pustuiosus species group and three other
congeners as outgroups. Using these data we have estimated calls at ancestral nodes and tested tOngara frog
female preferences for these calls. Here we address the follovring questions: (1) How conservative is the evolution
of various call characters; (2) How do individual call rriiaracters infiuence advertisement call recognition
(heterospecific call versus white noise) and discrimination (heterospecific call versus conspecific call); and, (3) Does
the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character differentially influence call recognition and discrimination. Our results
suggest that: (1) calls do not evolve as tightly coordinated suites of characters, but instead are arrays of more or less
plesiomorphic or derived characters; (2) that call discrimination and recognition might be influenced differently by
some call characters than others; and, (3) that the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character might have some effect
on these tasks.

ambient noise levels, "nriey perform conspicuous visual displays by extending or ‘flagging' the posterior limbs.

observed patterns suggest that complex visual communication may have evolved under two ecological scenarios.

Caira, Department, of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of, Connecticut, Storrs, CT USA.
Spiral intestines of rays identified as Aetobatus narinari, from the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Thailand and the
Timor Sea were examined for tapeworms. Light and electron microscopy of these worms revealed faunal differences
among individuals from these localities. Rays from Mdxico hosted several different species in the order
Tetr^hyllidea. Rays from Thailand and Australia hosted species belonging to file order Lecanicephalidea, but, the
species of lecanicephalideans differed between the two localities. Although these differences may simply reflect

differences were seen in the angle of the anterior margin of the pectoral fins and in snout length. Combined these
data lead us to suspect that the of spotted eagle ray found in the Eastern Pacific might not be conspecific with those
found in the two localities In the Indian Ocean. In addition, based on our data, the conspecific identity of the spotted
eagle rays from Thailand and Australia is questionable.

    Buoyancy in deep-sea sharks from the Chatham Rise. New Zealand. B.M. Wetherfaee. Zoology Department,
    University of Hawaii, Honolulu, HI, USA.
    Although deep-sea sharks approach neutral buoyancy through a large oily liver that contains low-density lipids such
    as squalene, there have been few comparisons of buoyancy within and among species of sharks. Buoyancy and
    chemical composition of the liver oil of sharks collected in deep-water trawls from the Chatham Rise, New Zealand
    were compared. Although there appears to be strong selection for neutral buoyancy in these sharks, buoyancy
    characteristics of sharks varied with species, size, sex and reproductive state. Livers of smaller sharks contain more
    squalene and are less dense than livers of larger sharks. However, livers of larger sharks contain a greater
    proportion of oil than livers of smaller sharks, and the whole body of sharks is nearly uniformly neutrally buoyant
    regardless of size of shark. Livers of mature male sharks contain more squalene and are less dense than those of
    mature females, but the non-liver tissue in females is less dense than that of males, and the whole bodies of both
    sexes are equally neutrally buoyant. Regulation of buoyancy of species of sharks found in shallow water differs
    considerably from that of deeper species, and appears to rely more on hydrodynamic lift provided by lifting surfaces
    such as fins.

    Kinematics of shark pectoral fin movements and their implications for lift-production.                    M.P. Robinson,
    Department of Biology, University of South Florida, LIF 136,, 4202 E. Fowler Ave, Tampa FL 33620 USA.
    Elasmobranchs, negatively buoyant animals, must produce dynamic lift to avoid sinking. Current models of shark
    locomotion assume that lift is produced posteriorly by the heterocercal caudal fin and anteriorly by the pertoral firis
    and head. These two components of lift produce torques at the center of mass that negate one another. All inodels
    have assumed that the pectoral fins are static during swimming. Using a dual video camera system I r^orded spiny
    dogfish, Squalus acan&iias, swimming in a large flume. Marks placed on the fins divided them into separate
    segments. Three-dimensional kinematic analyses of these individual segments of the fins and head of the shark
    demonstrated manipulation of the pectoral fins by the sharks during swimming. The angle of the pectoral firi was
    modified during steady swimming and was correlated with the position of the caudal fin during its beat. An index of
    lift was calculated for each fraction of the pectoral fin and head. The head appears to produce significantly more lift
    during steady swimming and while the animal is ascending In the water column. The negative lift produced by the
    pectoral fins appears to be Important in angling the animal down when It begins a descent

     Consequences of pesticide accumulation in anuran populations. R.W. Russell. Great Lakes Lab for Fisheries
     and Aquatic Sciences, Dept, of Fisheries and Oceans, 867 Lakeshore Rd., Burlington, ON, L7R 4A6: S.J. Heonar
     Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1; G. Mouland, Point Pelee National Park, RR#1,
     Leamington, ON, N8H 3V4; G.D. Haffner, Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Science, University of Windsor,
     401 Sunset Ave., Windsor, ON, N9B 3P4. •

    Environmental contamination with anthropogenic chemicals has been implicated in the decline and disappearance of
    amphibians from many localities around the world. Point Pelee National Park in southern Ontario has lost 5 of 10
    amphibian species in the last 50 years. Habitat loss has occurred but cannot account for the number of amphibian
    extirpations documented in the park. Similar aniphibian losses have not occurred at nearby wetlands. Amphibian
    extirpations at Point Pelee follow a period of DDT application in orchards. DDT and metabolite concentrations were
    greatest in terrestrial arpphibians (Pseudacris crucifer and Bufo americanus} and least in aquatic amphibians (Rana
    clamilans and Rana pipiens). High pesticide concentrations were measured in reptilian predators of amphibians,
    however pesticide concentrations measured in predatory fish were much lower than in snakes of similar trophic
    position. Trophic magnification of pesticides was observed only in the terrestrial food web. Pesticide accumulation in
    amphibians was positively related to site contamination. These data collected in southern Ontario indicate that the
    historic use of pesticides may be an important determinant of local distribution of amphibians and their predators.

Trabecular prismatic cartilage: a novel solution to strengthening the jaws of a cartilaginous fish.                  A.P^
Summers. Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, UMASS Amherst, Amherst. MA 01003 USA.
A synapomorphy of the cartilaginous fishes (Chondriohthyes) is that some, or all, of the skeleton is composed of
calcified cartilage known as prismatic cartilage. The surface of prismatic cartilage is a mosaic of plates of calcium
apatite crystals called tesserae. These tesserae surround a core of hyaline cartilage much as the rind surrounds the
pulpy fruit of an orange and serve to stiffen the skeletal element. In both jaw cartilage of the cownose ray, Rhinoptera
bonasus, struts of calcification run through the hyaline cartilage core. Cownose rays feed on mollusks, ophiuroids
and other hard prey. Tooth plates of adults show distinct wear patterns where the prey is usually cnjshed. A sagittal
section through this 'trabecular cartilage' shows that the starts are positioned so as to prevent buckling in this area.
The common ancestor of cartilaginous and bony fishes is thought to have had a bony endoskeleton. The lamellar
bone of the tesserae and vertebrae of chondrichthians is evidence that the skeleton has not lost osteogenic potential
entirely. The data presented here indicate that a novel developmental and biochemical process is also at work in the
cartilage. Data from neonate individuals indicates that the process of trabeculation is not epigenetic, but rather is part
of a fixed developmental pattern. Bone is typically strengthened through endosteal deposition and trabeculation. In a
remarkable example of convergence, multiple layers of tesserae and stmt formation serve the same purpose in
cartilage.

Consequences of pesticide accumulation In anuran populations. R.W. Russell. Great Lakes Lab for Fisheries
and Aquatic Sciences, Dept, of Fisheries and Oceans, 867 Lakeshore Rd., Burlington, ON, L7R 4A6; S.J. Hecnar,
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1; G. Mouland, Point Pelee National Park, RR#1,
Leamington, ON, N8H 3V4; G.D. Haffner, Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Science, University of Windsor,
401 Sunset Ave., Windsor, ON, N9B 3P4. •
Environmental contamination with anthropogenic chemicals has been implicated in the decline and disappearance of
amphibians from many localities around the world. Point Pelee Nation^ Park in southern Ontario has lost 5 of 10
amphibian species in the last 50 years. Habitat loss has occurred but cannot account for the number of amphibian
exfirpations documented in the park. Similar amphibian losses have not occurred at nearby wetlands. Amphibian
extirpations at Point Pelee follow a period of DDT application in orchards. DDT and metabolite concentrations were
greatest in terrestrial amphibians (Pseudacris crucifer and Bufo americanus) and least in aquatic amphibians [Rana

however pesticide concentrations measured in predatory fish were much lower than in snakes of similar trophic

amphibians was positively related to site contamination. These data collected in southern Ontario indicate that the
historic use of pesticides may be an important determinant of local distribution of amphibians and their predators.

Amphibian monitoring, varlablltty, and sample size: lessons from the literature. P.C. Eagle. Pennsylvania
State University, c/o Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, 12100 Beech Forest Road , Laurel, MD 20708-4038 USA;
S. Droege, Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, 12100 Beech Forest Road , Laurel, MD 20708-4038 USA; J.P.
Gibbs, Slate University of New York, Syracuse, NY 13210 USA.
Counts of amphibians over time were compiled from published accounts. At ths time this abstract was written, 37
studies have yielded 110 separate count series for 45 amphibian species. Counts were analyzed to determine
series mean, detrended standard deviation, and subsequent coefficient of variation (CV). Studies have been
categorized according to taxonomic group, sampling method, study region, and count type (index vs. population
estimate). Initial analyses indicate significant differences among count CVs based on count type, with CVs from
population estimates being significantiy lower than index CVs (p = 0.016). While sample sizes were low, there are
further indications that CVs of counts of terrestrial and stream salamanders are much lower than most anuran and
pond-breeding salamanders. We are currently adding counts to the database as new studies arise. We will also
demonstrate the impact of variability on power and sample size requirements for monitoring programs using the
program MONITOR. Finally, we plan to use studies providing within season data and multiple site data to
characterize the various components of count variance among sampling error and yearly variation.

Trabecular prismatic cartilage: a novel solution to strengthening the Jaws of a cartilaginous fish.                  A.P.
Summers. Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, UMASS Amherst, Amherst, MA 01003 USA.
A synapomorphy of the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) is that some, or all, of the skeleton is composed of
calcified cartilage known as pnsmatic cartilage. The surface of prismatic cartilage is a mosaic of plates of calcium
apatite crystals called tesserae. These tesserae surround a core of hyaline cartilage much as the rind surrounds the
pulpy fruit of an orange and serve to stiffen the skeletal element. In both jaw cartilage of the rxnvnose ray, Rhinoptera
bonasus, struts of calcification run through the hyaline cartilage core. Cownose rays feed on mollusks, ophiuroids
and other hard prey. Tooth plates of adults show distinct wear patterns where the prey is usually crushed. A sagittal
section through this 'trabecular cartilage' shows that the struts are positioned so as to prevent buckling in this area.
The common ancestor of cartilaginous and bony fishes is thought to have had a bony endoskeleton. The lamellar
bone of the tesserae and vertebrae of chondrichthians is evidence that the skeleton has not lost osteogenic potential
entirely. The data presented here indicate that a novel developmental and biochemical process is also at work in the
cartilage. Data from neonate individuals indicates that the process of trabeculation is not epigenetic, but rather is part
of a fixed developmental pattern. Bone is typically strengthened through endosteal deposition and trabeculation. In a
remarkable example of convergence, multiple layers of tesserae and strut formation senre the same purpose in
cartilage.

Automated acoustical monitoring of anuran amphibians In New Brunswick, Canada. K.L. Oseen. Department
of Biology, Dalhousie University, Halifax NS, B3H 4J1; R.J. Wassersug, Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology,
Dalhousie University, Halifax NS, B3H 4H7.
As part of a long-term amphibian monitoring program, automated acoustical recorders were placed at five sites in
two national parks in New Bninswick during the summer of 1997. Each recorder took a one minute long acoustical
sample every hour from early May until the end of August, for an average of 110 recording days per recorder.
Analysis of acoustical samples revealed the presence of five anuran species, Pseudacris crucifer, Rana catesbeiana,
Rana clamitans, Rana syh/atica, and Bufo americanus. A sixth species, Rana pipiens, was detected on only one
occasion. Three species also found in New Brunswick (Hyla versicolor, Rana palustris, and Rana septentrionalis')
were not detected at any of ths sampled sites. Chorus activity patterns changed over the breeding season for each
species. In general, chorus activity was highest between the hours of 10 pm and 5 am, although calling individuals
were frequently recorded throughout the day. We also compared two acoustical sampling protocols (one min every
hour vs. 12 s every 15 min). Both strategies detected the same species richness, but showed subtle differences in
anuran activity patterns. Comparison of calling activity with meteorological data is currently underway.

 Are you considering transplantantion as a management tod? Be cautious - mixing gene pods may be more
 harmful than helpful due to outbreeding depression. J.P. Hernandez-Martich. The University of Georgia
 Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802 USA.
 Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of
 between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts
 inbreeding depression (ID) tor offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness
 increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (I. e., OD occurs).
 Populations of eastern mosquitofish {Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from foe Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two
 drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms.
 OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were
 significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage
 sections (7of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower
 for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined
 potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best
 predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.nypotnesis is true Decline is occurnngj. vieany we wani nign power in our moniionng programs so as lo minimize
the chance of making a Type II error (i.e., failing to detect a decline that is occurring). However, many amphibian
monitoring programs likely do not have the necessary power to satisfactorily reduce the possibility that actual
declines are occurring, even though some studies suggest stability and have data-sets that exceed 10 years. Here,
we review the concepts of statistical power as they apply to detecting population declines. We then calculate an
estimate of power for long-term data on bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and wood frogs (Rana sylvatica] to investigate
the problems associated with maximizing power In amphibian monitoring programs. We also comment on how an
