Quick and accurate identification of triggerfishes (Balistidae) using PCR with species-diagnostic
mitochondrial (12S/16S) primers. H.A. Balchowsky. Nova Southeastern University, Oceanographic Center, 8000
Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA.
Identification of ichthyoplankton (eggs, larvae, and juveniles) can be a challenging task due to their small sizes and
dynamic development. This problem is particularly acute for tropical and subtropical ichthyoplankton, most of which
can be identified to family-level only. As part of a broader initiative to develop molecular markers for tropical and
subtropical fish identification, we report on the utility of mitochondrial ribosomal gene sequences for triggerfish
species identification. A 1,510 bp fragment, containing portions of the mitochondrial ribosomal genes (12S, 16S) and
the complete tRNA valine gene, was sequenced from six triggerfish species (4 genera) inhabiting the western central
Atlantic Ocean. Forty-three sequences were examined to assess intra- and interspecific variation. Intraspecific
differences were minor (less than 0.5%); however, sufficient interspecific differences occur within this locus to allow
the design of robust species-specific PCR primers. When tested in a multiplex PCR assay, these primers yielded
species-diagnostic size fragments that unambiguously identified all 4 genera and 4 of the 6 species. Distinction
between the two Canthidermis congeners (0.9% interspecific variation) was not possible using this approach;
however, these congeners were readily distinguished using RFLP analysis of the PCR amplicon, we suggest that
molecular genetic approaches can provide a robust and rapid method to tackle long-standing problems in the
identification of fish species.

method based on the molecular phylogeny was used to reconstruct the evolution or key characters traditionally used
in the classification of the group such as: trophotaeniae (external projections of the embryonic gut that absorb
maternal nutrients), karyot^es, and tooth and jaw structures. The phylogeny agrees with some but not all
conclusions from earlier studies regarding phylogenetic relationships and reproductive and trophic character

Are you considering transplantantion as a management tod? Be cautious - mixing gene pods may be more
harmful than helpful due to outbreeding depression. J.D. Hemandez-Martich. The University of Georgia
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802 USA.

Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of
between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts
inbreeding depression (ID) for offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness
increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (i. e., OD occurs).
Populations of eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two
drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms.
OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were
significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage
sections (7of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower
for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined
potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best
predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.

Evolution of the biomechanical attributes of long bones in fish, amphibians, and reptiles.               G.M. Erickson.
Biomechanical Engineering Division, Mechanical Engineering Department, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305-
3030 USA.
Long bones are the major skeletal elements of vertebrate appendages. The radiations of many vertebrate clades
were facilitated by locomotory innovations Involving these elements (e.g. the terrestrial diversification of tetrapods)
and thus it is necessa^ to understand how these elements changed biomechanically to more fully understand
vertebrates evolution. Biomechanical attributes of long bones such as strength, modulus, and loading conditions are
well documented in avian and mammalian taxa. However, data for taxa from outgroup clades are virtually non­
existent and the results from the few studies that have been conducted are not in accord with those obtained for bird
and mammal bones. In order to provide a better understanding of skeletal evolution, I conducted a series of
biomechanical tests on long bones from a diversity of fish, amphibians, and reptiles that possessed basal locomotory
attributes within their respective clades. Evolutionary trends were assessed using phylogenetic character analysis.
The results suggest; 1) material properties (strength, modulus, and failure strain) did not vary throughout evolution,
2) in vivo strain regimes increased Independently in birds and mammals, 3) the capacity of long bones to functionally
adapt is a plesiomorphic osteichthyan trait, and 4) size and shape changes were the primary means by which long
bones changed to meet evolutionary locomotory challenges.

Light attenuating molecules In the lens of the fish eye.            M. Posner. Dept, of Biological Sciences, Univ, of
Southern California, Los, Angeles, CA, 90089; Section of Vertebrates, Natural History Museum of Los, Angeles
County, 900 Exposition Blvd., Los Angeles, CA, 90007 USA.
The ocular lens of fishes contains mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), which attenuate short wavelengths of light.
The causes for the varied distribution of MAAs in the lenses of different fish species are still in question. In this study
I examined the lenticular MAA content of 42 flatfish species (order Pleuronectiformes) from nine families to
investigate the controlling factors on lens pigmentation and changes in pigmentation during ontogeny. MAAs were
actively transporteri and concentrated by fie lens from the surrounding humors in the eye. These MAAs produced
two absorbance peaks when analyzed spectrophotometrically, one near 320 nm and another near 360 nm. The
relative amounts of different MAAs in the lens was correlated with phylogeny, while the total MAA concentration
reflected the depth distribution of each species. Species living in deeper water contained lower concentrations of
MAAs. Both the total amount of MAAs and their relative proportions changed during ontogeny. MAAs began
accumulating after settlement, and increased in concentration with standard length. The phylogenetic trend in the
relative proportion of MAA peaks suggests that lens pigmentation is under genetic control. This control is not
exerted by the lens itself, but may occur at the level of food metabolism.

Comparative physiology of metabolic rate and thermal tolerance: physiological parameters for Investigating
macroecological patterns. W.l. Lutterschmidt. University of Oklahoma, Dept, of Zoology, Univ, of Oklahoma,
Norman, OK 73019.
Distributional patterns of species result in part from their ability to tolerate physiologically the environmental extremes
characteristio within their geographical range. Macroecology attempts to reveal relationships between organisms
and their environments by investigating statistical patterns of abundance and distribution. In such analyses, species
serve as replicates where the relationship between range and body size is used to understand how physical space
and ecological resources are partitioned to create fie unique distributions of species. However, these studies often
fail to consider the underlying physiological capacities and tolerances that are most likely to be the limiting factors in
determining distributions. I measured temperature dependent metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance in
several ectothermio species in a attempt to investigate two subsidiary principles of Shelford's law and determine if
physiological parameters are better predictors of distributional patterns than are measures of body size. After
controls tor phylogeny, I found species-specific plasticity of metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance to predict
better the statistical patterns of ger^raphic range size and latitudinal range among the fishes and snakes studied.
These findings support Shelforas idea that the distributions of species often are governed by the environmental
factor for which species have the narrowest tolerance range or least adaptability.

Patterns of variation in spring emergence by black rat snakes (Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta). G. Blouin-Demers.
P.J. Weatherhead and K.A. Prior, Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, On,
K1S 5B6.
Substantial individual variation in timing of emergence from hibernation has been reported among reptiles, although
few studies have addressed the causes of that variation. Here we report patterns of spring emergnece by black rat
snakes (Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta}, observed at 13 communal hibernacula in eastern Ontario from 1992 to 1997.
Although we found significant variations in timing of emergence among years and among hibernacula, we found no
evidence of a simple latitudinal gradient in mean emergence dates. Within hibernacula, significantly more snakes
emerged on days with high maximum air temperatures, but maximum air temperature only explained a small amount
of the variation among years in emergence dates. Larger individuals emerged earlier than smaller individuals and
females tended to emerge earlier than males. Condition was not a significant factor determining timing of
emergence in our black rat snake population. Based on these results, we proposed the preparation for reproduction
hypothesis which states that mature individual snakes emerge earlier than immature individuals to prepare their
gonads for reproduction.

available forest rxjnnectivity and snake pathways. Snakes used certain plants in disproportion to their occurrence in

Do incubation-induced changes to a lizard's phenotype affect its vulnerability to predators? S.J. Downes and
R. Shine, School of Biological Sciences, University of Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia.
Recent work on a variety of reptiles provides strong evidence that incubation temperatures can influence many
aspects of a hatchling's phenotype (i.e., size, shape, activity, locomotor performance, etc.). However, although these
traits seem likely to affect the hatchling's fitness, few studies have tested this assumption. Vulnerability to predation
is one plausible way that phenotypic modifications could affect an organism's fitness. Therefore, we incubated the
eggs of lizards at temperatures similar to the extremes of natural nests, and examined both the response of
hatchlings to predator (snake) scent and actual vulnerability in staged encounters in the laboratory. We used two
species of montane Australian scincids: one heliotherm (Lampropholis delicate} that deposits eggs in relatively warm
nests, and one thigmotherm (Nanoscincus maccoyf) that lays In relatively cool nests. For both species, our results
show that incubation temperature affects both an individual's response to predator scent and its vulnerability to
predation. These patterns are complex, and change with the age of the hatchling, perhaps through differential growth
rates and changes in activity patterns. Nevertheless, these experiments support the notion that incubation-induced
modifications to a lizard's phenotype may be biologically significant, and that some of these effects are mediated
through predator-prey interactions.

Ecology of an equatorial African leaf-litter herpetofauna, Kibale National Park, Uganda.                    J.P. Vonesh,
Department of Zoology, 223 Bartram Hall, University of Rorida, Gainesville, Forida 32611, USA.
Plot sampling was used to compare the wet and dry season litter herpetofaunas of three forest types in Kibale
National Park, Uganda. Species richness, abundance, and evenness were measured in pristine, selectively logged,
and exotic pine forests, A repeated measures design was also employed to examine whether Reus natalensis
fruiting events influence litter arthropod and herpetofaunal abundances. The diets of the six most common leaf lifter

rouqhly equivalent species richness but at higher densities. This paucity of litter herpetofauna at Kibale does not
appear to result from low prey availability, for though the abundance of many prey arthropods increases under
fruiting F. natalensis, there is no corresponding increase in herpetofaunal densities.

The fathead minnow (Pimephales promeias} In western boreal lakes:        Will forest harvesting affect
population-level processes? A.J. Danylchuk. Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alberta, ,
Edmonton, Alberta, Canada T6G 2E9,.
Harvesting of Alberta's boreal forest is increasing dramatically. Predicted effects of forest hanresting on lakes in this
region involve increases in nutrient loading and primary productivity. In turn, these changes may affect fish by
modifying food resources and increasing winter oxygen depletion rates. The fathead minnow is common to small
lakes in the western boreal forest. Because it is often the most abundant, or only fish present, the fathead is an
important component of aquatic food webs in this region. However, little is known about the basic ecology of fathead
populations inhabiting these lakes. The objectives of my research are to determine: 1) what factors regulate fathead
populations in boreal Alberta lakes; and 2) how potential changes in environmental conditions resulting from forest
harvesting may affect these populations. My research is divided into three components: i) the intensive study of four
fathead populations before and after experimental forest harvesting; ii) an extensive survey of populations inhabiting
lakes throughout the boreal forest of Alberta; and iii) mechanistic pond experiments. Together, these three
components should provide important insights into the factors and mechanisms regulating fathead populations, and
allow ms to assess the effects of forest harvesting on fathead populations in this region.

Phylogeny of anoles: morphological and combined analyses. S. Poe. Texas Memorial Museum; Department of
Zoology, University of Texas at Austin; Division of Amphibians and Reptiles, National Museum of Natural History,
Washington, DC 20560 USA.
Anole lizards (Anoiis, Phenacosaunjs', formerly Chamaeleolls, Chamaelinorops) are important study subjects for
organismal and evolutionary biology. Evolutionary interpretation of the numerous comparative data tor these species
requires a phylogeny. The content of and relationships within several small groups of anoles have been clarified by
many workers. Despite recent molecular work and reanalysis of morphological data, the higher level phylogeny of
anoles has remained unresolved due to the paucity of characters used and the large number of species (at least

species groups, 3) test the monophyly of Anoiis relative to other anole genera, 4) Test whether this new
morphological estimate is significantly in conflict with existing molecular data sets.

Using GIS to analyze the spatial distribution of nests of the common snapping turtle, Chelydra serpentina.
J.J. Kolbe. Iowa State University, Department of Zoology & Genetics, Ames, lA, 50011, USA.
Few studies exist that attempt to analyze the spatial distribution of turtle nests. This study utilizes the analytical
capabilities of Geographic Information System (GIS) software to examine the spatial distribution of common
snapping turtle nests in relation to each other and to the physical characteristics of the landscape. Seven years of
nest location data from a sand prairie along the eastern snore of the Mississippi River are included in this analysis.
Nests were found to be significantly clustered in their distribution over the entire study site. Additionally, a higher
proportion of nests were located in sand blowouts (i.e., areas of exposed sand with no vegetation) than expected
based on area ratios of landcover. Other factors, not included in the spatial analysis, were identified as potential
influences on turtle nest location. This study highlights the utility of GIS in the area of spatial analysis.    349      .                  16:00 Sunday                           .       GS2                             .PCH

Pennsylvania using PCR-SSCP. F.K. Ammer. R.J. McPherson and C.J. Lee, Biology Department, Clanon

the summer. This result is suggestive that recreational disturbance may increase larval mortality in high distumance
areas. Interestingly, a major flash flood event at the end of the summer effectively "reset*; the sy^em, redistnbuting
fish species equally between low and high recreational disturbance areas and Increasing diversity in both areas.

Initial results in a resampling survey of Nebraska amphibians as a test for declines. D.S. McLeod. School of
Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE 68588-0188, USA.
 An inventory of historical sites for amphibian larvae was conducted to verify or reject the hypothesis that amphibian
populations have declined in Nebraska over the past twenty years. In the early 1970’5 larval sampling was used as
a means of surveying these ponds as a part of an exercise in mapping amphibian distributions within the state.
Because amphibian larvae remain in a pond for a much longer time than do the reproducing adults, such a
methodology allows rapid acquisition of distributional data. Larvae were found al 100% of the ponds sampled during
the 197O’s, with a range of one to five species found per pond. During the 1997 field season between one and four
species were found at any one site (accounting forthose ponds which has no lanzae present). More importantly, only
58% of the ponds sampled were occupied by amphibian larvae. Of the 10 commonly occurring species of
amphibians in Nebraska, two (Hyta chrysoscelis and Bufo cognatus) were not found represented by larvae during the
sampling period, and one species {Acris crepitans) was found at only one site. Spea bombifrons, found at 25% of
the sites sampled in the 197O’s, was found at only 8% of the sites during 1997. While conclusions cannot be made
until further work is completed, this data suggests that declines have occurred in Nebraska's amphibian populations.

with high levels of recreational disturbance and in river areas with low levels of recreational disturbance during the

mollispinis) and desert sucker {Catostomus dark!). Community divers!^ was similar in both areas at the beginning of
the summer but was significantly lower in high disturbance areas later in the summer due to lower abundance of
desert sucker in these areas. Benthic algal biomass is being compared between low and high disturbance areas to
test the hypothesis that lower abundance of desert sucker in high disturbance areas is a result of lower algal
biomass, their primary food source, in these areas. Recreational disturbance primarily disturbs the river substrate,
possibly reducing algal biomass in high disturbance areas. Surveys for lanral fish indicate that larval densities were
similar in low and high disturbance areas early in the summer but significantly lower in high disturbance areas later in
the summer. This result is suggestive that recreational disturbarice may increase larval mortality in high disturbance
areas. Interestingly, a major flash flood event at the end of the summer effectively "reset* the system, redistributing
fish species equally between low and high recreational disturbance areas and increasing diversity in both areas.

Phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial ND2 and ND4L genes in the genus C)rprinella and related cyprinid
fishes. R.E. Broughton. Section of Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-2701 USA; J.R.
Gold, Department of Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences, Texas A&M University, USA.
We have obtained sequences of the entire mitochondrial ND2 and ND4L genes (1344 nucleotides) from 30 species
of North American cyprinid fishes. Twenty-four of these are currently recognized as members of the genus
Cyprineiia, or have been suggested to be included in Cyprinella. For most species, several individuals from
geographically distant localities were included for a total of 59 OTUs. Phylogenetic analysis, employing equal
weighting of all characters, yields a single most parsimonious tree. This tree is similar to Gibbs' phylogeny of
Cyprinella and supports his scattered-tuberoles and linear-tubercles groups except for the placement of C. caerulea.
The mitochondrial phylogeny also has substantial similarity with Mayden's analysis of Cyprinella and supports his
placement of C. caerulea in the linear-tubercles group. The primary difference with Mayden's phylogeny is
placement of the root. In the present case, C. callistia appears to be most basal while the C. lutrensis group of
southwestern species, and its sister group of C. spiloptera, C. whipplei, and C. venusta, appear most derived. When
transversion changes were weighted three times transitions, a single tree was obtained that differed from the equal­
weight tree in the placement of a clade containing C. caerulea, C. leedsi, C. callitaenia, C. callisema, and C. nivea.
This placement is inconsistent with both Mayden's and Gibbs' analyses suggesting that unequal weighting is
unjustified. Our analysis also suggests that recognition as Cyprinella of some species formerly considered Hybopsis
may be warranted.

Notograptidae: sister to Acanthoplesiops (Acanthoclininae, Plesiopidae). R.D. Mooi. Vertebrate Zoology,
Milwaukee Public Museum, 800 West Wells St., Milwaukee, Wl 53233-1478 USA; A.C. Gill, The Natural History
Museum, Cromwell Rd., London SW7 5BD.
The family Notograptidae contains one genus, Notograptus Gunther, and five nominal species known only from
northern Australia and New Guinea. Monophyly of the family is supported by numerous apparent autapomorphies
(e.g., anterior expansion of the median ethmoid, highly reduced gill-arch skeleton, composite A1+A2 section of the
adductor mandibulae, which originates broadly on the skull). Traditionally, the family has been considered a
blennioid or trachinoid, but in 1993 we suggested a relationship with acanthoclinine plesiopids. Here, we re-examine
this relationship and find strong evidence to place Notograptus among acanthoclinines (continuous free margin of
lower lip; head naked; dorsal and anal fins with high numbers of spines and low numbers of segmented rays;
reduced number of branched caudal-fin rays and total rays). Additional evidence supports a sister taxon relationship
with Acanthoplesiops, a derived acanthoclinine genus (symphyseal flap on lower lip; reduced hypural 5; reduced
hypurapophysis). This hypothesis helps to resolve the relationships among Acanthoplesiops by clanfying the polarity
of an otherwise equivocal character (autogenous middle radials of dorsal- and anal-fin pterygiophores). It also
produces a general pattern of distribution of the Notograptus^-Acanthoplesiops clade that compliments that of its
congeners.

A review of western north Atlantic species of Bembrops, family Percophidae, with descriptions of three new
species and additional comments on two eastern Atlantic species. B.A. Thompson. Coastal Rsheries Institute,

Ths Atlantic members of the genus Bembrops were examined from approximately 700 specimens, using meristic,
morphometric, and pigment characters to redescribe six species: B. anatirostris, B. gobioides, B. greyi, B. heterurus,

elongated in males and B. macromma Is unique in having the dorsal surface of Its eyes scaled. The eastern Atlantic
fonri presently considered the same species, B. heterurus, found off eastern South America, may represent an
undescribed species. The nine species are generally separated by depth strata within each geographical region,
with few syntopic collections.

Gambusla and Belonesox are sister taxa but Brachyrhaphis is not a Gambuslini (Cyprinodontiformes:
Poeciliinae). C.M. Rodriquez. Museo Nacional de HIstoria Natural, Plaza de la Cultura, Santo Domingo, Dominican
Republic.

moqjhological data, and this action was corroborated by Rauohenberger (1989). On the basis of cytochrome b gene
of the mithochondrial genome, Mojica et al (1997) found that Belonesox was not closely related to the other two

A first glance at pelagic shark catches in the Azores. A.A. Silva. G. Menezes and J.J. Pereira, Universidade dos
Acores, Departamento de Oceanografia e Pesoas, PT-9900 Horta, Portugal.
This paper reports a first attempt to estimate pelagic shark catches in the northeastern Atlantic Ocean around the
Azores. Blue shark (Prionace glauca} and shortfin mako {Isurus oxyrinchus) commercial catches reported for the
Azorean archipelago as well as non-reported fishing data from logbooks of swordfish longliners operating in the area
are presentee! for the period 1993-1996. Three major fleet components catching pelagic sharks are identified
according to vessel characteristics and fishing regime: open deck wooden boats, small covered deck boats (gross
tonnage less than 100 tons) and large covered deck boats (GRT exceeding 100 tons). The latter vessel class lands
most of the catches In Portuguese and Spanish mainland ports, accounting for 86-89% and 71-85% of the total
estimated blue shark and mako catches taken In the Azores during the study period. Catch rates for blue shark and
swordfish exhibit a pronounced seasonal and asynchronic nature. While the highest catch levels for the former
species are obtaineefin the Spring (averaging 807 Kg/1000 hooks), the fishing season for the latter targeted species
is from August to February. The implications of this pattern for future management are discussed. Blue shark bycatch
represents a major proportion of the total catches taken by the Azorean swordfish longline fishery, reaching a
minimum and a maximum of 39% and 91% respectively dunng October and June. Blue shark catches have been
gradually increasing over the period 1993-1996, peaking at an estimated maximum of 2,433 mt in 1996. Shortfin
mako catch levels have increased to an estimated maximum of 76 mt in 1995, followed by a decline to 54 mt in
1996. An observed increase of pelagic shark catch rates over the study period is probably due to a shift of fishing
effort towards pelagic sharks during times of low abundance of swordfish.

The Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is
responsible for management of Atlantic tunas, swordfish, billfish and sharks. Thirty-nine species of Atlantic sharks
are grouped into 4 management units - large coastal sharks, pelagic sharks, small coastal sharks, and prohibited
species. In the 'Report to Congress: Status of the Rsheries of the United States’ (September, 1997), NMFS

include rebuilding plans submitted for Secretarial review within one year (September, 1998) and that NMFS
establish an advisory panel for each FMP or amendment. The HMS Management Division is developing a

prepared separately. An update on the status of the HMS plan will be provided.

Experimental homing in juvenile lemon sharks, Negaprion brevlrostris, at Bimini, Bahamas. S.M. Clermont.
Zoological Institute, University of Copenhagen, Tagensvej 16, 2200 Copenhagen, Denmark; S.D. Gruber, Bimini
Biological Reid Station, RSMASAJniversity of Miami, 4600 Rickenbacker Causeway, Miami, FL 33149-1098.
This study represents the first eimerimental trials on an elasmobranch's ability to return home from an unfamiliar
area. Ten juvenile lemon sharks (66.0 to 96.0 cm total lengths) were tagged with ultrasonic transmitters and their
home ranges determined over a minimum of 3 days of tracking. Thereafter they were recaptured and experimentally
displaced 4 km off shore, south of the island. From late October 1997 to February 1998, seven displacements during
daylight and three displacements at night were performed. Sharks were tracked for between 2 and 14 hours, and in
all ten cases successfully returned to their home ranges. Ths behavioral pattern of the sharks at the time of release
was characterized by circling and vertical migrations suggesting that they were attempting to orient to sensory cues
in a way similar to homing pigeons. Further, sharks released at night appeared to change course to a more direct
route home at sunrise, suggesting that visual cues may play an important role in the final stages of homing.
Therefore, we are testing the hypofriesis that sharks are able to use the position of the sun as a cue for orientation.
Rnally, we are carefully documenting the behavior of sharks at the time of release to give insight into possible
mechanisms of orientation. Supported by the Rorida State Department of Education with a grant to SHG.

A preliminary demographic analysis of the bigeye thresher shark, Aloplas superclliosus. C.T. Chen and K.M.
Liu, Department of Rshery Science, National Taiwan Ocaean, University, Keelung 202, Taiwan.
Population growth and exploitation of Alopias superciliosus were estimated by demographic analyses using best
known life history parameters. Life history tables were constmcted by using both estimates of natural mortality (M) of
0.1316 and age-specific natural mortality for maximum ages of 30. Fecundity was 1 and age at maturity was at age
12. With age-specific mortality, the population increase rate was 1.2%/year, and the generation time was about
16.45 years without exploitation. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the mortality of juvenile stage was the most

A comparison of a stage-based model and a yield per recruit model of the sandbar shark (Carcharhinus
plumbeus}. K.K. Brewster-Geisz and T.J. Miller, Chesapeake Biological Laboratory, University of Maryland Center
for Environmental Science, Solomons, MD 20688, USA.
A stage-based model of sandbar shark populations indicates that fishing mortality (F) needs to be reduced to 0.08 to
ensure sustainability of the population. This model assumes the natural mortality (M) is 0.10. However, stage-based
models do not consider the effect size limits may have on the fishery. We have used a yield per recruit (YPR)
analysis to examine the effects of adopting different size limits in the fishery. We used various growth parameter
estimates, an age of recruitment of 1, and M = 0.10. Based on estimates from Casey ef. al (1985), peak YPR occurs
at a combination of F = 0.40 and an age of first capture of 10 years or approximately 144 cm fork length (fl). When
growth parameter estimates from Casey and Natanson (1992) are used, peak YPR occurs at a combination of F =
0.30 and an age of first capture of 10 years or approximately 99 cm fl. Maximum YPR for F = 0.08, predicted by the
stage-based model, is approximately 80% of the peak YPRs found above, and occur at an age of first capture of
approximately 6 years. With growth parameters estimated for 1991 to 1992 from Sminkey and Musick (1995), peak
YPR occurs at an F = 0.45 and an age of first capture of 9 years or approximately 124 cm fl. In this case, maximum
YPR for F = 0.08 is approximately 75% of the peak YPR estimated and occurs at an age of first capture of
approximately 5 years. These results suggest that in order to have a stable population, YPR for each set of growth
parameter e^’mates must be 20 to 25% smaller than the peak YPR.

Local occurrence of basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus Gunnerus) in relation to spatio-temporal patterns
of zooplankton abundance. TJ. Thom. M.J. O'Connell, M.C. Lucas and L. Joplin, Department of Biological
Sciences, University of Durham, DH1 3LE, England, UK; A. Downie, Scottish Natural Heritage, Maritime Group 2
Anderson Place, Edinburh, EH6 5NP,Sootland, UK.
The distribution of basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus} around the Isle of Arran in the Clyde sea area on the west
coast of Scotland, UK was investigated during July 1997. A network of shore based volunteers conducted visual
searches between 06-00 and 22-00 from seven vantage points for a total of 1538 hours over 20 days between July 6
and 28. Twenty-nine sightings were recorded. A plankton sampling programme was carried out in the same area
and over the same time period. The majority of shark sightings occurred in the afternoon and evening corresponding
to an increase in zooplankton abundance during this period. Three peaks in shark sightings occurred over the study
period which followed peaks in zooplankton abundance with a lag of one to three days. The spatial distribution of
shark sightings was also associated with the distribution of zooplankton in the area. Increases in the number of
sharks occurred when zooplankton dry weights were at the maximum normally found in the area. This study, has
shown, therefore, that fine-scale spatio-temporal variability in the distribution of basking sharks can be explained in
terms of patchiness in the distribution and abundance of zooplankton.

Sharks associated with the gulf menhaden Brevoorlla patronus fishery and their relevance to shark
populations of the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. J.A. de Silva. Department of Oceanography and Coastal
Sciences, Louisiana State University, 153 Howe-Russell Geoscience, Baton Rouge LA 70803. USA; R.E. Condrey
and BA Thompson, Department of Oceanography and Coastal Sciences, Coastal Fisheries Institute, CCEER,
Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge LA 70803-7503. USA.
We describe the shark bycatch in the U.S. gulf menhaden fishery; their species composition, fates, distribution and
estimate the annual number of sharks caught by the fishery. Ten species of sharks were identified, with blacktip
sharks Carcharhinus limbatus accounting for 50% of those obsenred. Approximately 75% of the sharks encountered
died, 12% were released disoriented and 8% were released healthy. Using loglinear and logit models we determined
spatial and temporal patterns in the shark bycatch. Contrasts revealed the odds of observing a fishing set with shark
bycatch was significantly greater in June-August than September-October. The odds of observing shark bycatch
during April-May was also significantly different from September-October. However, these differences were only
apparent east of 93 degrees W (central Louisiana). For the 1994 and 1995 fishing seasons we estimated an annual
take of approximately 30,000 sharks. Stomach analyses on sharks indicated that the menhaden schools were
functioning as a foraging base tor those sharks captured. While detailed age and growth information were not
collected, comparisons to length distributions in the literature indicated that the fishery appears to be impacting the
summer nursery grounds of sharks in the northern Gulf of Mexico.

Length-at-birth of the sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus, in Delaware Bay. R.R. Merson. Department of
Biological Sciences, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, Rl 02881, USA; H.L. Praft(Jr.), National Oceanic and
Atmospheric Administration, National Marine Fisheries Service, Northeast Rsheries Science Center, 28 Tarzwell Dr.,
Narragansett, Rl 02882-1199, USA.
Young-of-the-year sandbar sharks grow in length before their umbilical scars are healed. This study takes that into
account by separating umbilical scar healing stages and produces a more accurate length-at-birth than studies which
report the tenths of sandbar sharks with open umbilical scars. We examined 798 sandbar sharks captured by gill
net or longline in Delaware Bay between 1995 and 1997. Six distinct umbilical scar healing stages were termed cord­
remains, open-fresh, partly-healed, mostly-healed, well-healed and none. Sharks with the three earliest umbilical
healing stages did not differ in length, thus represented the length-at-birth. The mean length-at-birth is 49.3 cm ±0.3
cm fork length (95% confidence interval, n=238) with a range of 40 to 55 cm fork length in Delaware Bay. Our
results are comparable to published reports of sandbar length-at-birth along the US east coast and therefore do not
support the hypothesis that sandbar sharks are bom 'somewhat' smaller in the northern pupping range.

The fishery for dogfish (Squalus acanthias} of British Columbia is one of the oldest shark fisheries in the world. This

Density effects of oophagous tadpoles of Chirbtaius elffingeri, (AnuraiRhacophoridae): Importance of
material brood care. Y.-C. Kam and Y.F. Tsai, Department of Biology, National Changhua University of
Education, Taiwan; C.F. Lin and Y.S. Un, Dept of Zook, National Taiwan University, Taiwan.
  We studied the density-dependent aspects of growth, development, and survivorship of arboreal tadpoles of
 Chirixaius eifUngeri in bamboo forests at the Experimental Forest of the National Taiwan University at Chitou,
Taiwan, from May-Septeinber 1995. Newly hatched tadpoles were randomly assigned to one of the three
treatments: low (LD), medium (MD), and high density (HD) (six, 18, and 54 tadpoies/bamboo stump, respectively),
and each treatment consisted of 15 replicates. Tadpoles are obligatorily oophagous; thus, growth, development, and
survivorship of tadpoles are totally dependent upon trophic egg availability. Tadpoles in all treatments increased in
mass during development, but LD and MD tadpoles grew faster and weighed signifioantly heavier than HD tadpoles
by week 5. During the first 5 weeks of development, the biomass increase of tadpoles (BMI) in successful nests was
substantially greater than zero and was significantly different between treatments, indicating that female frogs are
capable of increasing the supply of trophic eggs as the tadpole number increased in MD and HD treatments. Body
size at metamorphosis was density-dependent but the time required to reach metamorphosis was not, which was
different from earlier studies on pond breeders. This discrepancy is probably due to the different feeding habits (i.e.,
herbivory versus oophagy) and size-selective feeding behavior. Results suggest that the energetic reserves of
female frogs for brooding strongly affect the growth, development, and survivorship of tadpoles.

Contributions to the life history of the redback salamander: preliminary evidence for kin recognition. D.C.
Fgreslgr and C.L. Anders, Biological Sciences, Towson University, Towson, MD 21252 USA.
We tested two questions critical to the reproductive life history of the redback salamander (Pielhodon cinereus): (1)
Do females recognize and preferentially brood their own eggs during pair-wise discrimination trials? (2) Are
hatchlings able to recognize their mother using substrate-bome chemical cues, and if so, is this ability innate or
learned? To address the first question, we tested brooding females collected from the field within a few days of
oviposifion. They were given a choice of their own eggs and those of a conspecific female, and their association
monitored over a 24 h period. To address the second question we cottected 60 females within 24 h post-oviposition,
and divided thern into two groups. The eggs of group 1 were raised by their mothers until they hatched. The eggs
of group 2 were isolated on filter paper throughout development. Beginning at 2 weeks post-hatching, each juvenile
was tested twice (24 h each) in pair-wise trials contrasting unmarked filter paper with filter paper scented with
matema odors. Our results confinn maternal egg recognition in P. cinereus, and we present preliminary data
suggesting that juveniles chemically imprint on their mother during the prolonged maternal brooding period.

Mating system of the green anaconda (Eunectes murinus') in the Venezuelan Llanos.             J.A. Rivas. University of
Tennesse, Dept of FEB. Knoxville TN 37996-0900.
Sexual selection and mating system theories predict that individuals will be more selective the higher the mating
investment they make. Hence, animals that do not make a high reproductive investment will increase their fitness by
increasing number of matings, while animals that have a high investment per mating will be “choosy”. While studying
the mating system of the anaconda, we opportunistically collected 45 breeding aggregations for six years. Femies
lie apparently passive in shallow wafer while the males coil around her (males number from 1 to 17, with a mean of
3.8). No fights or ritualized displays were seen among the males. Each female is attractive to males for about four
weeks throughout the breeding season, which lasts from mid-February to mid-May. Longer males were found with
heavier females (r= 0.48; p= 0.008) and the latter were courted by a greater number of males {r= 0.44; p= 0.02 ).
This suggests that males prefer to court females with higher fecundity and breeding status, since random mating
would not produce this tendencies. Due to the short time that the breeding season lasts (in respect to the duration
of the breeding ball), and the fact that receptive females are not clumped together, it is unlikely that one male can
find many females in one season. Although a lot remains to be studied, it appears that the mating system of the
anacondas is polyandric; where males select the more fecund females.

Diet and reproduction of the Common Death Adder (Acanthophis antarcticus} from Papua New Guinea: Lack
of ecological convergence with vipers? C.L. Spencer. Dept, of Herpetology, California Academy of Sciences,
Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, CA 94110-4599.
Common death adders (Elapidae) from Australia have convergent reproductive and dietary adaptations with vipers.
They reproduce biannually, show ontogenetic shifts from endothermic to ectothermic prey, and are ambush
predators. I examined 208 Acanthophis antarcticus from the collections of the California Academy of Sciences.
Morphometric data, sex, age, seasonal reproductive status, size of eggs or follicles, and stomach and hindgut
contents were determined. Preliminary results suggest that approximately 30% of snakes had hindgut or stomach

gravid in December, implying annual reproductivity. Thus these smaller snakes are not displaying convergent
ecological characteristics with vipers like their Australian counterparts.

Prediction and Interpretation of the abundance of alligators In lentic environments. J.D. Everf-r*. "Department
of Zoology, University of Rorlda, Gainesville, Rorlda, , USA 32611; **US Geological Survey- Biological Resources
Division,, Gainesville, Florida, USA 32653.

Previous analyses indicated that American alligator (Alliaator mississippiensis) population densities in 60 Rorida
lakes were significantly correlated with parameters historically used to evaluate system trophic state (total
phosphorus, total nitrogen, water column chlorophyll a, and water transparency). Recent examination of these and
other data have begun to reveal some interesting patterns regarding environmental factors and the abundance of
this crocodilian. Alligator density was uncorrelated with limnetic zone fish biomass and only slightly correlated with
littoral zona fish biomass, but was strongly correlated with whole-lake fish biomass (r® = 0.45, p < 0.0001). Other
environmental factors which were found to covary with alligator population size were lake color (r® = 0.37, p <
0.0001) and macrophyte coverage (r® = 0.28, p = 0.0015); those which were inversely related were mean lake depth
(r®= 0.49, p < 0.0001) and percentage of human-developed shoreline (r® = 0.38, p < 0.0001). Finally, while as
much as 55% of the variation in alligator population densities among lakes could be accounted for by total
phosphorus (p < 0.0001), multiple linear regressions using other parameters (plant coverage, water transparency,
and fish biomass) could account for up to 78% of the variation in abundance (p < 0.0001). These models are
discussed with respect to ecological processes present in lakes and their usefulness to game managers and to
scientists who attempt to detect human impacts on populations.

Environmental variation and socioecology. J.C. Maerz. Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton, NY
13902-6000 USA.
 Animal dispersion patterns are influenced by the distribution and abundance of resources and other individuals, both
of which are features of the local environment. A previous study indicates that moisture determines the extent to
which food and mates are limited for red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus}, so predictable differences in
moisture levels between populations may result in different dispersion patterns. I monitored shelter use and
cohabitation at two sites (wetter vs. drier) using mark-recapture to determine whether shelter fidelity and incidence of
cohabitation differ between sites. Both males and females at the wetter site demonstrated lower fidelity, but only
females at the wetter site exhibited greater incidence of intrasexual cohabitation. Welter site males showed low
occurrences of intrasexual cohabitation, as did drier site males and females. These results indicate that
salamanders in wetter habitats may not hold fixed territories, probably in response to increased food availability.
Low fidelity arid low intrasexual cohabitation by wetter site males may indicate the existence of ephemeral mating
territories. Differences in spacing patterns in response to local environmental conditions may have important
repercussions for salamander population dynamics and sexual selection.

reef fishes. C. Gerstner. School of Natural Resources & Environment; University of Michioan: 430 East University

Spatial isolation in drainage lakes ; implications for community ecology of fishes.                 J.D. Olden. Dept of
Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 365.
Although lakes are often Inter-connected waterbodies, few studies have examined isolation among lakes as a
determiiiant of fish species diversity and/or community composition. In this study I examine the fish species
composition and spatial arrangement of 52 lakes located within two south-central Ontario watersheds, and assess
the degree of spatial isolation between lakes. Measures of lake isolation incorporated watercourse distance, lake
elevation, upstream watercourse distance, and waterbodies as fish "stepping stones". Many of these isolation
measures were based on ecological considerations, i.e. the "challenges" a fish faces in moving between lakes, as
compared to the straight-line distance between sampling locations which is.often used in studies of this nature. Eight
isolation measures were examined for their degree of association with patterns in fish species composition. The
results indicated that conventional straight-line distance between lakes does not accurately portray the degree of
isolation. This study illustrates the Importance of examining alternative measures of lake isolation when exploring
patterns in fish species distributions, since the isolaflon of waterbodies increase the rate of local extinotion.
Therefore, interconnected lakes could potentially provide a "rescue effect" for lakes with threatened aquatic fauna.

Revisiting a "textbook example" of natural selection in the wild: a field test of threat display convergence In
threespine sticklebacks. R.J. Scott. Bioibgy. Clark University. Worcester. MA 01610. USA.

Freshwater populations of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) exhibit a tremendous amount of adaptive
variation in a number of traits. One classic example is male nuptial colouration in populations from the Chehalis
River drainage basin in Washington State. Males in these populations assume a jet-black nuptial colouration,
rather than the red underside and blue-green dorsum that is typical of the species. A widely cited, yet poorly tested,
hypothesis to account for the evolution of the black nuptial colouration in these populations is the threat display
convergence hypothesis. The hypothesis contends that the black nuptial colouration evolved in response to
competition for nesting territories with the co-distributed Olympic mudminnow (Novumbra hubbsi), which is also
black, territorial for nest sites and breeds at the same time of year as stickleback. The hypothesis produces the
prediction that mudminnows have a greater impact on the reproductive success of typical, red male sticklebacks
than on that of black male sticklebacks.         I tested this prediction by manipulating the presence/absence of
mudminnows and the colour type of stickleback present in screened exclosures in several wetland areas (typical
nesting habitat for both species). Also, I condurrted several field surveys of nesting sticklebacks to determine (i) the
frequency and outcome of interactions between nesting sticklebacks and mudminnows and (ii) the temporal
development of black nuptial coloration.

A molecular phylogenetic analysis of the relationships among the Iguanid lizard genus Liolaemus: testing
alternative biogeographic hypotheses. J.A. Schulte(ll). Washington University Campus Box 1137 St. Louis, MO
63130-4899 USA.
Liolaemus is a large genus of lizards in the family Iguanidae with greater than 160 species distributed throughout the
southern half of South America on either side of the Andes. Relationships among Liolaennjs species remain
unresolved. Approximately 1800 bases of aligned mitochondrial DNA sequence data were obtained from regions
encoding the ND1, ND2, COI, and eight transfer RNA genes. A phylogenetic hypothesis is generated for 55 ingroup
species and four outgroup species. Four alternative biogeographic hypotheses are suggested for the early
diversification of Liolaemus. The most parsimonious tree is highly suggestive of an east-west vicariant split due to
the uplift of the Andes at least 10-15 million years ago.

We surveyed tnitoohondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variation in the sagebrush lizard (Sceloponjs graciosus) from
throughout California, as well as populations from Oregon. Utah. New Mexico, and Baja California, including all three
currently recognized subspecies. We used these data to estimate the intraspecific phylogeny and to develop a

Freeze avoidance and terrestrial overwintering in the northern cricket frog, Acris crepitans.                 J.T. Irwin.
Department of Zoology, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio 45056 USA.
Anurans inhabiting northern locales survive the winter by avoiding cold through aquatic hibernation or burrowing, or
by tolerating freezing of their tissues. This study describes the ovenwintering strategy of the most aquatic of the North
American hylids, the northern cricket frog (Acris crepitans). Laboratory choice tests indicated that cricket frogs
choose terrestrial hibernacula, especially under leaf litter in shallow depressions, when faced with decreasing
temperatures. However, unlike Bufo and some Pseudacris, cricket frogs did not burrow when air temperatures
dropped, even when faced with desiccating conditions. Surprisingly, cricket frogs are not freeze tolerant like most
other nearctic hylids that hibernate in terteslrial sites. Given these data, field searches were conducted and cricket
frogs were found hibernating in crayfish burrows and other cavities along the pond's edge - sites which provide full
protection from freezing. In conclusion, cricket frogs can neither burrow nor sunrive freezing, and therefore require
pre-existing subterranean sites to successfully overwinter. Thus, I suggest that habitat quality and winter severity be
explored as possible causes of this species' decline in the northern portion of its range.

Adaptation to life in estuarine environments In the northern water snake (Nerodla sipedori). P.L. Martin and
W.M. Roosenburg, Ohio University, Dept. Bio Soi., Irvine Hall, Athens, Ohio 45701 USA.
The purpose of this investigation was to identify differences in resource allocation strategies between freshwater and
brackish water populations of the Northern Water Snake, Nerodia sipedon. Vfe also sought evidence that
populations of the Northern Water Snake ate adapting to estuarine environments. Gravid females were collected
from two brackish and two freshwater sites. The snakes' reproductive outputs were estimated using relative clutch
mass, adjusted for female condition. Neonates from each erivironment were raised in both freshwater and 25% sea
wafer to determine the environmental effects on growth, metabolism, and survival. Freshwater snakes allocated
40% more energy to reproduction than estuarine snakes. The growth rates of both groups were reduced in 25% sea
water. However, the freshwater neonates raised in 25% sea water became bloated and suffered 40% mortality. The
metabolic rates of estuarine snakes was significantly higher in both environments, llie results indicate that
freshwater snakes allocate a greater proportion of their energy to growth and reproduction, while estuarine snakes
incur a higher maintenance cost. Sufficient physiological and behavioral differentiation has occurred between these
ecologically distinct populations such that freshwater snakes suffer a substantially reduced fitness in estuarine
environments.

reproductiyo output in year two. In years one and two, paedomorphic individuals underwent metamorphosis during
the following Spring/Summer. Very few larvae were encountered in year three. As a result, relatively few efts
emigrated in the fall of year three. However, there was a large immigration of individuals (>2,000) from the
surrounding uplands. Although paedomorphosis occurred, the vast majority of reproductive newts were aquatic
adults in year three.

Variation In reproduction and its association with the maternal phenotype within a population of the
Galapagos lava lizard (Microlophus delanonis). M.A. Jordan. Department of Biology, University of New Mexico,
Albuquerque, NM 87131, USA.
Physical aspects of the maternal phenotype are recently recognized as important covariates of the nature of
reproduction (ie size vs. number of eggs). We document variation in reproductive phenology, total clutch mass,
clutch size and egg mass' among seasons and years within a natur^ population of Galpagos lava lizards
[Microlophus (=Tropidunjs) delanonis). Maternal size correlates with total clutch mass, clutch size, and egg mass
but does not affect the pattern of variation in these traits among time periods. We estimated maternal condition (a

characteristics explain some seasonal and annual variation In components of reproduction, we propose that
remaining temporal variation may be a response to differences between seasons In direct selection on eqqs and/or
hatchlings.

  Locomotor performance and reproductive success using DNA fingerprinting In male Eastern Fence Lizards,
  Sceloporus undulatus. G.J. Haenel and H.B. John-Alder, Cook College, Rutgers University, 84 Lipman Drive, New
  Brunswick, NJ 08901-8525, USA; LC. Seitz, Laboratoire d'Ecologie, CNRS URA 258, Universite Pierre et Marie
  Curie, 7 quai St. Bernard, Case 237, F-75252 Paris Cedex 05, France .
  Variatiori in locomotor performance may have important implications for fitness. Endurance can vary greatly (>10X)
  among lizards within a single population. We are using DNA fingerprinting in a natural population of the Eastern
  Fence Lizard, Sceloporus undulatus, to investigate the relationship of endurance to reproductive success. We
  studied a population of Eastern Fence Lizards in the New Jersey Pine Barrens to determine characteristics such as
  homerange, body size, and survivorship. Endurance was measured by running lizards on a treadmill at constant
  speed. Maternity was determined by having females lay their eggs in the lab. We established paternity by comparing
  minisatellite DNA fingerprint profiles of offspring hatched in the lab to the DNA fingeqjifnt profiles of their mothers
  and all potential fathers found on the field site. Reproductive success was measured as the number of clutches sired
  by each male. DNA fingerprinting data reveals a significant positive correlation between endurance and reproductive
  success. Male-female homerange overlap is a poor indicator of paternity in this population, and larger males tended
  to mate with larger females. Because endurance Is variable and positively related to reproductive success, selection,
  at least at the phenotypic level, can operate on endurance in this population.

Embryonic development of Sceloporus lizards: do cold climates favor rapid development? R.M. Andrews, T.
Mathies, C.P. Qualls and F.J. Qualls, Department of Biology, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University,
Blacksburg, VA 24061, USA.
Rapid embryonic development is a potential adaptation to cold climates. We tested this hypothesis for nine species
of Sceloporus lizards from four species groups and one species of Urosaurus, an outgroup, using observations
corrected for incubation temperature and hatchling size. Phylogenetioally based comparisons indicated that relatively
rapid development is characteristic of the scalaris species group and relatively slow development is characteristic of
the undulatus species group. Comparisons within these lineages were therefore used to determine if developmental
rate was related to climate, as judged by elevation and latitude. Within the scalaris species group, the
developmental rates of cool climate populations of S. aeneus and S. scalaris were not faster than that of a warm
climate population of S. scalaris. Within the undulatus species group, the developmental rate of a cool climate
populations or species were faster than that of a warm climate population or species for only one of five comparisons
(S. undulatus hyadnthinus from both Missouri and Virginia had tester development than S. wood! from Florida). In
general; developmental rates of Sceloponjs are lineage specific and do not appear to be adapted to local climates.

Developmental arrest determines embryonic stage at ovlpositlon In the lizard, Urosaurus omatus. T. Mathies
and R.M. Andrews, Department of Biology, Virginia Polytechnic Institute, Blacksburg, VA 24061 USA.
Determinants of embryonic stage at oviposition in the oviparous lizard, Urosaurus omatus were investigated to gain
insight into the reason(s) that most squamate reptiles oviposit when embryos reach stage 30. Eggs experimentally
retained in utero past the normal time of oviposition were compared with control eggs that were obtained at the
normal time of oviposition and incubated in incubation medium. Retention resulted in developmental arrest of
embryos at embryo stages 30.0-30.5. Embryogenesis could be re-initiated at any time up to at least 29 days pqst the
normal time of oviposition by removing eggs from the oviducts and incubating them in incubation medium.
Developmental arrest per se, did not affect the time it took eggs to hatch once eggs were removed from the oviducts.
Hatching success of these eggs was high (87%). Snout-vent length, hydration of body tissue, and locomotor
performance of hatchlings, were negative^ related to the time spent in developmental arrest. Retention of eggs had
no apparent adverse efrects on females. Developmental arrest, if widespread among squamates, would account for
the obsenred distribution of embryo stages at oviposition and may constitute a major constraint on the evolution of
viviparity.

The spatial distribution and timing of sexual receptivity of female snakes are important determinants of snake mating
systems. We examined spatio-temporal aspects of timber rattlesnake mating behavior through radiotelemetric
monitoring of female snakes. The onset of mating activity, indicated by the the arrival of courting males, was
synchronized within a four day period in late July, despite females being 1-5 km apart. Most pairings (7 of 9)
occurred during the first three weeks of August. Females enhanced their spatial predictability by becoming attractive
to males during shedding at discrete rock outcrops, and by moving between spatially distant outcrops when
receptive. Our findings suggest female rattlesnakes increase male competition, and hence the quality of mates,
through active advertisement of sexual receptivity at low personal cost.

Geometric morphometries as cladistic characters; evaluation using armored catfishes.                     S. Schaefer,
Department of Ichthyology, American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th Street, New York, NY
10024-5192, U.S.A.
Zelditch and Rnk have argued that the method of thin-plate splines decomposed by its partial warps can yield
phylogenetically informative characters, which can be subjected to the same tests of homology and character
independence as are applied to conventional morphological characters. Suitability of the method for cladistics has
been challenged on both theoretical and empirical grounds. The hypoptopomatine lorioariids were used to evaluate
the method by examining the extent to which geometric morphometric characters thus identified are congnient with
respect to the generic-level phylogeny for the group established on the basis of independent morphological
characters. Of 15 partial warps describing head shape derived from 18 homologous landmarks, six yielded
potentially infomiative contrasts between six ingroup and two outgroup taxa. Two contrasts were congruent with the
phylogeny, three were incongnrent, and one was autapomorphio. Two incongnient characters mapped identically
onto me cladogram, suggesting non-independence. Partial warp homology and the extent to which the method
converged upon stable definitions of characters were examined via empirical simulations involving permutation of
key parameters.

Revision of the loricarild catfish genus Cochliodon and the evolution of wood-eating.              J,W- Armbruster,
Division of Ashes, Smithsonian Institution. Washington, DC 20560, USA.
In fishes, only two distantly related groups of suckermoufh armored catfishes (Loricariidae) are known to eat wood:
Panaque and the Hypostomus cochliodon species group. The two groups share several modifications to the skull for
increasing muscle attachment sites and have large, spoon-shaped teeth set in highly angled Jaws which they use to
remove small shavings from submerged logs. Studying the morphological evolution of wood-eating in Panaque is
made difficult because Panaque is part of a larger group of fishes which share many of the modifications necessary
for wood-eating but which do not eat wood. The H. cochliodon group, on the other hand, appears to have been
derived from strictly algivorous species; thus, the transition to wood-eating can be better examined. The H.
cochliodon group was found to contain several undescribed species including several that appear to have teeth
intemiediate between the long, thin teeth used lor algivory in most Hypostomus and the short, spoon-shaped teeth
used for xylophagy in the H. cochliodon group. In this study, the H. cochliodon group was revised and a phylogeny
was produced containing most of the species groups of Hypostomus to assess the evolution of the morphology
associated with xylophagy.

Phylogenetic relationships of the suckermouth minnows, genus Phenacoblus, inferred from parsimony
analyses of nucleotide sequence, allozymic and morphological data (Cyprinidae: Cypriniformes). W.W..
Dimmick. University of Kansas, Museum of Natural History, Lawrence. KS 66045; B.M. Burr, Department of Zoology,
Southern Illinois University al Carbondale, IL 62901, U.S A
We investigated the phylogenetic relationships among the five species of the genus Phenacoblus (Cyprinidae;
Cypriniformes) using a combined analysis of molecular and morphological characters. The nucleotide characters
were comprised of 208 potentially infomiative sites among a total 1773 aligried base pairs from several segments of

The Labridae is a diverse, circumtropioal family of marine fishes composed of over 700 species in over 80 genera.
Relationships among labrid genera, among the labrid subgroups cunently recognized, and affinities between the
Labridae and other perciform families are poorly understood. In this study, a character survey of labrid osteology,
musculature, connective tissues, neuroanatomy, and internal organs is presented. Taxa examined included
members of all labrid tribes, as well as scarid and odacid fishes that are nested within the Labridae. Outgroups
examined include cichlids, pomacentrids, embiotocids, gerreids, sparids and other perciform taxa. New osteological
features include morpholo^ of the neurocranium, axial skeleton, and pterygiophores. Phylogenetically Informative
characters were discovered in the abductor musdes of the pectoral fins, the inclinator muscles of the dorsal fin,
caudal musculature, and the shape of the myomeres. Useful characters of internal anatomy include the coiling
Eattems of the gut and neuroanatomical features. Brain structure is particularly character-rich. Conclusions: The
  abridae are clearly monophyletic based on numerous new characters. Weak support continues for labroid
monophyly. Most previous labrid tribes and subfamilies are not natural groups. Scarids and odacids are labrids.

analyses of nucleotide sequence, allozymic and morphological data (Cyprinidae: Cypriniformes). W.W.
Dimmiek. University of Kansas, Museum of Natural History. Lawrence, KS 66045; B.M. Burr, Department of Zoology.
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale. IL 62901. U.S.A.
We investigated the phylogenetic relationships among the five species of the genus Phenacobius (Cyprinidae:
Cypriniformes) using a combined analysis of molecular and morphological characters. The nucleotide characters
were comprised of 208 potentially informative sites among a total 1773 aligned base pairs from several segments of
mitochondrial genes encoding the large and small RNA subunits, the valine transfer RNA. and the ND2 protein
coding gene. Allozyrne products from 23 polymorphic loci and 9 morphological characters that were taken from the
literature were also included in the total evidence analysis. Third position codon sites were demonstrated to be
saturated for transitional changes and unsuitable for phylogeny reconstruction among the species studied here. The
total evidence phylogeny is isomorphic with Mayden's (1989) morphological hypothesis. Phenacobius mirabiiis was
found to be basal, followed in ascending order by P. teretuius, P. catostomus, P. crassiiabrum and P. uranops.

sometimes breeds successfully in the presence of fish. I investigated the co-occurrence of breeding A. maculatum

importance of the effects of the presence/absence of fish, pH, Secchi depth, lake area, and the forest type
surrounding the lakes on the density of egg masses in lakes. Variation in egg mass density among the lakes was
significantly related to the presence/absence of fish (excluding Salvelinus fontinalis}, but was not related to any of the
other habitat variables. The lanrae were palatable to fishes, but lanrae successfully reached metamorphosis in at
least one lake despite the presence of fish. Although presence of fish was the most important factor in the suitability
of a breeding site to A. matxrlatum, fish did not completely exclude A. maculatum. The use of refuges, spatially
complex habitats, and a bet-hedging life history, are potential ways in which A. maculatum can reproduce despite the

muscosa in Dusy Basin. Kings Canyon National Park. K.M. MaHhews. K.L. Pope''’ and D.B. Court, 'US Forest
Service Pacific Southwest Research Station, P.O. Box 245, Berkeley, CA 94701, USA; California Polytechnic State
University, San Luis Obispo, Department of Biology, San Luis Obispo, CA 93407, USA.
Rana muscosa was once common throughout high elevation areas of the Sierra Nevada but has declined pnmarily
due to widespread stocking of non-native trout. To understand Rana muscosa habitat needs, we initiated a
telemetric study in 1997 to determine home ranges and movement patterns during the summer and fall when their
high elevation habitats (>3000 m) are accessible. We used radio transmitters and GPS to map the ocations of 24
frogs in Dusy Basin. During the summer frogs were distributed throughout the basin in a variety of lakes, m August
12 tagged frogs showed no movement away from the small lakes where they were originally captured and tagged,
and their home ranges were small (within 50 m). In September 8 of 9 frogs moved up to 200 m away from their
original capture lakes. By October, when lakes began freezing, frogs were found in only two lakes along the

more widely distributed during the summer, and become more restricted in their distribution as the lakes freeze.
Future restoration strategies should ensure their access to their summer and winter habitats.

Overwintering habitats of radio-impianted green frogs, Rana clamitans. V.S. Lamoureux and D.M. Madison,
Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton, N.Y. 13902-6000 USA.
Winter's freezing temperatures exert a major selective force on temperate frogs and toads. The selection of an
overwintering site that provides protection from freezing is critical forthose species without freeze tolerance. Many
freeze intolerant frogs, such as the green frog (Rana clamitans}, are commonly assumed to overwinter at the bottom
of shallow, eutrophic, breeding ponds. Although anurans overwintering in pond bottoms would avoid freezing, these
environments are highly anoxic for the majority of winter. Since adult ranids cannot tolerate anoxia for even limited
periods of time, it is unlikely that pond bottoms would be suitable overwintering sites. Anurans may need to undergo
extensive movements in search of suitable overwintering sites that remain unfrozen and provide adequate oxygen for
survival We used radio implants to determine overwintering habitats of the green frog in southern New York state.
In late fall, green frogs moved 80-480 m from their summer breeding ponds to streams and seeps that remained
flowing and unfrozen throughout winter. We suggest that these sites are chosen because they remain unfrozen and
remain well oxygenated.

How vsnom-conductlng fangs are formed. K, Jackson, Museum of Comparative Zoology. Harvard University
Cambndge,, MA 02138, U.S.A.

Venom-delivery systems occur in at least four families of snakes. In viperids, elapids, and atractaspidids, the venom-
aehvery system is front-fanged, and consists of a hollow fang and a venom gland associated with compressor
muscles, which squeeze venom into a duct, which cam’es it to the proximal end of the fang, where it enters the
wnom canal. In venomous colubrids the fang is grooved rather than hollow, and positioned at the posterior end of
me maxilla. It is not known how many times the venom-delivery system has been independently derived in snakes.
This study was initially undertaken to determine how venom-conducting fangs form during development in differerit
groups of snakes, in the hope that fois might shed light on the question of how venom-conducting fangs were arrived

Application of a modified index of biotic integrity to detect changes in fish assemblages in a historically
de^aded river system. R.B. Evans. The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996 USA.

The New River, a tributary of the Big South Fork of the Cumberland River in northeast Tennessee, has been
degraded by siltation associated with coal mine drainage. Electrofishing samples from 42 localities in 1996 revealed
recent increases in ths range of intolerant species and the return of extirpated fishes to the river system. A modified
index of biotic integrity (IBI), relative to the New River, was compiled using components of fish assemblages
(metrics) that reflect the impacts of siltation. Replicate fish samples were obtained by using a bootstrap resampling
algorithm that enabled tests for significant differences among IBI scores. Comparisons of IBI scores from 13
electrofishing samples completed in 1977 and repeated during 1996 indicate that the health of fish assemblages and
water quality have improved during the past two decades.

freeze intolerant frogs, such as the green frog (Rana clamitans), are commonly assumed to overwinter at the bottom
of shallow, eutrophic, breeding ponds. Although anurans overwintering in pond bottoms would avoid freezing, these
environments are highly anoxic for the majority of winter. Since adult ranids cannot tolerate anoxia for even limited
periods of time, it is unlikely that pond bottoms would be suitable ovenwintering sites. Anurans may need to undergo
extensive movements in search of suitable ovenwintering sites that remain unfrozen and provide adequate oxygen for
survival. We used radio implants to determine ovenwintering habitats of the green frog in southern New York state.
In late fall, green frogs moved 80-480 m from their summer breeding ponds to streams and seeps that remained
flowing and unfrozen throughout winter. We suggest that these sites are chosen because they remain unfrozen and
remain well oxygenated.




How vonom-conducting fangs are formed.                K. Jackson. Museum or Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.
Cambridge,, MA 02138, U.S A.

Venom-delivery systems occur in al least four families of snakes. In viperids, elapids, and atractaspidids, the venom­
delivery system is front-fanged, and consists of a hollow fang and a venom gland associated with compressor
muscles, which squeeze venom into a duct, which carries if to the proximal end of the fang, where it enters the
venom canal. In venomous colubrids the fang is grooved rather than hollow, and positioned at the posterior end of
the maxilla. It is not known how many times the venom-delivery system has been independently derived in snakes.
This study was initially undertaken to determine how venom-conducting fangs form during development in different
groups of snakes, in the hope that this might shed light on the question of how venom-conducting fangs were arrived
at evolutionarily. It was found that published descriptions of fang formation in snakes disagree about how fangs are
formed. This disagreement is discussed along with developmental differences between fangs in embryonic snakes
and replacement fangs in adult snakes, and their implications for reoonstrocting the evolutionary history of snakes.

A description of flight in the flying snake, Chrysopelea paradisi. J.J. Socha. Department of Organismal Biology
and Anatomy, University of Chicago, 1027 East 571h St., Chicago, IL 60637 USA.
Passive (gliding) flight has been studied in some vertebrate fliers, but is essentially unexplored in the flying snakes of
the genus Chrysopelea. Four specimens of Chiysopelea paradisi were videotaped in flight from a height of 11
meters. Seventy-five total flights were recorded. For comparison, locomotion of the snake in water and on land were
also recorded. Chrysopelea is capable of beginning its flight either in mid-air or from a controlled launch. In a
launch, the body is coiled back against the substrate, then sprung forward horizontally. By the end of the launch, the
body is flattened dorsoventrally from head to venL In Hight the snake undulates laterally in a swimming-like motion
with the body in a plane parallel with the ground. The amplitude of undulation in air is more than twice that of
undulation in water. Over the course of a flight, the frequency of undulation decreases. Upon landing, the snake
contacts the ground tail first, then body, and head last. The snake is capable of extensive maneuvering in flight, able
to turn ninety degrees within a meter. Video clips of the flight will be shown.

Tale of two puffers: Do motor patterns change with a shift in muscle insertion?                     J.E. Austin and P.C.
Wainwright, Dept, of Biological Sciences. Florida State, University, Tallahassee, FL 32306 USA.
Durophagous fishes of the order Tetraodontiformes use stalwart teetii and jaws to process prey. Idiosyncratic in their
reliance on oral manipulation and crushing during feeding, they possess a relatively complex adductor mandibulae
musculature as compared to those fishes of the ancestral, pharyngeal jaw-processing persuasion. A1 and A2
adductor mandibulae muscles orchestrate the closing and biting forces. Dog-faced pufferfishes in the genus Arothron
possess a plesiomorphic insertion of the A2 muscle on the lower jaw. Southern puffers of the genus Sphoeroides, in
contrast, have a novel shift in A2 insertion from the dentary to the maxilla. Lack of linkage between anatomical
change and subsequent functional consequence serves to reinforce motor pattern conservation during muscle
evolution. Electromyographic recordings of jaw muscles from both genera were taken as puffers fed on prey of
varying texture (fiddler crabs and shrimp). Quantified with EMG variables Including burst duration, relative onset and
intensSy, motor pattern differences were manifest only in an across-the-board earlier onset of adductor firing in
Southern puffers.

A field population of bullfrog tadpoles with a highly female-biased sex ratio. L.C. Rania and C.R. Propper,
Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff. Arizona 86011, USA.
The timing of the occurrence of sex differentiation is variable among anuran amphibians. While some frog species
erdiibit sexual differentiation after metamorphosis, others differentiate during the larval period. In order to determine
the timing of sexual differentiation in the bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana, we collected 82 tadpoles from a fish hatchery in
northern Arizona. Upon histological examination we found that differentiation was evident by Gosner Stage 35.
Furthermore, among differentiated animals, 88,6% of the popijlation was female, with only 11.5% of the population
being male. Two of the male specimens had poorly organized seminiferous tubules with oocytes embedded within
the testicular tissue. One female had a polynuclear oocyte. We cannot say what may have affected this population
of bullfrog tadpoles, but our histological results suggest that these animals may have been exposed to some form of
xenobiotic contamination.
