The effects of xenobiotics on larval development in the bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana}.         S.G. Faraoher, L.C.
Rania and C.R. Propper, Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University. Flagstaff, Arizona 86011,
USA.
Xenobiotic compounds have been hypothesized to disrupt normal growth and development and induce gross
morphological mutations and abnornialities. Embryonic exposure to endocrine disnjpting compounds may alter the
formation of endocrine tissues, leading to abnormalities in the timing or outcome of the sexual differentiation of
gonadal tissue. Previous research demonstrated the occurrence of gonadal abnormalities in juvenile alligators
collected from a contaminated lake site (Guillette, Crain, and Rooney, 1997). In a study examining the
developmental timing of sexual differentiation of Rana catesbeiana from a local fish hatchery, we were surprised to
find a highly skewed, female biased sex ratio (Rania, ef al., personal txjmmunication). Histological preparations
revealed abnormalities in the differentiation of the gonadal tissue of many of these individuals. One hypothesis from
this result is that some xenobiotic compounds may be affecting sexual differentiation in R. catesbeiana. Vie
conducted two experiments to test this hypothesis. First, we treated larval R. catesbeiana with endosulfan, a locally
sprayed pesticide that is known to be weakly estrogenic. We found significanf differences in weight and mortality
among 4 treatments (3 concentrations anti a control) over a three week period. Next, we treated larval fl.
catesbeiana with zineb, a commonly used herbicide in the U.S.. We found no statistical differences in weight or
length among 5 treatments (4 concentrations and a control), although there were significant differences in mortality.
These data suggest that larval bullfrogs exposed to pesticides may suffer deleterious effects.

changes In photoperiod and temperature. However, there is little direct evidence concerning environmental control
of downstream migratory behavior. Seasonal timing of physiological and behavioral changes associated with
increased temperatures was examined. Atlantic salmon parr and pre-smolts were tagged with passive integrated

influence on migration must be considered when contemplating survival of hatchery and wild smolts to the marine
stags.

Declining temperature Influences the osmoregulatory physiology of American shad, Alosa sapldissima,
restricting the timing of seaward migration. J. Zydlewski‘° and S.D. McCormick’-*', "Conte Anadromous Rsh
Research Center, BRDAJSGS, 1 Migratory Way, Turners Falls, MA 01376 USA; ‘University of Massachusetts,
Department of Biology, Amherst, MA , USA.
Osmoregulatory abilities of American shad must be coordinated with migrations between fresh water (FW) and
seawater (SW). Shad develop the ability to tolerate SW at larval-juvenile transition (26-45 d post-hatch) coincident
with 3.5 and 10-fold increases in chloride cell (CC) number and gill Na’,K*-ATPase activity respectively. Although
only early development is limited to low salinities, shad remain in FW for 5-6 months (until autumn). During autumnal
migration juveniles lose the ability to osmoregulate in FW, evidenced by a decline in plasma chloride (20%). Shad
kept in the laboratory through Dec. experience large declines in plasma chloride (68%) and high mortality. Gill
Na+,K*-ATPase activity increases 3-fold and gill CC's on the primary and secondary lamellae Increase 2-fold and 1.5-
fold; these are likely to be compensatory mechanisms for increasing ion uptake. Changes in plasma chloride, gill
Na'',K-’-ATPase, and CC's are reduced and delayed if shad are maintained at 24°C versus a natural decline in
temperature. Impaired osmoregulatory ability, as influenced by temperature, may serve as a proximate cue for
migration. Changes In temperature (e.g. global warming) will likely alter the timing of migration.

Dept. Biology, York University, North York Ontario M3J 1P3; M.S. Ridgway, Aquatic Ecosystems Science Section,

Among salmonines (trout, salmon, char), there is a consistent trend for large females to spawn before small ones
within a breeding season. This pattern may be related to competition for limited spawning sites or, alternatively,
small females may delay reproduction as an adaptive tactic to minimise brood loss. Females routinely lose broods
through the subsequent use of nest sites by other females. Broods of small females are more likely to be lost by this
distuitiance because nest depth is related to body size. We tested these alternative hypotheses by detaining the
largest females in a marked population of lake-spawning brook trout (Saivelinus fontinalis). The competition
hypothesis predicts small females would breed earlier in the absence of large females, whereas the adaptive tactic
hypothesis predicts delayed breeding. Consistent with our second hypothesis, small females spawned significantly
later during the experimental year (1996) compared to the previous two years. Furthermore, brood loss was
significantly reduced. Within seasons, brood loss was significantly higher for small than large females. Site choice
may also play an important role in reproductive success. We show that small females increase reproductive
success by delayed reproduction and suggest that this adaptive tactic may be socially mediated.

The effects of population structure on the timing of reproductive    activity In male fathead minnows

Size-dependent asynchrony in the seasonal timing of reproduction has been well documented tor fish in temperate

differences in eriergy allocation do not account for differences in their phenology. Preliminary analyses also indicate
that the production and size of young produced by small 'uninhibited' males was not significantly different from the

Seasonal aspects of resource allocation In Ambystoma opacum: Implications for population dynamics. D.£_
Scott, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802 USA.
Marbled salamanders (Ambystoma opacum') inhabit woodlands throughout much of the easterri United States.
Adults typically migrate to temporary pond breeding sites en masse in early autumn, where courtship, breeding, arid
terrestrial oviposition occur over a 3-4 week period. Energetically "spent" adults leave the site with virtually all lipid
stores depleted. Experimental manipulations of food level suggest that adult reproductive frequency is dependent on
prior food acquisition; thus food availability in the terrestrial habitat may partly explain the wide
among-individual variation in year-to-year breeding patterns.
Larval success is highly dependent on the timing of pond filling and drying: hydroperiod directly affects mortally
and strongly influences competitive and predatory interactions. Per-capita food resources in the larval stage
determine larval growth rates, larval period, body size at metamorphosis, and a suite of post-metamorphio adult
traits Although variation in larval period can be substantial, there is surprisingly little vanation in the absolute date
of metamorphosis. Larvae from eggs hatched 3-mo apart generally metamorphose within a few weeks of each other,
regardless of whether the aquatic habitat remains suitable for growth. Later-hatching larvae therefore metarnorphose
at a smaller size in spite of the strong relationship between body size at metamorphosis and traits related to adult
fitness.
Food resources available to individuals in both the aquatic and terrestrial stages of the life cycle affect the resource
allocation “decisions' a salamander makes. Understanding allocation decisions is critical to modeling the population
dynamics of Ambystoma opacum.

Differential timing of maturation and reproduction the salamander, Ambystoma talpoldeum.                     T.J. Byan*'.
■Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken SC 29802 USA; R.D. Semlitsoh, ‘■Divsion of Biological
Sciences, Univeristy of Missouri, Columbia MO 65211 USA.
Variation in abiotic parameters determines the timing of reproduction in many semi-aquatic amphibians; hence, ^e
timinq of first reproduction is constrained by extrinsic (e.g., temperature and rainfall) rather than intrinsic (e.g., the
rate of qametogenesis) factors. Adaptations that release organisms from extrinsic factors may have important
Individual- and population-level implications. We describe the pattern of metamorphosis and maturation in natural
and experimental populations of the salamander Ambystoma talpoideum. Prior to first reproduction (usually at 1-yr
post-hatching), individuals that metamorphose are sexually immature when leaving the aquatic envirorimerjt, and
must mature in the terrestrial environment. Maturation, however, may precede metamoyhosis. Individuals, that
mature prior to metamorphosis remain in the aquatic environment (i.e., become "paedomorphic ), are physiologically
capable of breeding at the start of the breeding season, In the early fall. Terrestrial adults, however, must wait for the
proper suite of environmental conditions to initiate migration to the aquatic breeding habitats, which may be delayed
until mid to late winter. The result is a potentially large difference in the timing of reproduction be^een the two
morphs. The consequences of differential maturation and reproduction among individuals may collectively have
larger population-level effects.

Soil composition and moisture influence the cold hardiness of hatchling painted turtles (Chrysemys picta).
J.P. Costanzo and J.D. Litzgus. Department of Zoology, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio 45056, USA; J.B. Iverson,
Department of Biology, Earlham College, Richmond, Indiana, 47374, USA; R.E. Lee(Jr.), Department of Zoology,
Miami University, Oxford, Ohio 45056, USA.
Painted turtles [Chrysemys picta) hatch in late summer but usually remain in the nest during winter. Hatchlings earn
survive subzero temperatures in the nest either by tolerating the freezing of their body tissues, at temperatures ,,-4
°C, or by avoiding ice nucleation and remaining supercooled (unfrozen) to temperatures at least as low as '12 °C.
We investigated the effects of soil composition and soil moisture on susceptibility to ice inoculation in hatchling
turtles endemic to the sandhills of Nebraska, where soil moisture in winter is variable (range 4-14%). Turtles cooled
in frozen, native soil (predominantly sand) froze at -1.6 °C, whereas turtles cooled iri frozen soil to which clay or peat
was added supercooled to -13 °C before freezing. Avoidance of inoculation by environmental ice in turtles exposed
to frozen native soil was possible only when the soil contained liffle moisture (<4%). Thus, survival of relatively low
nest temperatures, by supercooling, may be greater for turtles hibernating in sandy soils containing little moisture, or
in soils containing clay or organic matter. However, the winter microenvironment contains numerous ice nuclei (e.g.,
inorganic particulates, microorganisms) that may nevertheless promote inoculative freezing.

Field and laboratory studies on active and resting body temperatures of a nocturnal, tropical snake (Boiga
irregularis). N.L. Anderson. B. Coupe. G. Perry, T. Hetherington and J. Williams, The Ohio State Universrty,
Department of Zoology. 1735 Neil Ave., Room 104 Botany and Zoology Building. Columbus, Ohio 43210, USA.
Although studies of body temperature (Tb) are extensive for snakes living in temperate regions, few studies have
focused on tropical, nocturnal snakes. Temperature sensitive radiotransmitters were used to record coelomic

actively thermoregulate. The situations for active snakes is unclear. Captive snakes with access to temepratures
between 22 - 43 °C attained greater Tb while active al night (30 - 33 °C) than free ranging snakes (25 - 26 °C) limited
to ambient temperatures between 24 - 26 °C. The difference in Tb might represent selection of a 30 - 33 °C Tb by
captive snakes or be an artifact of movement patterns through the thermal mosaic.

Constraints on life histories of temperate-zone snakes: is the price of viviparity very high?                  P,T. Gregory,
Dept, of Biology, University of Victoria, P.O. Box 3020 STN CSC, Victoria B.C. V8W 3N5.
In the highly seasonal environments of the north temperate zone, ectothermic animals such as snakes suffer
significant temporal constraints on their annual cycles, with consequences for their life histories and demographies.
For example, cold winters prohibit any activity at all, but summers also may be cool, further restricting activity. In
presumed evolutionary response to this, most temperate-zone snakes are viviparous; gravid feipales exhibit precise
behavioural thermoregulation, apparently providing optimal developmental conditions for their young. Howevec
thermoregulation often conflicts with other activities such as feeding. In fact, in many species, gravid females feed
liffle or not at all, even in captivity. The main demographic consequences of this are reduced future reproductive
output, especially through decreased reproductive frequency of individual females. Nonetheless, this tradeoff may be
relatively unimportant in the long run because many snakes are long-lived “bet-hedging" species and compensate for
low reproductive output in one year by surviving to reproduce at a later date. I illustrate these ideas with data for
garter snakes (Thamnophis) and rattlesnakes (Crotalus).

Among the most critically endangered sturgeon species worldwide are those in the genus Pseudoscaphirhynchus
(Scaphirhynchinae), which are endemic to the Syr Darya (P. fedtschenkoij and Amu Darya (P. kaufmanni and P.

Phylogeny and biogeography of ricefishes (Beloniformes,Adrianichthyidae) L.R. Parent!. National Museum of
Natural History,, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., 20560.
Ricefishes, known best by the medaka, Oryzias iatipes, are classified in the family Adrianichthyidae in the
atherinomorph order Beloniformes. The approximately twenty-five ricefish species range throughout fresh and
brackish waters of eastern Eurasia, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, across the Indo-Australian archipelago,
crossing Wallace's Line, to Timor. Throughout most of their range, ricefishes are small, reaching about 40 mm SL; in
the tectonic lakes of Sulawesi, however, ricefishes are relative giants, reaching about 200 mm SL. Ricefishes are
monophyletic and comprise two monophyletic subgroups or lineages, one large bodied and one small, diagnosed
here by morphological characters. Outgroup comparison using traditional morphology supports a transformation
from large to small, whereas preliminary molecular data supports a transformation from small to large. Sulawesi
ricefishes are not monophyletic but, instead, include members of each of the two lineages. As expected, the sister
taxa have an area of overlap, or sympafry, in Sulawesi. This distribution pattern is found in other fish taxa,
supporting the idea that neither lineage is primitive to the other, but that there was a widespread ancestral taxon,
and, once sister lineages diverged, some members of one or both lineages dispersed into the range of the other.

P.E. Bartelt. Waldorf College, Forest City, lA 50436 USA; C.R. Peterson, Idaho State UniversiN, Pocatello, ID
83209 USA.
Understanding the thennal biology of ectotherms is fundamental for understanding factors that affect their
movements and habitat use. For wet-skinned amphibians, one of these factors is different rates of evaporative water
loss among habitats. Comparing botty temperature variation of amphibians to variations in the thermal and hydric
conditions among habitats will help biologists to better understand how habitat modifoation may affect amphibian
movements and habitat use. For a one month period during 1995, we monitored the body temperatures (Tb) of adult
western toads and used physical models to monitor the environmental conditions of fore^ed habitats they used. We
surgically implanted temperature-sensitive transmitters into four toads and used an automated data recording system

operative temperatures every 15 minutes and calculated rates of evaporative water loss over four hour blocks of
time, in shaded and exposed microsites among four habitats. Nighttime toad Tb's were higher than model
temperatures, suggesting that toads remained under cover or in burrows at night. Daytime toad Tb's were warmest
in the shrub habitat, rather than in the regenerating clearcut, and coolest in the forest canopy.

by temperature. Other characteristics are more variable and the effects of temperature on these will be discussed.

studied in the white sturgeon, Adpenser transmontanus, using 3-D kinematics, electromyography, and quantitative

Department of Biology, Pepperdine University, Malibu, CA 90263-4321.
Gnjnion fish (Leuresthes tenuis} exit the ocean to spawn on sandy beaches. Both males and females move about
actively during terrestrial spawning. In a previous study, grunion that were removed from water in the laboratory and
forced to be active showed increased lactate concentrations in white muscles and blood. In this study, grunion of
both sexes were caught in the field before spawning, and following completion of normal spawning activity. These
were compared with grunion that had not emerged from water, and with a group of fish that had emerged but not
spawned, then were exercised to exhaustion in air. Lactate concentrations from white muscle and the heart were
measured for males and females in all four treatments. There were no significant differences between males arid
females in the field, before or after spawning, in lactate in white muscle and heart muscle. Values were within
nomial field or resting ranges for ectothermic vertebrates. Fish exercised to exhaustion in air showed significantly
higher lactate in both white muscle and heart than other fish. We suggest that grunion do not employ anaerobiosis
during normal emergence and spawning out of water.

IChilomycterus schoepli). We were particularly interested in how these fish modulated adductor mandibulae muscle

Food tiabfts of the european wall lizard, Podardt slcuta. Introduced to L.ong Island, New York. N. Patel and
R.L. Burke, Department of Biology, Hofstra University, Hempstead, NY, USA, 11549.

We studied the stomach contents of 150 European wall lizards, Podarcis sicula, collected from several populations in
western Long Island, New York, throughout their active season in 1997. Their diets were made up of a wide variety
of ants, insect larva, beetles, spiders, and millipedes. The list of prey included many introduced species. We
compared our results to those reported for this species and conspecifics in their native habitat

Wo found a correlation between prey size and head width, which suggests that head width or a morphological factor
associated with head width, may constrain the size of prey that Individual lizards can consume. We further noted
that some individuals had eaten several prey items of the same species, which is surprising in cases of prey species
that do not normally congregate. This suggests that individual lizards may specialize on particular prey species, and
actively forage for that species. We also tested for differences In food habits of males and females, independent of
body size.

A comparison of the movements of indigenous and displaced long-term captive ornate box turtles
(Terrapene omata) in the Sand Hills of Nebraska. D.L. Claussen. T. Luncan and K. Zemko, Dept, of Zoology,
Miami Univ., Oxford, OH, USA 45056.

Herpetologists often release animals after laboratory study in a laudable attempt at conservation. However, the
subsequent fates of such animals are generally unknown. We hypothesized that the behavior of these animals
would be markedly altered, possibly compromising their survival. We compared movements of turtles, captured in
the field and fitted with thread-trailers, with a matched group released simultaneously after one year of captivity. We
trailed each animal for 200 m (two or three days) and we subsequently mapped these trails, computing for each the
minimum convex polygon area, the maximum recorded speed, and three measures of trail sinuosity (the square root
of area divided by trail length (L), the greatest distance between two points divided by L, and the fractal dimension
(D)). The variance of the captive turtle data was significantly greater than that for the native turtles for trail area and
for two of the three sinuosity measures. However, contrary to expectations, none of the mean values differed
significantly between these groups, nor were there any obvious trends. Although we have no survivorship data, long­
term captivity and release in an unfamiliar location does not appear to markedly affect the short-term movement
patterns of ornate box turtles.

Prior. Endangered Species Division, Canadian Wildlife Service, Hull, Quebec KOH 1A3; H.L. Gibbs, Department of
Biology, McMaster, University, Hamilton, Ontario L8S 4K1; P.J. Weathertiead, Department of Biology, Carleton

We used DNA sampled from black rat snakes {Elaphe o. obsoleta} and eastern massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistnjrus

scales of management, and a method for testing the efficacy of conservation actions.

We collected European wall lizards, Podarcis sicula, from separate but similar populations in western Long Island,
New York, throughout the spring and summer of 1997, and assessed their reproductive condition. Diagnosable adult
females ranged in size from 44 to 77 mm SVL; the smallest female with eggs was 57 mm SVL. Of the 57 adult

 Origins of the American snake fauna. H.G. Dowling and J.V. Jenner, Rendalia Biologists, Talladega, AL 35160;
T. Pinou, Dept. Biol. Yale Univ., New Haven.,.

  Recent geological, paleontological, morphological, and molecular studies provide identification and better
definitions of the diverse clades that comprise the present American snake fauna. No single field provides a clear
zoogeographic narrative of these faunal elements but the consilience of information from multiple sources offers
such a base. Not unexpectedly, the oldest surviving clades are also the most ancient ones in the Americas. The
typhlopids and leptotyphlopids of the Neotropics and Africa probably date from the mid-Cretaceous splitting of
Gondwana by the Atlantic Ocean. The anomalepedids and Anilius in contrast are ancient South American
endemics without known relatives, although the latter may be a Recent relative of the Cretaceous +Dinilysia. The
Neotropical (true) boids appear to represent an ancient henophidian fauna that ranged from Madagascar across
Antarctica to South Arnerica. Conversely, the American erycids, tropidophiids (and              ?ungaliophiids and
?Loxocemus) derive from the Cretaceous-to-Eocene connection of eastern North America with Europe. This also
may be true of the caenophidian “North American Relicts.' The main American caenophidian fauna (crotalids,
elapids, xenodontids, dipsadids, colubrids s.s., and nafridds) did not arrive until later. Both paleontological and
molecular data support two or more Miocene entries of these snakes from the Old World via Bering Strait

The angle-headed dragons, Gonocephalus sensu lato have often been given as an example of a vertebrate that

agamids. Gonocephalus and Acanthosaura dadistically belong with the Calotes and Agama radiation in Asia and
Africa. The Eocene agamid Tinosaurus from North America has been compared with these two dades and falls
with the former.

Department of Biology, University of Richmond, Richmond, VA 23173 USA.

The genus Gastrophryne comprises 5 species: G. usta, G. carolinensis, G. olivacea, G. elegans, and G. picHventris.

carolinensis and G. olivacea represent the northernmost range of the genus and are widely distributed in the USA.

Investigating monophyly in the sub-family Petropedetinae Noble 1931 (Anura: Ranidae). E. Scott. A. Dawood
and A. Channing, Zoology Department, University of the Western Cape, Private Bag XI7, Bellville, 7535, South
Africa.

In an attempt to establish the outgroup of the genus Cacostemum Boulenger 1887, a preliminary' molecular
investigation into the relationships among the genera of the sub-family Petropedetinae was conducted. Additional
exemplar sequences from the sub-family Raninae Gray 1825 were induded in the analysis, which used
mitochondrial 12s sequence data. Parsimony analysis of the results shows the genera of the Petropedetinae to be
interspersed with genera of the Raninae, refuting monophyly of both sub-families as currently recognized. Although
this result is by no means surprising, and has been found by other workers (e.g. Ford 1989,1993), it does highlight
problems associated with ranid ph^ogenetics in general. There is a need to find monophyletic dades within the
small African ranids in order to understand their phylogeny, so that evolutionary and biogeographic hypotheses

Freeze tolerance and cryoprotectant mobilization in the gray treefrog (Hyla versicolor).                       J.R. Layne.
Department of Biology, Slippery Rock, PA 16057 USA.

 This study characterized freeze tolerance and cryoprotectant levels in H. versicolor tram Illinois. Frogs were frozen
in the laboratory at -1.5, -3.5, and -5.5 C. All frogs tolerated freezing at -1.5 and -3.5 C but the survival rate declined
at -5.5 C (<50%). Calorimetry revealed that 46.2% of the body water froze at -1.5 C. Plasma glucose and glycerol
were substantially elevated, 14X and 5X respectively, in recently thawed frogs vs. unfrozen frogs. Three unfrozen
frogs had levels of plasma glycerol tanging between 17.1-36.8 mmol/L, suggesting an anticipatory response to
freezing, but another three unfrozen frogs had glycerol at 1.1 mmol/L. No correlation existed between levels of
plasma glucose and glycerol in unfrozen frogs and recently thawed frogs. Inverse relationships existed between
glycerol content and ice content and between plasma osmolality and ice content. The levels of freeze tolerance and
related protective measures appear sufficient for H. versicolor to successfully overwinter beneath forest floor debris
in Illinois.  505                         16:00 Tuesday

present a biologically realistic protocol to study the effects of pulsed exposures of pe^iades on amphibian egg
masses and larvae. We will examine effects of three insecticides on survival, growth, behavior, and development ot
several amphibian species. Eggs and larval stages of three amphibian species will be exposed to three

and pesticides are rapidly absorbed by sediment.

Taxonomic status and geographic distribution of Bryconamerlcus elgenmanni Evermann and Kendall, 1906
(Characiformes, Charaadae). A.M. Miquelarena, Institute de Limnologia "Dr. Raul A. Ringuelet*, C.C. 712, (1900)
La, Plata, Argentina.; A.E. Aquino. American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th Street,, New
York, NY, 10024, USA.

Evermann and Kendall (1906) described Bryconamericus eigenmanni based on two specimens of Rio Primero
(Cordoba, Central Argentina), after which there were no more records of the species. The similarity between S.
eigenmanni and B. iheringi was noted by several authors, though finally keeping both as separate species. The need
of comparison of good population samples from ths areas of distribution of bo^ nominal species was suggested by
Malabarba and Kindell (1995), however misplacing ths type locality of B. eigenmanni within the Rio Parana system,
when actually the former belongs to an endorheic basin. The objective of our study is to provide evidence supporting
the validity or B. eigenmanni on base of material from ths type-locality drainage. A redescription using morphometric,
meristic and osteological characters, an analysis of the geographical distribution as well as a comparison with B.
iheringi, are provided. It is concluded that B. eigenmanni can be distinguished from other species of the genus by a
combination of characters including number of maxilla teeth, premaxilla shape, body depth, eye horizontal diameter,
and secondary sexual dimorphism of male pelvic fins. The distribution range suggests that the species is endemic to
endorheic drainages of Central Argentina.

Development of an index of biotic integrity for the mid-atlantic highlands region. F.H. McConnick. US
Environmental Protection Agency, 26 W. Martin Luther King Dr., Cincinnati, OH 45268 USA; R.M. Hughes,
Dynamac International, c/o US Environmental Protection Agency, 200 SW 35fh St., Corvallis, OR 97333, USA; P.R.
Kaufmann and A.T. Herlihy, Oregon State University, c/o US Environmental Protection Agency, 200 SW 35fh St,
Con/allis, OR 97333 USA; D.V. Peck, US Environmental Protection Agency, National Health and Environmental
Effects Laboratory, 200 SW 35th St, Corvallis, OR 97333 USA.

From 1993-1995, fish assemblage data were collected from 298 streams in the Mid-Atlantic Highlands region as part
of the USEPA's Environmental Monitoring and Assessment Program (EMAP). We examined responses of fish
community metrics to physical, chemical, habitat and landscape indicators of catchment disturbance. Univariate and
multivariate analyses of relationships among fish community metrics, habitat integrity and anthropogenic disturbance
were used to develop an index of biotic integrity (IBI) for the assessment of stream condition in the region. Metrics
are scored continuously from 0-10 and the resulting 16 metric IBI ranges from 0-100. We assessed the condition of
the fish community based on hypothesized reference criteria reflecting historical conditions. We established scoring
criteria of 85% for excellent biological integrity, 70% for acceptable, and 50% for impaired. Only 19.6% of the stream
length had excellent or acceptable fish communities. Forty-two percent of the total stream length was marginal and
37% was impaired.

Migration and population structure of the porbeagle Shark, Lamna nasus, in Canadian Atbntio watery WJi-
Jovce. Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, B3H 4H6: P.C.F. Hurley. Fishenes Biologist, Manne R^sh Division
(Maritimes Region), Bedford Institute of Oceanography, P.O. Box 1006, Dartmouth, Nova Scotia B2Y 4A2.

Seasonal movements of the porbeagle shark, Lamna nasus. in Canadian Atlantic waters were deteimined using size
and sex composition of catches sampled by Fisheries Observers in the porbeagle longline fishery. Males and
immature females predominate porbeagle catches on the Scotian Shelf edge in March and April. The data suggest
ttiat mature females segregate from the main body of the population during this penod. The The proportion of mature
females in catches increases in May and June. Porbeagle move onto the Shelf in May and northeastward along the
Shelf in May and June, moving into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and onto the Grand Banks m late June and early July.
Larger porbeagle move off the Shelf into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and onto the Grand Banks first, followed by
vounger porbeagle. Large porbeagle begin to leave the Gulf in September and large females prodominatG catches
on trie Grand Banks in September to November. Porbeagle move out of the Gulf and off the Grand Banks in
November and out to the Shelf edge in December. Migration of the porbeagle shark in Canadian Atlantic waters is
complex and catch rate analyses should incorporate size and sex composition of catches on a seasonal basis.

Preliminary results of stock discrimination of Dolly Varden char, Salvelinus malma, and Arctic char, S.
alpinus, from Iwavik National Park, Yukon Territory, using mIcro-PIXE analysis of otolith sfrOTtiurn.
Babaluk and J.D. Reist, Fisheries and Oceans Canada, 501 University Crescent, Winning, MB, R3T 2N6, V.A.
Sahanatien, Dept, of Canadian Heritage, Parks Canada, P.O. Box 1840, Ini^k, NT, XOE OTO; N.M. Halden, Dept, of
Geological Sciences, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, MB, R3T 2N2; J.L. Campbell, Dept, of Physios, University of
 Guelph, Guelph, ON, NIG 2W1.
 Micro-PIXE (proton induced X-ray emission) analysis was used to determine the content of strontium in the core area
 of otoliths from Dolly Varden and Arctic char from the north slope of the Yukon Territory. Otoliths are composed
 primarily of calcium carbonate (as aragonite). Trace elements such as strontiurn which are'.present in the water the
 fish inhabits and which are chemically similar to calcium are often incorporated into the otoliths. Because otoliths do
 not undergo resorption of constituents, they contain a permanent record of the environments occupied by the fish
 throughout life. The otolith core is formed at the site where the individual was spawned; thus, environmental yanation
 in the levels of strontium and other trace elements has the potential to differentiate biological groups of fish. M^^h
 strontium levels in otolith cores from populations of Iwavik char ranged from 280 to 520 ppm and were assoaated
 with the habitat occupied. Strontium differences in otoliths have the potential to discnminate biqlogica st^ks of
 chars in Iwavik National Park and may also be useful in identifying fish from mixed groups to their stock of ongin.
 This work confirms biological stock stmeturing observed in these char through other methods.

energy may be used in reproductive strategies in a seasonally fluctuating environment. We have developed an

Is spawning phenology sufficient to explain adult recruitment in smallmouth bass populations? M.S.
Ridgeway and B.J. Shuter, 1 Harkness Laboratory of Fisheries Research, Aquatic Ecosystems Science Section,
Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, Third Floor North, 300 Water St., Peterborough, Ontario K9J 8M5; M.J.
Gross, Department of Fisheries and Wildlife, University of Minnesota, USA.

The timing and duration of spawning in smallmouth bass populations are closely tied to body size and spring
warming rates. A repeatable pattern of large males preceding small males In the timing of reproduction has been
obsenred at a number of sites. The alternating life history hypothesis proposes that the potential gains made by
young-of-year as a consequence of this seasonal pattern of spawning are sufficient to predict size of maturity and
spawning time of individu^s. We present three lines of evidence that together indicate the acquisition of home
ranges in the late juvenile stage is a key process in adult recruitment in our study population in Lake Opeongo. DNA

fidelity to home ranges, areas of concentrated use and a daily movement pattern suggesting spatial memory.
Finally, a 60 year record of age-specific abundance and growth demonstrates that density-dependent growth occurs
at ages 2-3; a period of time after their initial restricted distribution in their first summer and prior to the adult home
range phase. We believe this transition phase is the key to understanding adult recruitment and that spawning
phenology may interact with this element of bass ecology rather than a direct connection to adult maturity as a
proposed in the alternating life history hypothesis.




     525 .                      15:30 Tuesday                                   SE                                 THN
Adaptation-by-time within pacific salmon populations.               A.P. Hendry. School of Rsheries, University of
Washington, Box 357980 Seattle, WA, USA.

Correlations between breeding date and the life histo^ or energy stores of individuals might arise owing to two
different mechanisms; condition dependence or adaptation-by-time. Condition dependence is the conventional view,
and predicts that individual size, condition, or status influence breeding date. This concept has been profitably
applied to iteroparous. Income breeding species with flexible breeding times. It seems poorly-suited, however, to
some semelparous, capital breeding species that have less flexible breeding times. For these species, a more
plausible explanation is that heritable maturation schedules allow temporally-isolated population components to
adapt to selective regimes specific to their breeding times (adaptation-by-time). The fundamental difference between
the two hypotheses is that condition dependence considers breeding date within a season to be a proximate effect of
variation in life history traits or energy allocation, whereas adaptation-by-time considers breeding date to be an
ultimate cause of such variation. I present evidence for limited gene flow among temporal components of Pacific
salmon populations and evidence that they exhibit adaptive variation tailored to selective regimes that vary through
the breeding season. Adaptation-by-time appears relevant to temporal trends in body size, reproductive life span,
patterns of energy allocation, and the development rate of embryos.

State-dependent timing of breeding In fishes: proximate explanations and ultimate implications. E.T. Schultz.
Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs CT 06269-3042 USA.

The seasonal timing of reproduction may vary with individual characteristics (or 'state variables'), such as size and
energetic state. I review this phenomenon in fishes. I show that the pattern is widespread, in taxonomic terms and
across reproductive modes and behaviors. I show that there is evidence that individual state can affect the timing of
first reproduction in the season (onset) as well as the last breeding effort of the season (termination), in serially-
spawning fishes. The most common observation is that large individuals commence breeding activity earlier in the
season than small individuals. State dependence in phenology is considered at several levels of organization. The
physiological effect of state variables, in tenns of how they affect the endocrine system to influence timing, is poorly
understood. Clarification of the relationship between state variables and timing is needed, and perhaps best
addressed with eiqierimental manipulation of individuals. State-dependence in timing is meaningful from an ultimate
perspective. Optimization of breeding time is often viewed in terms of single fitness components, especially survival
of offspring. State-dependence suggests that the situation is more complex. I show that fish systems are promising
subjects for tests of various models of optimal breeding times.

Is it all just walking pterygoids? An exploration of feeding mechanics in snakes. B.A. Young. Dept, of Biology,
Laibyette College, Easton, PA. 18042 USA.

Classic descriptive and functional studies of ophidian feeding have resulted in a detailed, and supported, hypothesis
for the mechanics of prey ingestion in snakes. This hypothesis, commonly known as the pterygoid walk, centers on
the sequential protraction and retraction of the contralateral palato-maxillary arches. Given the phylogenetic history
and cephalic staictural diversity of snakes, as well as their variation in prey preference, it would seem unlikely that all
snakes use the same prey ingestion mechanics. The diversity of feeding mechanics was explored through a
morphological examination of the mandibular syphysis, a region generally taken to have no special function in prey
ingestion. Serial sections through the syrnph^is of over 180 species revealed substantial variation in tissue
composition and structural arrangement. Suites of characters suggest this anatomical region may perform different
functional roles in different species. Observations of ophiophagous snakes reveal prey ingestion accomplished with a
highly modified pterygoid walk. In these cases only unilateral displacement of the palato-maxillary arch functions in
prey ingestion, with the caudal portion of the pterygoid displacing the prey posteriorly.

The ontogeny of morphological variation: sex, family, and testosterone effects on head, body, and tail
growth in the garter snake, Thamnophls sirtalis. R.B. Kino. Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Illinois
Univeristy, DeKalb, IL, USA 60115.

The evolution of population- and species-level differences requires heritable variation in phenotype. However,
phenotypic variation may have physiological and environmental as well as genetic causes. In an effort to elucidate
the proximate causes of morphological variation in the garter snake, Thamnophls sirtalis, offspring born to 26 wild-
caught females were reared in captivity. Within each litter, males and females were assigned at random to two
treatment groups and received sham or testosterone-containing subcutaneous implants for a three month period
starting at three months of age. Growth in head dimensions, body size, and tail length was monitored until snakes
were six to 14 months old and was analyzed using repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance. Family
membership had pervasive effects on growth in all traits. These effects may be attributable to penetic variation or
maternal effects arising from the common in utero environment shared by litter-mates. Sex had significant effects on
growth in all traits but the magnitude of these effects was small, suggesting that differences in body size seen in
adult garter snakes do not arise until later in life. Elevated testosterone levels had significant but small negative
effects on growth in body size and head dimensions.

Gordon Walls (1940, 1942) constructed an elegant logical story for the early origin of snakes as burrowers, based
upon the anatomy of the eye. Independently, Mahendra (1938) suggested that burrowing snakes, such as Typhlops,
represented the most basal snake lineages, also underscoring the hypothesis of a fossorial ancestry for snakes.
This hypothesis, with Some modification, has been widely accepted (Underwood, 1970; Rieppel, 1988). Recent
phylogenetic research by Caldwell and Lee (1997) suggested an alternative to the fossorial ancestor hypothesis,
reviving an early hypothesis for an aquatic origin of modem snakes. Can the ophthalmic characteristics so forcefully

many of ^ese same ophthalmic characteristics are observed in aquatic taxa. The shape and relative size of the lens
and the method of accommodation in modem snakes are typical of aquatic animals and suggest an aquatic ancestry
for snakes. Other characteristics of the eye are less obviously attributable to an aquatic ancestor but are still
consistent with this alternative hypothesis. In light of the revised nistorioal framework, this alternative hypothesis for
ths ecological origin for snakes merits closer inspection.

Studies of lung-based hearing in amphibians and reptiles. T.E. Hetherington. Department of Zoology, Ohio
State University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210-1293 USA.

Lungs have been shown to function in reception of airborne sound in snakes and species of frogs that lack tympanic
middle ears, and this lung pathway may represent the most primitive mechanism of hearing in tetrapod vertebrates.
Laser vibromefric studies were extended to investigate the acoustic responsiveness of the lateral body walls and
lungs of salamanders and lizards, and additional studies analyzing potential routes of sound energy transfer from the
lungs to the inner ear were conducted on frogs. The body walls of several species of salamanders and lizards were
found to be responsive to sound, typically showing a low frequency peak in motion (< 300 Hz) and a higher
frequency peak from 800-2000 Hz depending on body size. In contrast, the body wall of lungless plefhodontid
salamanders showed a reduced low frequency peak in motion and completely lacked the higher frequency peak.
Neurophysiological studies on fire-bellied toads (Bomblna orientalis) suggest that sound energy is not transferred
from the lung to the inner ear via respiratory pathways. Vibrometric experiments suggest instead that the operoularis
system may be involved. Sound-induced motion of the suprascapula decreased dramatically when sound was
blocked from reaching the body wall/lung. Lung-induced motion of the suprascapula may be relayed via the
operoularis muscle to the operculum in the oval window of the inner ear.

A new look at what the eye Impllee about the early ancestors of snakes. C.L. Capretle. Evolution, Ecology, and
Organismal Biolog, Ohio State University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210 USA.

Gordon Walls (1940, 1942) constnicted an elegant, logical story for the early origin of snakes as burrowers, based
upon the anatomy of the eye. Independently, Mahendra (1938) suggested that burrowing snakes, such as Typhlops,
represented the most basal snake lineages, also underscoring the hypothesis of a fossorial ancestry for snakes.
This hypothesis, with some modification, has been widely accepted (Underarood, 1970; Rieppel, 1988). Recent
phylogenetic research by Caldwell and Lee (1997) suggested an alternative to the fossorial ancestor hypothesis,
reviving an eariy hypothesis for an aquatic origin of modem snakes. Can the ophthalmic characteristics so forcefully
argued by Walls for a fossorial origin of snakes equally support an argument for an aquatic origin for snakes? In fact,
many of these same ophthalmic characteristics are observed in aquatic taxa. The shape and relative size of the lens
and the method of accommodation in modem snakes are typical of aquatic animals and suggest an aquatic ancestry
for snakes. Other characteristics of the eye are less obviously attributable to an aquatic ancestor but are still
consistent with this altemative hypothesis. In light of the revised historical framework, this alternative hypothesis for
the ecological origin for snakes merits closer inspection.

Evaluation of a by-catch reduction device to reduce diamondback terrapin [HXalaclemys terrapin} mortally bi
crab pots. J.P. Green. Ohio University, Athens, OH, USA; W.M. Roosenburg, Dept, of Biological Sciences,, Ohio
University, Athens, OH 45701 USA.
Diamondback terrapins, Malaclemys terrapin, frequently drown due to incidental capture in crab pots. Crab pots
selectively capture male and young female terrapins, thereby skewing sex ratios and removing individuals with high
reproductive value. We tested a by-catch reduction device (BRD) to determine its ability to reduce tenapin
enbapment and the effect the BRD had on the size and number of crabs that were caught in crab pots. We tested
three size BRDs, 4 cm x 10 cm, 4.5 cm x 12 cm and 5 cm x 10 cm, on both standard crab pots and modified crab
pots designed to prevent terrapin mortality. We found that the 4 cm x 10 cm BRD effectively prevented turtle entry,
however, eliminated crabs based on height. Neither the 5 cm x 10 cm nor the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRDs affected crab
size or the number of crabs caught, but the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRD reduced terrapin by-catch by 82 percent, whereas
the 5 cm X 10 cm BRD only reduced terrapin by-catch by 50%. We stress the importance of using BRDs to reduce
terrapin captures throughout their range, thus preserving the biodiversity of wetland ecosystems and restoring or
maintaining natural sex ratios of terrapin populations.

Ecology of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terraperi}, with implications for conservation and
management. KJt. Buhlmann and T.D. Tuberville, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, SC,
29802, USA; R.H. Kerr and D. Booher, Institute of Ecology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602, USA.

We investigated populations of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terrapen}, a species endemic to Jamaica. We
sampled turtles at four sites-- three along the southern Jamaican coast and one in northwest Jamaica. We captured
turtles in a variety of habitats, including a permanently ponded wetland, farm ponds, and a stream in a karst
landscape. Turtles were also found in a series of seasonal ponds where they retreat into nearby cave refugia. The
refugia remain flooded, thus allowing the slider population to exist in this seasonally arid landscape. We did not
observe or capture turtles during limited sampling in a large river and a brackish mangrove swamp. Individuals from
the northwest population appeared morphologically distinct from turtles captured along the south coast and
descriptions of T. terrapen provided in the literature. The native people hanrest turtles whenever they are found
incidentally. Concentrated populations, such as those in the cave refugia, are heavily exploited. We found red­
eared sliders (Trachemys scripts elegans} in Jamaican pet stores and suspect they could become established in
Jamaica, possibly hybridizing with the native slider. Our preliminary research suggests that T. terrapen is a highly
threatened species needing conservation action in order to insure its persistence.

Effects of human disturbance on five-line'd skink (Eumeces fasciatus) abundance and distribution at Point
Peiee National Park, Canada. S.J. Hecnar and R J. Brooks, Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph,
ON, N1G 2W1; R.T. M'Closkey, Department of Biological Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, ON, N9B 3P4.

The five-lined skink is widely distributed in eastern North America but its populations are disjunct and of conservation
concern in the northern portion of its range. Canadian populations are presently considered "vulnerable". We
studied effects of human disturbance on five-lined skinks at Point Peiee National Park, from 1990 to 1997.
Surveys Indicated low skink abundance and a lack of woody debris in areas heavily used by humans. A population
dedine, concurrent with high disturbance levels, occurred from 1990 to 1996. Skinks used woody debris as refuge
sites and showed preferential use of large moderately decayed logs and boards having greater surface area. Human
disturbance resulted in degradation and removal of debris. To test the hypothesis that skink absence in human high-
use areas was caused by a lack of suitable debris, we placed artificial microhabitats in areas which previously
lacked debris and skinks . Experimental boards were quickly colonized and heavily used despite high disturbance
rates. Results suggested that skinks are resilient to minor disturbances such as board displacements, but not to
removal or degradation of debris. Habitat restoration by moving large woody debris from open beach to the
stabilized dune began in 1996 and resulted in increased skink abundance in 1997.

The effects of road mortality on two threatened snake species on Peiee Island, Ontario. R.J. Willson. B.D.
Porchuk and R.J. Brooks, Department of Zoology. University of Guelph. Guelph. Ontario, NIG 2W1.

Road mortality is becoming an increasing threat to endangered and isolated reptile populations. Reptiles killed by
motorized vehicles and found on Peiee Island's roads (68 km in total) were collected and locations recorded from
1993 -1996. During the three years of intense surveys, the roads were scanned approximately every two days. In
1998, sections of road that had high numbers of roadkilled blue racers {Coluber constrictor mx'i) and eastern fox
snakes {Elaphe gloyd!) during the roadkill surveys, will be scanned intensively to determine suitable methods to
mitigate the effects of vehicular mortality. The blue racer is endangered in Canada, and threatened status for the
eastern fox snake is pending review. In three years 78 blue racers (11 adults/year) and greater than 100 eastern fox
snakes were found dead on Peiee Island's roads. Many adult females that are killed on the roads are moving to or
from shoreline oviposition sites. In the fall of each year, many hatchlings are also found dead on the roads. For
example, from 1993 - 1996, 75 hatchling eastern fox snakes were recorded as roadkills. As a result of continuing
development in the form of summer cottages, and growing tourism, vehicular traffic continues to increase on Peiee
Island's roads. Ths future impact of increased traffic flow and continued road mortality on the blue racer and eastern
fox snake remains to be seen. Our data suggest that road mortality will be a significant factor leading to the decline
of both snake species on Peiee Island.

The Impact of roads on snake populations in eastern Texas. D.C. Rudolph. S.J. Burgdorf, R.R. Schaefer and
R.N. Conner, Soulhem Research Station, Box 7600, SFA Station, Nacogdoches, TX 75962 USA.

Radio-telemetry studies of timber rattlesnakes {Crotalus horridus) and Louisiana pine snakes {Pituophis mthvem}

timber rattlesnake records in relation to road densities supported the hypothesis ffiat mortality associated with roads
has resulted in the extirpation of this species from significant portions of the landscape. The hypothesis that existing
road networks depress populations or large snake species was tested using a trapping protocol to sample snake

Habitat use, home ranges and hibernacula of the copperbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta}
in southern Indiana and northwest Kentucky. C.J. Coppola and R.A. Kingsbury, Department of Biology, Indiana-
Purdue University, R. Wayne, IN 46805 USA.

The copperbelly is federally listed under the Endangered Species Act as Threatened in the northern part of its range,
and protected to the south by the Copperbelly Water Snake Conservation Agreement. Snakes from two populations
were radio-tracked at the Sloughs Wildlife Management Area, Kentucky, and in the Patoka National Wildlife Refuge,
Indiana. The movements of the snakes were monitored to elucidate patterns of home range size and habitat use.
including hibernacula sites. Habitat use was seasonally compared between sexes. Home ranges and activity
centers were calculated using minimum convex polygons. Individual snakes occupied widely different habitats,
demonstrated pronounced fidelity to selected habitats for much of the season. Buttonbush sloughs and areas of
shallow water with emergent vegetation were most frequently used, while closed canopy forested habitats away from
the sloughs and targe bodies or open water were not. Habitat use shifted towards palustrine forest edges as the
season progressed. The hibernacula of most snakes were crayfish burrows or stumps near or within the floodplain.

Phylogeography of the anchovies (Genus Engraulis). W.S. Grant, Northwest Fisheries Science Center, National
Marine Fisheries Service, 2725 Montiake Blvd East, Seattle WA 98112 USA; B.W. Bowen. Department of Fisheries
and Aquatic Sdences, University of Rorida, 7922 NW 71st Street, Gainesville FL 32653 USA.

Anchovies (genus Engraulis) inhabit temperate upwelling zones and boundary currents across the globe, including
locations in Europe (E. encrasicolus), southern Africa (E. capensis), Australia (E. australis}, Japan (E. japonicus},
Mexico-California (E. mordax}, Chile-Peru (E. ringens}, and Argentina-Brazil (E. anchoita}. Comparisons of mtDNA
cytochrome b sequences reveal four major lineages corresponding to three New Worid spedes and a single lineage
including all four Old Worid species. The relationships among haplotypes in the Old World anchovies demonstrate
recent colonization events between Japan and Australia, and between Europe and southern Africa. A previous
population in southern Africa (possibly the progenitor of the European population) may have gone extinct and been
recently recolonized from Europe. A comparison of anchovies to sardines (genus Sardinopd), which have a similar
geographic distribution, reveals a dramatically different distribution of mtDNA lineages. These data prompt two
conclusions about the biogeography of temperate marine fishes. First, a vicariance model alone is inadequate to
explain the distribution of evolutional lineages in these taxa. Both vicariance and dispersal events are strongly
implicated. Second, the principle of gener^ized tracks, in which species with similar distributions have similar
evolutionary histories, is contradicted by a comparison of phylogeographic patterns in sardines and anchovies.

History and diversity of Great Basin fishes. G.R. SMITH. Museum of Zoology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor,
Ml 48109-1079, USA.

Hubbs' and Miller's research on the Great Basin emphasized changes at ths level of races and subspecies; these
changes apparently occurred rapidly, in hundreds to thousands of years. Miocene to Pleistocene fossils of these
fishes, in contrast, suggest unexpectedly slow changes at the species level, i.e., over hundreds of thousands to
nearly 10 million years, with infrequent evolution of new spedes. Resolution of this incongruence requires
clarification of the relative frequency of short-term differentiation, species origins, and extinction. The Great Basin
evidence demonstrates that fluctuating pluvial-interpluvial cydes result in rapid proliferation of new subspedes, but
eventual extinction of all but generalist survivors, often as relict endemics. The frequent extinctions and infrequent
persistence of new spedes in the Great Basin seem to be the consequence of repeated loss of habitat during
interpluvial stages of Pleistocene cycles. The result seems to be rapid but superficial changes in morphology without
long-tenn charge. Great Basin fish faunas exhibit low diversity and high endemism characteristic of tectonically
actave areas. The low diversity suggests that high extinction rates were caused by high elevations, high gradients
(low habitat diversity), and dimatic variability.

Flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae are distributed in marine waters across the entire northern hemisphere. The

Ocean. Some species inhabit wide ranges inhabiting Pacific, Atlantic and Arctic waters, while many others have
more limited distributions. An area cladogram using a recent cladistic hypothesis of relationships within
Pleuronectidae allows for the interpretation of this geographic distribution. A trans-arctic dispersal appears to be a
repeated pattern within taxonomic subgroups of Pleuronectidae. Associated with this extensive distribution is a wide
range of life history traits. Feeding behavior, spawning season, age and size at maturity all exhibit variation at
different taxonomic levels, induding within spedes variation for some of the widely distributed spedes. The extent to
which inheritance versus geographic distribution, and corresponding environmental factors influence these life
history variables will also be presented.

Sangre de Cristo and other local color from Mexico; geographic variation in sexually selected characters?

The variable platyfish, Xiphophorus variatus, has the broadest range of any species of Xiphophorus. Most work on
this species has concentrated on populations in the Rio Tamesi drainage, towards the northern end of its
distribution. Here, we report on the populations toward the southern end of the range, in the Rios Nautla, Solteros,
Tecolutla and Cazones. These populations differ from the ones in the north by exhibiting pronounced local variation
in adult male coloration patterns. One variety, termed Sangre de Cristo in the aquarium literature, is characterized
by deep red coloration on the belly and throat of adult males. Another color variety is vivid yellow coloration of the
gonopr^ium. These color variants, and others, ate extremely restricted in geographic distribution. Sangre de Cristo
occurs in an area no larger than ten by fifteen kilometers, with the frequency of the variant highest towards the center
of the range. Yellow gonopodium is know from only a single locality. In contrast, adult male color variants in the
north seem more broadly distributed. Population genetic data suggests that populations in the south may be more
isolated from one another than in the north. AP-PCR (RAPD) analyses reveal less band variation in the southern
populations than in the northern populations. There is also less variation at the autosomal tailspot locus in southern
than in northern populations and greater tailspot variability among populations in the south. If is hypothesized that
the evolution of local color variants is promoted by reduced gene flow among populations. This is of great interest
because vivid adult male colors in poeciliids are generally believed to be sexual selected characters and these
results suggest a potential role of small population effects in their origin.                              .14:15 Tuesday                                CF14                                AXL

 ANOVA. Preliminaiy results show increased densities inshore, with predictable cycling over the sampling period.

     Use of GIS in taxonomic collections and its relevance to assessing biodiversity, spatio-temporal
     distributions, and field work validation. J.R. Ruiz-Carus. F.D.E.P., Florida Marine Research Institute, 100 Eighth
     Ave. SE, St. Petersburg, FL 33701-5095, USA.

     A system that analyzes and displays spatially referenced data is known as a geographical information system (GIS).
     The use of GIS technology has facilitated understanding of complex relationships between organisms and their
     environment. In ichthyology, GIS could facilitate access to information associated with taxonomic collections. It
     could provide spatial analysis within and among species using distribution patterns of morphological and genetic
     characters: accurately analyze geographical distributions of morphological characters and correlate them with
     ecological parameters; and provide an objective measurement of the status of an ecosystem, which has generally
     been done based on human perception but lacked data. Taxonomic collections of voucher and type specimens and
     their associated environmental data are abundant sources of unexplored information. This information is highly
     relevant for management of natural resources because taxonomy has been built upon it. This information, when
     analyzed with GIS, could be used to address these areas and to provide the foundation for measuring fish
     biodiversity and evaluating the dynamics of spatio-temporal patterns of fish. The FDEP's FMRI is applying GIS
     technology to analyse the robust databases associated with its voucher collections. Further study of voucher
     specimens will allow us to produce maps of morphological characteristics of fish linked to ecological parameters. We
     also intend to produce synthesized information for ecosystem management in a format amenable to spatial- and time­
     analysis study.

     Borders and biodiversity: a plight for Pacific salmon.           B.E. Riddell. Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Padfio
     Biological Station,, Nanaimo, B.C.

     If Pacific salmon are a cultural icon, then their treatment in the past century is certainly inconsistent with this value.
     Recent reviews of their status in Canada and the Pacific northwest report about 1,000 populations extinct or at risk,
     and several stocks are listed or proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Causes of the declines
     are numerous, usually attributed to someone or something else, and always debatable. The history of impacts can
     be broadly characterized as: an initial uninformed and rapid expansion of fisheries; then decades of rapid economic
     expansion in many sectors plus heightened competitive over-fishinQ of hatchery and wild salmonids; and finally, 20-
     30 years of extensive regulation, confrontation, and change. Dunng the latter period, the issue of "borders" in
     management and conservation has become very evident. The Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and
     Canada (1985) provided the first comprehensive agreement on Pacific salmon and offered a means to cooperate in
     consenration and development. Unfortunately, it now exemplifies the problem of Bordets and’their risk to biodiversity
     in Pacific salmon. This talk will address the history of salmon conflicts, the complexity of salmon issues, and describe
     the risks associated with the present Treaty impasse.

Interstate striped bass managaement, 1977-1998. H.M. Austin. Virginia Institute of Marine Science, College of
William and Mary, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA; J.G. Travel stead, Virginia Marine Resources Commission,
P.O. 756, Newport News, VA 23607, USA.

Initially, under the auspices of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Interstate Fisheries Management
Program, and subsequently the operation of the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC), striped bass
(Morone saxatilis) management of the mid-Atlantic (Virginia-Maine) stocks have showed both an initial abysmal
beginning, and a final and unique result that can claim responsibility for the dramatic recovery of the heavily fished
mid-Atlantic stocks. Recommendations were made to the ASMFC as early as 1942 for the need for more stringent
unified regulations that transcended state boundaries: but it was not until 1981 that a Scientific and Statistics
Committee recommenced to the ASMFC Striped Bass Board that the spawning grounds be closed during the
spawning season, and that the minimum size limit be 14* coast-wide, while most of the states adopted such
measures in 1982 their enforcement was voluntary. It was not until the passage of the Federal Atlantic Striped Bass
Cohservation Act in 1984, requiring full compliance with the Act that each state fulfilled their obligations.
Subsequently, a combination of protective regulations and stringent enforcement, coincident with several highly
successful dominant year classes (1987,1989, 1993, and 1996) have led to an unprecedented abundance of large
(>24*, 600 mm) fish. So successful is the program that Congress has passed subsequent coast-wide legislation
(Atlantic Coast Cooperative Fisheries Consenration and Management Act of 1994) to protect other coastal migratory
species.

A bl-national effort to protect endangered Kemps ridley sea turtles. S.S. Heppell. Duke University Marine
Laboratory, 135 Duke Marine Lab, Road, Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 USA; R. Marquez-Milan, Institute Nacional
de la Pesoa-CRIP Manzanillo, Playa Ventanas S/N, A.P. 591, Manzanillo, Colima, Mexico 28200.

Kemp's ridley sea turtles {Lepidochelys kempi) nested in ths tens of thousands in the 194O's and were the most
abundant species in the Gulf of Mexico. Intensive egg harvest and mortality at sea caused the population to
plummet; by the mid-197O's, less than 1000 nests per year were counted at Rancho Nuevo, Mexico, the only known
nesting beach. Efforts to prevent extinction were initiated in Mexico in 1960s, and from 1966-1978 approximately
30,000 hatchlings were releaserJ per year. A United States-Mexico cooperative research and conservation program
was formed in 1978 which now protects 95% of the nests laid at Rancho Nuevo. The cooperative includes the
Mexican Ministry of Fisheries, U.S. National Parks Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, and National Marine
Fisheries Senrice. Additional research support and funding comes from the Glatts Porter Zoo in Brownsville, the
Texas Shrimpers Association and other groups. The National Marine Fisheries Service sponsored a captive
rearing program and efforts to re-establish a nesting colony at South Padre Island, Texas. Both nations passed
legislation that requires Turtle Excluder Devices on shrimp trawling gear to reduce incidental mortality. Today the
Kemps ridley population is still more than an order of magnitude below historical levels, but nests are increasing,
largely due to the dedicated efforts of two nations.

Northern Rmlts of reptiles: temperature-related constraints and adaptations.                      R.J. Brooks. Department of
Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, NIG 2W1.

Forty years ago, Bleakney pointed out that the factors limiting the ranges of herpetofauna had not been well studied.
This is still true. Presumably, limits are set by extreme climatic conditions in some if not all cases. The northern
limits are set by the severity of cold temperatures in winter or by the impact of summer temperatures on the

Biodiversity crossing borders: the invasive vector In fishes. E.J. Crossman and B.C. Cudmore, Centre for
Biodiversity and Conservation, Royal Ontario, Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario M5S 2C6.

Most often measures of biodiversity have been documented and expressed in regard to political boundaries, as
opposed to ecological areas. There have been extensive programs of intentional introduciions of nonindigenous
species by agencies in one political area without prior consultation with adjacent political areas. When this situation
involves international boundaries it can lead to greater concern. The present freshwater fish fauna of Canada could
be said to result totally from fishes that have "invaded or reinvaded" Canadian waters as those wafers appeared.
The process continues today. Records starting in 1949 indicate that at least eight species have entered Canadian
wafers by moving across or around the Great Lakes and interconnecting rivers. The list includes eight species
native to the United States and seven introduced there. If we include the potential of global warming there are an
aditional 41 species to the immediate south of Canada that might invade. If we extend the list to the whole of
Canada and the United States there is a total of 63 species that have achieved part of their distribution by this vector.

Northern borders and threatened species: endangered amphibians In Canada. D.M. Green. Redpath Museum,
McGill University, Montreal, Quebec H3A 2K6.

The northern range limit of a species is the dynamic result of local extinction versus establishment of new
populations. This, in turn, is dependent upon dispersal, habitat availability, habitat predictability, population
dynamics, and metapopulation dynamics. In Canada, all native species of amphibians reach their northen limits. For
some, this limit lies just inside the southern Canadian border and therefore these species are candidates for
Canada's endangered species list whatever their distribution or abundance in the United States. Canada has no
endemic amphibian species. To what extent are these Canadian endangered species an artifact of the position of the
Canada/US border? Or, in consideration of the genetic distinction and isolation that may occur among northern
limital populations, how much of a biolological imperative does designation of "endangered" in Canada carry? These
questions are best addressed on a case by case basis.

Evolution of freeze tolerance in turtles: what is known? R.L. Burke. Department of Biology, Hofstra University,
Hempstead, NY, USA, 11549.

Hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in western painted turtles (NE and various Canadian), midland painted
turtles (Ontario and OH), eastern X midland painted turtles (NJ ), and ornate box turtles (NE). Lack of hatchling
freeze tolerance has been reported in red eared sliders (IL anrJ LA), spiny soft-shelled turtles (NE), yellow mud turtles
(NE), and snapping turtles (NE). To this list I add wood turtles and common map turtles (IN) as not freeze tolerant,
and very preliminary data suggests that southern painted turtles (LA) are also freeze intolerant, while Blanding's
turtles appear to be freeze tolerant.

Understanding the evolution of this trait is complicated for several reasons. These include 1 .disagreement over the
importance of freeze tolerance vs supercooling in natural situations, 2. lack of a consistent standard for defining
freeze tolerance, 3. lack of comparable interpopulational freeze tolerance data for a species with large latitudinal
range and possible variation in this trait, and, 4. lack of a phylogenetic analysis of a clade with variation in this trait.

Forty years ago, Bleakney pointed out that the factors limiting the ranges of herpetofauna had not been well studied.

The ecophysiology of freeze tolerant frogs: surviving the big freeze. J.R. Lavne Jr, Department of Biology,
Slippery Rock University, Slippery Rock PA 16057 USA.

At least five species of frogs from North America survive extensive freezing of their body fluids. Their limits of
tolerance emanate from the combined interactions of freeze temperature and the duration of exposure. Frogs protect
their tissues from injury by accumulating massive quantities of glucose or glycerol and by relocating body water from
major organs. The roles of physiologic^ systems in the cryobiology of these frogs are varied. Some morphological
characteristics and systemic functions are key elements supporting freeze tolerance. For example, the integument
transmits ice crystals info body fluids preventing extensive supercooling of body fluids and the cardiovascular system
actively distributes cryoprotectant from central stores in the liver to other body tissues before arresting. In contrast,
the CNS and skeletal muscle function at temporarily reduced rates upon thawing that are in proportion to the
intensity of the freeze episode. This then may affect important organismal activities such as the ability of frogs to find
and interact with mates.

Molecular adaptations for freeze tolerance In amphibians and reptiles. K.B. Storey. Dept. Biology, Carleton
University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, Ontario K1S 5B6.

Various species of terrestrially-hibernating amphibians and reptiles are freeze tolerant, enduring long-term freezing
exposures with as much as 50-65 % of total body water frozen as extracellular ice. Studies in my lab explore the
biochemical adaptations underlying natural freeze tolerance. Recent studies have included analysis of the hormone,
B-adrenergic receptor, and second messenger responses underlying cryoprotectant (glucose) production by liver and
identitied a novel fbnn of Insulin in wood frogs. Other studies have madie the first analysis of freeze-induced gene
expression in vertebrate organs. Using a cDNA library constructed from livor of wood frogs (Rana sy/vatica) frozen
for 24 h at -2.5 degrees C °, we identified the freeze-induced upregulation of genes coding for the a and S subunits of
fibrinogen (a plasma dotting protein), the mitochondrial membrane ADP/ATP translocase, and a novel protein (about
90 amino acids, 10 kD) with a nuclear exporting sequence. Northern hybridization analysis showed that mRNA levels
for all three proteins (fibrinogen subunits paralleled each other) had distinct organ-specific patterns and responded
differently to freezeAhaw, dehydration, and anoxia stresses. Other studies have revealed that genes that are anoxia-
induced in freshwater turtles are also upregulated by freezing in hatchling painted turtles

Skirting the edge of hypoxia: overwintering In bullfrogs. A.W. Pinder. Dalhousie University, Halifax NS B3H
4J1.

It has long been a mystery how aquatically overwintering frogs, such as bullfrogs, sunzive winter hypoxia. There
have been anecdotal reports that frogs bury in mud, but anoxic frogs survived less than two weeks at 4°C in the
laboratory, and frogs did not bury in mud when it was available. In the field, while most of the pond bottom was
severely hypoxic, the frogs were found in very cold (0-1°) and relatively well oxygenated water at the extreme edge
of the pond, centimetres below ice cover. In the laboratory, frogs in a thermal gradient chose colder temperatures
when the wafer was hypoxic (Tatfersall and Boutilier; J. Exp. Biol. 200:1031-1038). Frogs have a high Q10 (around
5) below 4°C, thus metabolism is reduced In cold water at the pond edge. Anally, the metabolic rate of ovenwintering
frogs In hypoxic water gradually decreased by 60% over several weeks, reducing fuel consumption and the amount
of oxygen required in the water (Donohoe and Boutilier, J. Exp. Biol, in press). Aquatic frogs thus remain aerobic all
winter by choosing a low environmental temperature to reduce metabolic rate, choosing water with the highest
available oxygen, and reducing metabolic rate at a constant temperature.

Several terrestrial anurans and reptiles that live at high latitudes have developed elaborate physiological and
biochemical mechanisms for surviving cold winter temperatures. These animals can endure the conversion of up to
65% of their total body water into extracellular ice and then revive after freezing solid for days or weeks. Several
studies have indicated an important role for reversible protein phosphorylation in the regulation of freeze-induced
metabolic adaptations and documented changing patterns of activity of protein kinases A and C. New studies are
examining the roles of mftogen-acUvated protein (MAP) kinases in signal transduction in freeze-tolerant and anoxia-
tolerant frogs and turtles. Stress- and organ-specific changes have been found in ths responses of the extracellular
signal-regulated kinases (ERKs), the stress-activated protein kinases (SAPKs), and p38 that indicate differential
functions in cell response to stress. Other studies have monitored stress-induced changes in transcription factors by
Western blotting and electrophoretic mobility shift assays; these bind to DNA at the promoter regions of their target
genes and induce gene expression in response to cellular stress. The patterns of MAP kinase activation in stress-
tolerant animals suggest the importance of these modules in adapting to oxygen deprivation and severe osmotic

    climbs during nestling periods and 4 cimbs during post-fledgling periods). Inactive roosts were climbed 16 times,
    each having documented use of cavities by non-RCW species. Only three climbs were made upon active roost trees
    and none on random trees. In addition, 22 gray rat snakes were monitored via radio telemetry to assess home range
    size, habitat composition, spatial distribution and individual habitat preferences throughout Noxubee National Wildlife
    Refuge, Noxubee and Winston counties, Mississippi, during 1997. Data indicate random selection for any cavity
    using species by gray rat snakes, but, any chance selection for RCWs is important given the limited fecundity of this
    bird. Also, depredations upon RCW nest trees appears not to be random temporally. Snakes tend to visit RCW
    cluster areas only dumg the nesting season and seem to specifically target RCW nest trees during the nestling
    period. If non-iethal detenents to gray rat snake depredation can be found for RCW nest trees, the snake could serve
    as a management tool to eliminate competitors and predators of RCWs through depredation of these species, while
    presenting RCW nestiings.
