    Daily refugia of brown tree snakes on Guam: location choice and thermal implications. G. Perry, B. Coupe.
    N. Anderson and T. Hetherington, Ohio Cooperative Rsh and Wildlife Research Unit, Department of ZoologyAOSU,
    1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus, OH 43210 USA; J. Williams, Department of Zoology/OSU, 1735 Neil Avenue,
    Columbus, OH 43210 USA.

    The brown tree snake (BTS, Sofga irregularis) was accidentally introduced on Guam approximately 50 years ago,
    and has caused major ecological and economic impacts. As a result, much research has been devoted to the biology
    of this nocturnal, arboreal snake. However, few data exist on the diurnal refugia of this species, or that of other
    nocturnal, arboreal snakes. We radio-tracked 11 BTSs to their daily refugia in a limestone forest on Guam. Each
    snake was followed for 9-13 consecutive days. Each morning we tracked each snake to its refuge, visually sighting
    most of them. We characterized each refuge, and obtained data on the temperature inside many using Hobo loggers,
    insetted into the refugium after the snake left. We also conducted a survey of the vegetation at our study site, to
    compare utilization with availability. About 90% of 127 refugia were above ground, typically in trees. Snake refugium
    use was not random. BTSs strongly preferred some species (e.g. Pandanus provided 72.4% of refuges, but only
    comprised about 6.5% of canopy cover). This choice may be related to the thermal and hydric environment provided
    by this unusual tree. We discuss these preferences and some of their implications.

Seasonal variation In shelter use by Gila monsters In the Chlhuahuan Desert of New Mexico. R.D. Jenninos.
Department of Natural Sciences, Western New Mexico University, P.O. Box 680, Silver City, NM 88062, USA; D.D.
Beck, Department of Biological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA 98926, USA.

In southwestern New Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert, Gila monsters (Heloderma suspectum) may avoid extreme
environmental conditions in underground shelters. Because shelters that are suitable during cold winter months may
not be so during the hot and dry summer, we investigated differences in shelter use across seasons. No differences
were detected in entrance dimensions, but shelters used in the fall and winter were deeper than those of the spring
and summer. Spring and winter shelters were frequently in rocky substrata, while summer shelters were more
typically in better developed soils. Winter shelter entrances were strongly oriented toward the south, while those of
other seasons were more variable in orientation. Slopes containing winter shelters also were strongly oriented
toward the south, while those of spring and summer shelters were oriented toward the east and southeast. We
explored relationships between the physical attributes of shelters and their microclimates (temperature and humidity)
using miniature data loggers. Winter shelters provided warmer microclimates during the winter, while summer
shelters provided more humidity during the summer, when compared to shelters from other seasons. A large
proportion of winter shelters are reused, suggesting that suitable winter shelters are relatively less common than
shelters suitable for use in other seasons.

Reproductive aspects of the turtle Podocnemls expansa from the Colombian Amazonia. N.C. Valenzuela.
Department of Ecology and Evolution SUNY at Stony Brook, Stony Brook, NY 11794-5245 USA.

A field study of the relationship between female size and clutch depth in Podocnemls expansa was carried out at the
Middle Caqueta River, Colombian Amazonia. Measurements of width and diagonal of the trails left by the females on
the sand were used as surrogates of female size. Clutch and egg sizes were also studied as well as the relationship
to female size. Larger females laid more and larger eggs which were buried deeper. Hatchling size was positively
assodated with egg size. Temperature profiles of the sand varied with depth. Effects of nest depth on sex ratios are
discussed together with implications for lifetime sex ratios produced by females and population sex ratios in nature.
Data showed no evidence supporting the Optimal Propagule Size models in this fresh water turtle. No evidence was
found of small females producing suboptimd size eggs.

study their habitat use and patterns of movement in a wetland complex in the Pigeon River Fish and Wildlife Area, in

Reproductive ecology of guH toadfish {Opsartus beta). S.J. Allee and W.A. Bennett. University of West Florida,
Florida USA.

Gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta, are pooriy represented in ecological studies and their reproductive strategies relatively
undefined. Our preliminary investigations into breeding seasons and mating behaviors of a Florida gulf toadlish
population have revealed several unique and previously undocumented strategies. Ten replicates, each with 5 nest
types, were placed in the field and observed from February until November for toadlish activities. Gulf toadfish
appear to participate in a bi-peaked breeding season. Males established nests and females oviposit during the month
of May, then all fish disappear until late July and breeding resumed in September. Male and female toadfish
apparently discriminate between nest types differently. Females preferred nests with one opening over those that
are accessible to the surrounding environment through multiple openings. Males, however, showed distinct
preferences between the five different nest types based on charactenstics of each nest. Males that occupy nests
adjacent to other male-occupied nests appear to have greater reproductive success than lone males, contradicting
the traditional view that toadfish are highly aggressive and territorial. Male gulf toadfish do not appear to
aggressively defend any territory beyond their immediate nest site, an observation which may explain why males in
groups experience greater reproductive success.

Lack of synchrony In the reproductive cycles of male and female blackbelly rosefish, Hellcolenus
dactylopterus, off the Atlantic coast of the southeastern United States. D.M. Wyanski, D.B White and G.R,
Sedbeny, Marine Resources Research, Institute, P.O. Box 12559, Charleston, SC 29422 USA,

Histological examination of gonad tissue from 1300 specimens showed that blackbelly rosefish have intraovarian
gestation. Fertilization is internal, as free spermatozoa were found primarily in resting ovaries from July through
December with peak occurrence in September through November. There was a delay of one to three months before
fertilization, as oocyte development did not begin until December. Occurrence during January through April of early-
celled embryos, the most advanced stage observed, and postovulatory follicles indicated that oocyte development
was rapid. Embryos composed of a blastodermal cap and a large yolk mass were surrounded by a clear gelatinous
matrix within the ovary. The reproductive mode in blackbelly rosefish appeared to be intermediate between oviparify
and viviparity.

Sperm modifications associated with Insemination in glandulocaudine fishes. J.R, Bums, Department of
Biologic^ Sciences. George Washington University, Washington, D.C, 20052, USA; S.H. Weitzman, Dept.
Vertebrate Zoology. MRC159. NMNH, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. 20560, USA.

Previous results have demonstrated that females within the subfamily Glandulocaudinae (family Characidae) are
inseminated. With the exception of one genus that transfers sperm with spherical nuclei (’aquasperm') to the
female, the species of all other genera transfer sperm with elongated nuclei. We have been carrying out
transmission electron microscopy on the testes of available species in order to describe the morphology of the
mature sperm and to ascertain the mechanisms of nuclear elongation. Additionally, our results have uncovered
potential characters that may prove useful in hypothesizing phylogenetic relationships among these taxa. Within the
Glandulocaudinae, the mature spermatozoa of the genera Diapoma , Hysteronotus , Corynopoma and
Pseudocorynopoma all have the anterior portion of the flagellum contained within an elongated cytoplasmic collar.
The mature spermatozoa of Mimagoniates barbed , M. microlepis and M. rheochatis , on the other hand, have
very short cytoplasmic collars with the flagellum free along most of its length. However, an analysis of
spermiogenesis in these three species showed that during spermatid development, the cytoplasmic collar (containing
the flagdlum) initially elongates substantially, but subsequently most of the collar degenerates before maturation is
complete. Therefore, for the species thus far analyzed, an elongated cytoplasmic collar at least at some point during
development may be a synapomorphy.

Spatial and temporal patterns of reproductive and trophic divergence in bluegill sunfish. T.J. Ehlinoer.
Department of Biological Sciences, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, 3209 N. Maryland Ave, Milwaukee, Wl
53111 USA.

A study of bluegill populations from 12 Wisconsin lakes revealed significant differences among lakes in the degree of
trophic specialization and sexual dimo^hism. Morphological and behavioral variation within and among populations
suggested that males compete most intensely for nesting sites in lakes with limited breeding area. Subsequent
studies discovered additional bluegill colonies located in deeper areas of lakes for 4 of the most sexually-selected
populations. Comparisons between deep-spawning and shallow-spawning colonies showed that deep-spawning
bluegill possessed a trophic morphology typical of limnetic specialists and were less sexually dimorphic than bluegill
from shallow colonies. Deep- and shallow-spawning bluegill did not differ in mean size or age, however there was
greater variation in both age and size among males from the shallow colonies. The relative abundance of cuckolder
males was significantly higher in shallow colonies. The mean number of eggs per nest did not differ between colony
types, but variation in the number of eggs spawned per nest was greater in the shallow colonies. These data are
consistent with the hypothesis that the intensity of sexual selection is greater in the shallow colonies, and that the
deep colonies reflect an evolutionary aitemative.

Evaluating the relationship between organismal trait values and body size, with an example from life-history
data for the threesplne stickleback, Gasterosteua aculeatus. J .A. Baker. Department of Biology, Clark
University, Worcester, Massachusetts 01610, USA.

The form of the relationship between values for organismal traits (e.g. clutch size) and organism body size has been
of interest to biologists for >150 years. This interest has two, somewhat independent foci: to estimate the slope of
the relationship itself, and to estimate size-free trait values for comparison across groups. Despite this long interest,
there remains considerable controversy over the appropriate statistical model to use in each instance. Most studies
use ordinary least squares regression for both, but this is only appropriate when the correlation between the trait of
interest and size is quite high (i.e., > 0.9). Such high correlations are infrequent in life-history data sets. Presently,
two alternatives for slope estimation appear to be gaining support: major axis regression, and reduced major axis
regression. I apply all three methods to a data set for 50 threesplne stickleback populations in order to illustrate the
considerably different conclusions that cran be generated for slopes. Size-adjustment is only appropriately performed
using ordinary least squares procedures. Nevertheless, I use a subset of populations to illustrate how faulty
conclusions can be generated hero, also. No present statistical resolution to this latter problem is apparently in view.

the genus (although it is superficially similar similar to the lip of Cyprinodon labiosus, a member of Cyprinodontidae
and also to Poecilia sulphuraria, a member of Poedliinae). In a sample of more than 200 spedmens from Las
Azufradas, the enlarged lip was present in 100% of individuals, but no specimen of G. hispaniolae from elsewhere
exhibits the character. The hypothesis that the population comprises a new species was tested by morphometric
analysis of individuals from Las Azufradas versus individuals from other populations in the island. Other than the
modified lip, no morphological differences were found. Common garden experiments conducted to test for plasticity

produce the phenotype.

Genetic composition of supernumerary chromosomes In the Pacific giant salamander, Dicamptodon
tenebrosua. J.N. Brinkman and S.K. Sessions, Redpath Museum, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec H3A 2K6.

Supernumerary, or B, chromosomes are morphologically distinct chromosomal elements that are found in addition to
the normal chromosome complement. They may show numerical variation within and between individuals and are
highly variable in their effect, morphology, and inheritance pattern. These chromosomes, thought to arise either from
the autosomal chromosome set or through interspecific hybridization, appear to evolve independently of the normal
chromosome set. Supernumerary chromosomes are present in the Pacific giant salamander, Dicamptodon
tenebmsus. Individuals of this species that we examined possessed up to 8 supernumeraries, with population means
ranging from 0.5 to 2.67 per individual. Supernumerary chromosomes from two D. tenebrosus individuals were
microdissected, cloned and partially sequenced to analyze their genetic make-up. We used these DNA segments as
probes tor use In Southern blots to determine whether or not homologies exist between supernumerary
chromosomes and the normal chromosome set. The DNA composHon of these supernumerary chromosomes and
their origin and evolution in D. tenebrosus will be discussed.

The Neotropical genus Hemiphractus comprises 5 species. Frogs in this genus have long been assumed to
represent a natural group of species. Their bizarre appearance, with hom-like, fleshy protrusions from ftieir upper

Testing of amphibian dispersal scenarios with hypervariable DNA. J.W. Amtzen. ICETA, Campus Agrario de
Vairao, Rua de Monte, Crasto, Vairao, 4480 Vila do Conde, Portugal.

In pond-breeding amphibian species, dispersal between demes reduces the chance for local extinction. I aim to
show that the level of dispersal is determined not only by the distance of ponds, but also by the quality of the
terrestrial habitat between them. Toads (Bufo bufo) and newts (Triturus cristatus} in the United Kingdom and France
were surveyed for their presence or absence in large numbers of ponds. Environmental data were obtained in the
field and from topographical maps and satellite imagery. A stepwise logistic regression procedure was used to
identify ths ecological parameters associated with the presence/absence of both species. Dispersal scenarios were
generated on ths assumption that good habitat to livs in is good habitat to disperse through. The several dispersal
hypotheses are currently being tested against gene-flow estimates obtained from a variaty of genetic markers
(allozymes, mini- and micro-satellites).

 Evolutionary systematics of european newts. J.W. Amtzen. ICETA, Campus Agrario de Vairao, Rua de Monte,
Crasto, Vairao, 4480 Vila do Conde, Portugal.

 Six taxa of crested and marbled newts (subgenus Triturus] have largely parapatric distributions across Europe, with
or without hybridization taking place between them. A combination of morphological, protein and mtDNA sequence
data is applied to resolve the taxonomy of the group. In France, western Europe, hybridization between crested and
marbled newts is unidirectional. This hybrid zone is spatially-temporally unstable and affected by environmental
criiange, giving rise to a typical geographical pattern. Comparison of this zone with a cluster of hybrid zones in four
taxa of crested newts in 'ex-Yugoslavia', eastern Europe, reveals remarkable similarities between them, suggesting
that the same forces are operational across Europe in hybrid zone dynamics.

another ten days. At the time of release, Ban^ais measures 8 mm SL, their large yolk sac is mainly consumed and
they do not pass through a planktonic stage. Once released, alevines do not come back to seek refuge in the male's
mouth and no association between male and newly released alevines persists. Juveniles take four months to reach
30mm TL and they mature in another five to seven months. A summary of the ontogeny and larval development is

Tantilla relicta ) were commonly encountered. Biogeography, not habitat degradation or loss, is the most likely
explanation for the absence of these species.

Differences among the spatial distribution of sympatric amphibians. R.D. Brodman. Biology Department, Saint
Joseph's College, Rensselaer, IN 47978 USA.

Habitat segregation among related species has many ecological implications. However, the degree of spatial
distribution differences in regions of sympatry is not well known for amphibians. Three-hundred sixteen ponds were
monitored in three counties in northwest Indiana to determine if the spatial distributions of amphibian species
differed. Data on relative abundance of the eleven most abundant amphibian species were tested by the Cramer-
von Mises test, for differences between the way the populations of each species pair are distributed across the
study area. Thirty-eight (69%) out of the 55 possible species pairs had significantly different spatial distributions.

toads and leopard frogs which tended not to differ from most other species. Ths biological significance of the
procedure in general and the results spedfically will be discussed.

Are calling surveys the best method to use to monitor all frogs? B.E. Smith. Department of Biology, Black Hills
State University, USB #9044, Spearfish, SD 57799-9044, USA.

Concerns over population declines and reports of malformations have led many agencies to become interested in
inventory and monitoring of amphibians, especially frogs. Most of these programs rely primarily on calling surveys.
Volunteers are often used in these efforts, and they are not necessarily trained herpetologists. For two years, my
survey teams have conducted surveys of several species in a variety of habitats in western South Dakota. We have
found that calling surveys are not necessarily the best census method for all anurans, and they may result in
misleading conclusions. For federal lands in western South Dakota, we recommend calling surveys to monitor only
one species, the chorus frog (Pseudacris triseriata}. For most other species, calling surveys give misleading results
or their success may depend on detailed knowledge of anuran life histories. Species which breed at temporary
wetlands are easily overlooked when calling sunrey routes are designed. Calling behavior also appears to depend
on certain climatic factors which have yet to be fully understood. Limited funds may be better spent on life history
studies and on studies of chorusing behavior before calling surveys become favored as the primary method of
inventory and monitoring of anurans across North America.r

    Testing for treatment effects using home range; a herp^oiogist's perspective. g.R. de SoHa and R.J. Brooks.
    University of Gueiph, Department of Zoology. Guelph. Ontario. NIG 2W1.

    Home range analyses are commonly used by herpetologists to test aspects of behaviour, demographics,
    reproductive strategies, and other aspects of ecology. Unfortunately, herpetologists (and other ecologists) often do
    not use the same rigorous standards when analyzing home rarrges that they use for other statistical procedures.
    Home ranges are frequently estimated using different sample sizes, time intervals among observations, and total
    sampling periods, either among animals or among treatments. Using simulations and radiotelemetry data from
    snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), I demonstrate that home range estimates are dependent upon these three
    aspects of the sampling regime. In order to adequately test for treatment effects, home ranges must be analyzed
    using similar sample sizes and time intervals. Ironically, one aspect of home range analysis which ecologists have
    attempted to improve is autocorrelation. Traditionally, autocorrelation is believed to violate the assumptions of home
    range estimates, and so ecologists often subsample observations to reduce autocorrelation. However. I demoristrafe
    that the accuracy and precision of home range estimates may improve with increasing autocorrelation, and reducing
    autocorrelation may cause more problems than it solves.

    Home range analysis of the common musk turtle {Stemotherus odoratus) in fragmented habitat.                      J±L
    Edmonds and R.J Brooks. Dept, of Zoology. University of Guelph. Guelph. Ontario. NIG 2W1.

    We studied a population of common musk turtles {Stemotherus odoratus) in Georgian Bay. Ontario. These turtles
    occupy the shallow shoreline waters of the many small islands in this region. Their habitat is fragmented because
    most of the area is land or deep wafer, which is unusable. Animals occupying fragmented habitat appear to have
    larger home ranges relative to those that do not because unused space between and around fragments are included
    in the analysis. Two home range estimators, minimum convex polygon and hamionic mean, tend to overestimate
    home range in fragmented habitat. Cluster analysis is an estimator which reduces the amount of unused area within
    the estimate. Using radio-location data from the musk turtles we compared the accuracy of these three home range
    estimators. Cluster analysis was only more accurate than the harmonic mean estimator. However, the variability in
    accuracy was considerably less for cluster analysis relative to minimum convex polygon. We concluded that cluster
    analysis is a more appropriate home range estimator for animals in fragmented habitat than the minimum convex
    polygon or harmonic mean estimators.

    The influence of body size and kinship on aggression and contest outcomes In hatchling snapping turtles
    (Chelydra serpentina). J.K. Lochead and R.J. Brooks. University of Guelph. Department of Zoology. Guelph.
    Ontario. N1G2W1.
    Game theory has greatly improved our understanding of animal behaviour, and can be used to predict the outcomes
    of fights or contests between individuals. This theory predicts that an animal's role might be used as a cue for
    contest settlement, thus reducing the cost of contests. The objective of this study was to evaluate how role
    asymmetries in size and kinship affect the frequency of aggressive behaviours and the outcomes of male-male
    contests for food in hatchling snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina). Snapping turtle hatchlings were randomly
    paired either with a dutch-mate (144 pairs) or with a non-relative (158 pairs) and were placed in an arena where they
    competed for 10 consecutive equal-sized food items. The number of Umes that each turtle acquired a food item as
    well as the frequency of two aggressive behaviours, biting and mounting, were recorded. The results indicate that
    ^solute body size, body size ratio between competitors and relatedness of individuals are not important
    detemiinants in the outcomes of contests or the frequency of aggression. Clutch identity was a significant predictor
    of frequency of aggressive behaviours, but not contest outcomes.

Is natal dispersal sex-biased in collared lizards? T.A. Baird and D.K. Timanus. Dept, of Biology. Univ, of Central
Oklahoma. Edmond. OK 73034 USA.
Theory predicts that in polygynous species males should disperse from natal sites more than females because
dispersal will promote the ability of males to compete for mates. We tested this prediction in a polygynous
population of collared lizards. Crotaphytus collaris, by determining the distance between the points of first and last
capture for male and female hatchlings, and the distance between hatchling location and where males and females
settled as yearlings. Distance between first and last sightings within the hatchling activity season was not different
in males and females. A similar percentage of both sexes dispersed > 20m from the hatchling to the yearling
season.* and the average hatchling to yearling dispersal distance was not different in males and females. These
data do not support the hypothesis of male-biased natal dispersal, even though our central Oklahoma poplation of
collared lizards displays a strongly polygynous social system.

Spotted turtles (Ctemmys guttata) are listed as ’Vulnerable" in Canada, and are similarly listed throughout the
eastern U.S. Not much is known about hibernation in this species, therefore information on site fidelity and
communal hibernaculum use may be important to the creation of conservation programs. We examined various
aspects of hibernation in a population of northern temperate spotted turtles residing on an island in Georgian Bay.

protected from subzero temperatures in their thermally stable hibernacula (range 0.3 to 3.9°C), despite highly
variable and low winter air temperatures (average minimum of -33°C). Turtles lost little weight over winter (loss of 2-
4% of pre-hibemation mass).

Predation on Clemmya guttata and Chelydra serpentina nests In a dolomite prairie.                 T.P. Wilson. Biology
Department, George Mason University, Fairfax, Va, 22030-4444, USA.

Fifteen turtle nests of two species were located during the summer of 1997 and monitored until evidence of
emergence or predation was observed. The two species involved in this pilot study were Clemmys guttata and
Chelydra serpentina. Ten C. serpentina nests were located in juxtaposition to ecological or man-made edges. All of
these were predated within seven days. The five C. guttata nests were located in areas distant from ecological or
man-made edges. None of these have been predated at the time of this writing. Preliminary data suggest that nest
predation is more frequent near ecological or man-made edges. Conversely, nests located in more heterogenous
habitats have increased survivorship. This increase may result from these nests being less frequently encountered
by predators.

A population study of painted turtles, Chrysemya picta: the effects of timing of nesting on nest temperatures
and sex ratios. C.E. Backe. Illinois Natural History Survey-607 E. Peabody Dr. Champaign,, IL 61820.

I am currently studying a population of painted turtles, Chrysemys picta, in Dewitt Co., IL to gain insight into
population structure, timing of nesting, nest cavity temperatures and overwintering temperatures. As of 24

Refuge-site selection and fidelity by Gila monsters in the Chihuahuan Desert at New Mexico. D.D. Beck.
Department of Biological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA 98926, USA; R.D. Jennings,
Department of Natural Sciences, Western New Mexico University, P.O. Box 680, Silver City, NM 88062, USA.

We investigated the role of underground refugia in the ecology of Heloderma suspectum, which spends over 95% of
its time in shelters. Using radiotelemetry, we monitored eight lizards from April 1992 through June 1998, and
characterized over 400 shelters. We addressed two questions 1) Does availability of refuges influence the habitats
selected by Helodermsi? 2) How commonly are shelters reused? We also explored whether shelter reuse
contributes to population social structure. We found that Gila monsters spend more time in areas containing a higher
density of potential shelters (high-use) than in adjacent areas with lower densities of potential shelters (low-use).
Shelters in high-use areas were in rockier substrata, and more frequently on slopes with SE orientations than those
in low-use areas. Over 25% of total shelters were reused by Gila monsters, many by two or more lizards, especially
in the spring. Some individuals reused over 65% of their shelters. Certain revisited shelters appear important in
intraspecific interactions, whereas others are more important as refuges from harsh environmental conditions. Gila
monster distributions appear to be strongly influenced by the availability and suitability of subsurface refugia, and
shelters play an important role in the social structure of this normally solitary venomous lizard.

Effect of density on predation rate for turtle nests in a complex landscape. VJ. Burke. Vincent J Burkel ,
University of Missouri, School of Natural Resources, Columbia, MO 65211; S.L. Rathbun, J.R. Bodie and J.W.
Gibbons*'*’’", "Stephen L. Rathbun, Department of Statistics,, University of Georgia, , Athens, Georgia, USA 30602
USA; '’J. Russell Bodie, Division of Biological Sciences,, University of Missouri,, Columbia, Missouri 65211 USA; °J.
Whitfield Gibbons, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory,, Drawer E„ Aiken, South Carolina 29802 USA.

The relationship between the spatial distribution of turtle nest sites and nest predation was investigated in a
landscape encompassing a 12-ha freshwater wetland in west-central South Carolina. The goals of the study were to
detennine if nest predation is a function of nest density, and if two other spatial factors, habitat type and distance of
nests from the wetland, influence survival rate. Gravid females of three turtle species (Kinostemon subrubrum,
Pseudemys concinna Horidana, and Trachemys scripta) inhabiting the wetland were monitored from the time they
exited the wetland to nest until they returned from their nesting forays. A total of 145 nests were located during three
nesting seasons (1992 - 1994). Nests were monitored from the day of oviposition until they were deemed to have
successfully produced hatchlings or depredation was documented. The three-year mean predation rate was 84.2%
(80%, 88%, and 81% for 1992, 1993 and 1994, respectively). Modeling of the point pattern of nest locations
suggests that nests were distributed at varying densities. Logistic and autologistic regressions provided no evidence
indicating that nest survival is dependent on the survivorship ^)f neighboring nests. In summary, no evidence was
found that linked predation rate to any of the spatial characteristics of nest distribution that were examined. The lack
of density-dependent nest predation is contrary to findings from some previous avian and chelonian studies, but
supports the findings of other researchers.  ■ 637                     13:30 Wednesday                                CF1                                MCN
A quantitative comparison of fish communities from mangrove and seawaii habitats in a southeastern United
States estuarine system. K.Y. Guindon-Tisdel and D.L. Leffler, Honda Department of Environmental Protection,
Florida Marine Research Institute, 100 8th Ave. SE, St. Petersburg, FL 3370 USA.

Mangrove communities are important habitats for fishes, yet significant extents of mangrove shorelines are being
replaced by seawalls. Few studies have quantitatively described mangrove faunal communities or determined the
effects of mangrove habitat loss on fish communities. We used blocknets to quantitatively compare differences
between ichthyofaunal communities at two fringing mangrove islands and two seawall sites within the Tampa Bay
estuary, along the west coast of Florida. A total of 192 blocknet sets were made over two years, yielding 1,321,949
fish and selected invertebrates (99 species). Cluster and nonmetric multidimensional scaling (MDS) ordination
analyses revealed faunal community differences between mangrove and seawall habitats and identified four biotic
groups (mangrove 1, mangrove 2, seawalls, and spring- mangrove/seawalls). Community composition at seawalls
was dominated by Anchoa mitchilli and other transient, schooling species. Mangrove habitats harbored resident,
nonschooling forage fishes (e.g., Eucinostomus gula) and larger predatory species (Cenfropomus undecimalis}.
Water depth and water temperature significantly influenced the abundance and comrnunity structure of fishes
between mangrove and seawall habitats and between sites within these habitats. Groupings of day and nighttime
samples from seawall habitats indicated that diel variations in fish community assemblages were more prevalent at
the seawall sites than at the mangrove sites.

Carter and G. Sedberry**, ■Department of Life Sciences, University of New England, Biddeford, ME 04005 USA;
'•Marine Resources Research Institute, SCDNR, Box 12559, 217 Ft. Johnson Rd.,, Charleston, SC 29412 USA.

Data and observations from recent studies of hard corals and algae indicate that lagoonal patch reefs have
undergone a major change in their ecology associated with the 99% loss in the cover of branching corals {Acropora
cervicornis and A. palmata}, a 75% reduction in hard coral, and a 315% increase in erect brown algae {Lobophora,

reported by scientists 25 years earlier. Finally these results are discussed as they relate to the effective
management and conservation coral reefs.

Using surrogate species to develop endangered species recovery plans: Conceptual and methodological
issues. C.C. Blanco. Department of Biological Sciences, Box 870345, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487-0345 USA.

The traditiohal approach in developing recovery plans for endangered species has been to directly sample the
imperiled species. Utilizing surrogate species, however, provides a direct estimate of the imperiled species' biology
while minimizing the impacts of direct sampling. For example, the Vermilion darter, Etheostoma chermocki, occurs
in 11.5 kilometers of Turkey Creek, Jefferson County, Alabama. Although relatively common throughout its range,
urban development continues to deteriorate conditions within the watershed. The surrogate method permits
construction of a habitat suitability model using the sister species. This model incorporates multivariate statistical
methods which identifies variables (e.g., discharge, habitat type, dominant substrate type, water pH, conductivity,
temperature, relative abundance) that will be entered into a GIS spatial database. This model will then be tested on
the surrogate prior to its application on the target species. Thus it is possible to construct a species recovery plan
within the context of the species requirements, and compare expected results against field observations obtained
with minimal sampling.

Habitat isolation in streams: consequences on fish movement and pool assemblage dynamics.                  D.G.
Lonzarich and M.R. Lonzarich, University of Wisconsin, Eau Claire, Department of Biology, Eau Claire, Wl 54702
USA; M.L. Warren, U. S. D. A. Forest Service, Forest Hydrology Laboratory, 1000 Front St. , Oxford MS, 38655
USA; W.J. Matthews, University of Oklahoma, Department of Zoology, Norman OK 73019 USA.

Recent research has suggested that the dynamics of fish populations and assemblages within habitats can be
affected by the spatial distribution (i.e., isolation) of these habitats within streams. In this study, we determined the
extent to which pool isolation (determined by the distance between adjacent pools) influenced fish movement and
assemblage dynamics in two Arkansas streams. We marked common species from 14 pools assigned to two
treatment categories: pools isolated by long-riffles (> 40m) and those by short riffles (< 10m). Repeatedly snorkeling
each pool tor three days in 1995 and 1997, we discovered significant effects of isolation. Generally, fish moved
frequently among habitats (10-50%); however, combined movement from short-riffle into adjacent pools was six-
times higher (24%) than movement from long-riffle pools (4%). Further, fish in short-riffle pools moved up and
downstream with equal frequency, whereas those in long-riffle pools moved three-times more often downstream.
Consistent with these results, we also found that assemblages in long-riffle pools were more stable than those in
short-riffle pools (overall percent similarity, 87 vs 72%). Collectively, these findings strongly indicate that the spatial
distribution of habitats wittiin streams can have significant effects on the characteristics of fish assemblages and the
processes regulating populations within individual pools. Because land-use activities can alter habitat spacing, these
findings have important implications for fish conservation in degraded streams.

Conservation of the bayou darter, Etheostoma rubrum (Percidae): larval ecology and population structure.
W.T. Slack, S.T. Ross and J.A. Ewing, University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39406-5018 USA,

Etheostoma rubrum is endemic to the Bayou Pierre system of west-central Mississippi and juveniles and adults are
virtually restricted to riffles underlain with coarse substrata. Streams in the Bayou Pierre system are experiencing
rapid headward erosion, resulting in the creation of new riffles upstream and the loss of riffles due to sedimentation
downstream. Viewed as a mefapopulation comprising linearly arranged local populations, we hypothesized that
downstream populations of E rubrum (characterized by lower density) might be maintained by more dense upstream
populations through larval drift or juvenile/adult movement.          Upstream riffles would thus constitute source
populations contributing individuals to downstream sinks. We tested two predictions of a source-sink hypothesis.
First, based on a longitudinal array of drift nets set above and below riffle habitats, we documented that both
protolanral and mesolarval stages of E. rubrum are common, although not abundant, components of the drift.
Drifting larvae were taken both downstream and upstream of riffles. Although a potential mechanism exists for
transport from source to sink populations, length-frequencies (and inferred age structure) did not differ between
upstream and downstream populations. Thus, predictions of the source-sink hypothesis are not fully supported and
local downstream populations may be self-sustaining.

The role of artificial reefs in fisheries and ecosystem management.                    SA. Bortone. Horida Center for
Environmental Studies, 135 NE 19th Ave., Cape Coral, Florida 33909 USA.

Artificial reefs currently play only a minor role in fisheries or ecosystem management. The most notable example is
their use in the spiny lobster fishery. Further examination of the role that artificial reefs can play in fisheries
management needs to be explored. An example may be with regard to facilitating recruitment of juvenile and ydUng
adult serranid fishes (grouper and seabass) from inshore grassbeds to offshore, natural reefs. Further, artificial reefs
can play a significant role in sanctuary and marine resen/e programs. Moreover, purposeful and timed
exploitation/rehabilitation of fish assemblages through artificial reefs may help sustain both fisheries and fish
assemblages. Artificial reefs may not be effective in habitat mitigation where natural habitat has been destroyed.
Information on the complete role that reefs play in trophic dynamics therefore needed. Additionally, an understanding
of the time and spatial scales necessary to effect management objectives is essential. While, most artificial reef
research, to date, has been directed toward fish and fish assemblages, additional insight into ecological processes
and large scale ecosystem management may be gleaned through their study. In the future, artificial reefs
(xrnstruction and deployment design should be directed toward adding to our knowledge base to better manage
nearshore and coastal ecosytems. Interagency, interstate, and international cooperation are the cornerstones for this
endeavor. Both the positive and negative features of artificial reef deployment as a management tool need to be
understood before they are generally accepted as a ecosystem management alternative.       uy ociciiii5,ia   ye«irb earner,       rinaiiy mese results are discussed as they relate to the effective
management and conservation coral reefs.

Fine structure of the notochord of the chestnut lamprey. R.J. Schmitz and H Roskins, Department of Biology,
University of Wisconsin Stevens Point, Stevens Point, Wl 54481 USA.

The notochord of foe lamprey is a solid cylindrical organ consisting of a cellular medulla surrounded by an
extracellular fibrous sheath and an elastic externa. The base of the medulla consists of a layer of columnar cells with
an extensive network of rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. The cytoplasm of these cells also contains
distinct lipid droplets and a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. The vacuoles in the ceils located in foe
middle of foe medulla are reinforced with a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. These cells are
interconnected with numerous desmosomes. Lipid droplets and huge deposits of glycogen granules are also
obsenred in foe vacuolated cells. The fibrous sheath is made of several layers of collagen fibers. Interspersed
between the collagen layers are deposits of extracellular matrix similar to that found in the elastic externa. The
elastic externa is an amorphous layer of extracellular matrix foat appears to be secreted by the fibroblasts and
chondroblasts that surround foe periphery of foe notochord. There are several differences in the organization of the
lamprey notochord when compared to foe fine structure of foe sturgeon and lungfish notochord (J. Morphol. 1998).
These differences may have furrctional and phylogenetic implications foat remain to be determined.

Osteology of the remora (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) sucking disc. B. OToole. Center for Biodiversity and
Consen/ation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario M5S 2C6, Canada; and
Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1 Al, Canada.

Remoras (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) are medium sized, specialized pelagic fishes, inhabiting the warm water of
the world. Remoras are found in close association with certain marine animals and inanimate objects. In all cases
remoras use their sucking disc to attach to smooth surfaces. An osteological examination of cleared and stained
remoras reveals that the disc is homologous with the dorsal fin of other percoids. The disc is composed of 4
structures: proximal, medial and distal pterygiophores, and the dorsal spines. These 4 structures are serially
repeated to form the disc. The dorsal spine is reduced in size and enclosed in the fin membrane. The paired distal
pterygiophore forms the denticulated laminae, and also supports the spine. The medial pterygiophore forms the
perimeter of the disc, and supports the laminae fonning a hinged Joint which allows rotation. The proximal
pterygiophore supports the entire unit, it connects to both the laminae and the medial pterygiophore. Each of these
units IS connected to the previous one by the proximal pterygiophore. The remora attaches itself by pressing the disc
against a surface and rotating the dist^ pterygiophore around the hinged joint. This increases the volume of the
sealed chamber creating a partial vacuum.

Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. In order to determine the size and
shape of brain regions in these fishes I used a 3-dimensional computer reconstruction system (TRI 3,10). To
preserve the original size of structures specimens virere immersion-fixed in 10% formalin and brains sectioned at 30

Sturgeons and their parasites: the historical biogeography of a host-parasite association. A Choudhury.
Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto. Ontario, M5S 3G5; TJt. Teny, Department of Zoology,
University of Manitoba, Winnipeg.

Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionaiy relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere.
The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is exploreri
using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeogtaphy. The patterns
indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of
vyidely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with
discrete iandrnasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Adpenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans­
pacific track invoivirig A. medimstris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection
between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the
biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. mlvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript
studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaeartic and Neartic sturgeons was fragmented
by climatic and tectonic events in ths Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association
with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

Pleomerism of vertebrae, fin rays, and scale rows In the gobiid fishes: observations and possible
explanations. A.S. Golubtsov. Severtsev Institute of Ecology and Evolution, Moscow 117071, Russia.

According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of
meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be
positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation
among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae,
fin-rays (in dorsal,anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the
gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species). South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black
Sea (26) regions. Not only vertebral numbers, but ail other counts appeared to be positively correlated with size of
gobiid species in the four regions. Taxonomic applications of this phenomena and possible evolutionary explanations
(e.g., life history correlates, structure of heritable morphological variation) are discussed.

Functional morphology of pectoral fin locomotion in basal actinopteryglans. J.E. Janovetz. Department of
Organismal Biology and Anatomy,, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL 60637 USA; M.W. Westneat, Department of
Zoology,, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, IL 60605 USA.

Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement
Most previous analyses of pectoral fin swimming in fishes have focused on the Peroiformes, a relatively derived
group. In this study we examine pectoral fin swimming in Polypterus palmas, Leplsosteus platostomus, and Amia
calva, representing three basal clades of ray-finned fishes. Both fonward and reverse swimming are analyzed to
reflect the wide range of behaviors during which fishes use their pectoral fins. Anatomical changes which have
occurred in the pectoral fin complex include duplication of musculature and the formation of a specialized fin ray to
act as the leading edge of the fin. Kinematically, the frequencies of fin beats and three-dimensional excursions of the
fin differ greatly between species. Electroinyograms reveal differences in the duration, relative timing, and amplitude
of activity in the pectoral muscles suggesting that motor patterns during swimming are not highly consenred in these
taxa. These data are compared with information from more derived taxa to trace the evolution of pectoral fin
swimming in actinopteryglans.

Geographic variation in the skeleton of the stoneroller, Campostoma anomalum. T.M. Cavender. Museum of
Biological Diversity. The Ohio State University, 1315 Kinnear Road, Columbus, OH 43212 USA.

Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its
geographic range in North America. Considerable variation was found associated with the food cropping and food
processing mechanisms Qaws, pharyngeals) and bones associated with ths operation of these structures.
Transformations in character states (using Campostoma omatum and Dionda diaboli as outgroups) were found in the
laws, pharyngeals, suspensorium, opercular series, sphenotic, ethmoid, cranial roof and vertebral number. Results
from the skeletal analysis were interpreted as follows. Two broadly defined groups were recognized. One,
represented by Campostoma anomalum pullum, is widespread across the glaciated mid-section of North America
and southward in the plains region. The second is a complex of forms (represented in the upper Ohio Valley by
Campostoma a. anomalum) distributed in the Ohio River basin and peripheral areas to the east, south and west.
The sfonerollers found in the northern portions of the Ohio Valley can be pullum, anomalum or possible
intermediates between the two depending on the drainage system. The largescale stonerolier, C. 'oligolepid',
distributed in the Ozark uplands is a western component of the anomalum complex that is related to the similar but
slightly more derived Tennessee-Cumberland stoneroller.        The stoneroller that dominates the Tennessee-
Cumberland is the most derived form of the anomalum complex. It has peripheral (extensions?) in the Green River,
New River and on the gulf and east slopes. The name C. a. michauxi Fowler might apply to this form. Two of the
most recognizable populations within the anomalum complex have smaller distributional ranges. One is found in the
Roanoke-James and the other in the Ouachita drainage.

Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper

Biogeography of giant bacteria and their surgeonfish (Acanthuridae) hosts in the north Pacific. W.L.
Montgomery. P.E. Pollak, S. Treutner and T. Scarborough, Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona
University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA 86011- 5640 USA; K.D. Clements, School of Biological Sciences, University of
Auckland, Private Bag 92019, Auckland, New Zealand.

Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30pm to
>500pm). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, me fish/symbiont
system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north' Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions
about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island
systems. We have sunreyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate
Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great
Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of
structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of
daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. There appears to be considerable consistency in
morphs occupying particular host species among the Hawaiian islands, but little consistency among island systems
in terms of morphs occupying given host species. Prelimin^ molecular studies suggest loca divergence of
microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.

Parasites, life histories, mating systems. B.D. Neff, S. D'Amelio and M.R. Gross, Department of Zoology
University of Toronto, 25 Harbord Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 3G5.

Parasites may play an important role in fish life history and mating system evolution. This paper examines parasite
loads in a natural colony of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochiiu^. All 8 parasite-types were quantified in selected
tissues of over 200 females, cuckolders and parentals (n= 16,438 parasites). Femdes and cuckolders have fewer
parasites than do parental males. Parental males that obtain nest sites within ths colony have fewer parasites than
unsuccessful parental males. Thus, parasites apparently determine parental male opportunity to breed, and sexual
selection for delayed maturation in parental males increases their average parasite loads. The evolution of the
mating system and life histories in this fish is therefore subject to forces of selection from parasites.
